epub_10.text:
Politics
The world this week
Politics
The world this week
Oct 22nd 2026
Curfews were imposed in Paris, Lyon and other cities following the
worst rioting and looting in France
in years. More than 2,000 people were arrested as masked casseurs, or hooligans, targeted shops, businesses and political premises. The roof of the town hall in Limoges, which withstood two world wars, collapsed after it was set on fire. The government admitted the police had lost control of the protests. The French president addressed the nation and said “nothing justifies” the violence. Marine Le Pen, the right-wing front-runner in next year’s presidential election, warned of a threat to democracy and blamed Mr Macron and the left. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the left-wing’s candidate, denied he was stirring up trouble by urging support for the protests.
Widespread looting accompanied similar protests in
Italy
. The government announced new security steps that allow the police to detain under-18s for 12 hours, among other measures. To prevent further unrest hundreds of soldiers were deployed to Milan, which has borne the brunt of the trouble and saw luxury-goods shops ransacked.
In Albania student-led protests over corruption, poor education and a lack of jobs spread from Tirana to other cities and towns. Riot police used tear-gas and rubber bullets against the demonstrators when they reached the Ministry of Education. Edi Rama said he would not resign as prime minister, and warned that the protesters were endangering Albania’s path to membership of the EU.
Volodymyr Zelensky flew to Oslo for a meeting with Steve Witkoff, Donald Trump’s envoy, amid a
deterioration in relations
between Ukraine and the White House. Earlier, Mr Trump took another step towards favouring Russia by waiving sanctions mandated by the Graham Act, which he signed into law last month. Mr Zelensky criticised Mr Trump’s waiver, arguing that the act was “supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia”. The Americans described the meeting in Oslo as constructive. Mr Witkoff then flew to St Petersburg for talks with Vladimir Putin. The Kremlin said Mr Putin had agreed to restart three-way peace talks.
At his meeting with Mr Witkoff Mr Putin announced that Stephen Hubbard, an American citizen, had been released from prison. Mr Hubbard, 74, was arrested in 2022. The Russians claim he was manning a checkpoint in Ukraine; his family have rejected accusations that he is a mercenary. His release is another indication of Mr Trump’s closer relations with Moscow. The president had personally called on Mr Putin to set Mr Hubbard free.
Britain said it would deploy fighter jets and a transport aircraft to
Saudi Arabia
to help defend the kingdom against attacks by the Houthis, Yemeni rebels backed by Iran. The jets will help protect infrastructure and residential areas, but will not conduct offensive strikes against the rebels. In Yemen the Houthis fired missiles at a training camp for government forces, killing at least 73 people. The Yemeni government is allied with the Saudis.
Egypt’s president, Abdel-Fattah al-Sisi, also pledged to help the Saudis, and asked parliament to approve the deployment of combat forces. The extent of any Egyptian involvement in the conflict is unclear. Turkey’s parliament was also considering  a plan to send military personnel to Saudi Arabia.
More than 80 people were killed in a drone strike near a market in southern Sudan, most of them commuters on their way home from work. The Rapid Support Forces, which controls the area, blamed the strike on the army, which it is fighting in a civil war. Another drone hit a town in a disputed region near the border with South Sudan, killing at least 150 people. Such attacks causing mass civilian casualties have become increasingly common in the three-year conflict.
A former Rwandan soldier and vocal critic of Paul Kagame, Rwanda’s president, was found beheaded near Kampala, the capital of neighbouring Uganda. Robert Kabera, who fled to Uganda in 2020, had recently posted on social media that he feared for his life. He is not the first exiled Rwandan dissident to turn up dead in gruesome circumstances.
Nigeria confirmed its first case of Ebola since the Democratic Republic of Congo announced an outbreak of the disease in May. Authorities said the patient had travelled to Nigeria from Uganda. The Ugandan government said there were currently no active cases of the disease in the country.
America’s State Department reported that 300,000 visas have now been revoked during Donald Trump’s second term, up from the 175,000 that had been tallied up to early August. Announcing the new numbers an official reiterated the administration’s policy: “zero tolerance for foreigners here on visas who break the law”.
A non-binding referendum in Alberta saw more than 75% of voters back an option to remain a province of Canada, rather than start the process of holding a binding referendum on splitting away. Mark Carney hailed the outcome as a victory for “unity”. “Canada ​is so much greater than the sum of its parts,” he said. However, Albertans did back other measures in the referendum to give the province more control over immigration.
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro debated each other ahead of
Brazil’s presidential election run-off
on October 25th. Polls show the race has narrowed since the first round on October 4th, when Mr Bolsonaro took 47% of the vote to Lula’s 45%.
Marco Rubio, America’s secretary of state, met Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, India’s foreign minister, in Mumbai for talks on finalising a trade deal. The pact has been held up for months because of tensions over American tariffs and India’s purchase of Russian oil. But Mr Rubio now says an agreement is “very, very close”.
More than 9,500 police officers were deployed in Jakarta to deter student-led protests that were called to mark the second anniversary of
Prabowo Subianto’s
inauguration as Indonesia’s president.  The deterrence worked, as few students gathered to demand Mr Prabowo do more to tackle the cost of living and other grievances. The president’s approval rating has plunged since taking office. MSCI, a global index service, warned that it might remove Indonesia’s emerging-market status because of its “market dysfunction”. Downgrading Indonesia would force many tracking funds to sell their Indonesian assets.
Japan’s space agency
launched a spacecraft
on a five-year mission to collect samples from Phobos, one of two small moons that orbit Mars, the first-ever return journey from the planet’s system. The spacecraft will enter Martian space in August 2027, landing on Phobos at some point in the following years.  A rover will use a robotic arm to collect moondust. If all goes well, the spacecraft will depart  in 2030 and return to Earth in 2031.

epub_11.title: Business
epub_11.text:
Business
The world this week
Business
The world this week
Oct 22nd 2026
Elon Musk floated the possibility of merging SpaceX and Tesla. There is a “lot of merit” in combining the companies, he said, and the boards of both have created independent committees to explore their options (as the boss and largest shareholder in both firms Mr Musk is not on the committees). A merger would bring together Mr Musk’s AI ambitions for data centres, driverless cars and robots. SpaceX, meanwhile, reported quarterly revenue of $14.6bn, up by 161% year on year, $7.6bn of which came from AI (which it calls SI, or super intelligence). Mr Musk has pledged to give every child in America one SpaceX share, currently worth nearly $160, next year.
Tesla earlier demonstrated its new Roadster sports car; the demonstration vehicle was modified with SpaceX-derived thrusters and able to flip mid-air and land safely again. The electric-carmaker reported a surprise positive cashflow in its latest earnings.
Market jitters resurfaced about the huge investments being made in AI.
CoreWeave
, which rents out data-centre capacity, saw its bonds and share price plunge amid worries that it will not be able to service its debt. The sell-off spread to other “neocloud” companies. Meanwhile, the share price of Elice, an AI-infrastructure company, fell by 32% on its first day of trading in South Korea.
Anthropic registered a net loss of more than $80bn in the first half of this year, according to press reports, mostly because of an accounting charge related to bonds that could be eventually converted to shares. The frontier-AI firm is expected to make its stock-market debut in mid-November. Anthropic is to hand over 5% of its shares to a new public-benefit fund it has created to work in AI safety and examine AI’s impact on the jobs market, among other things.
Meta’s third-quarter revenue grew by 26%, year on year, to $64.6bn. The company rolled out its Muse personal AI agent in September. Meanwhile, a court in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25bn to the state after it was found to have misled users about privacy.
Barclays, a big British bank, revealed that it is cutting 5,000 jobs this year because of efficiencies from adopting AI. Most of the jobs will be among developers and other support services.
Stock in Netflix slid again after the streaming giant reported its slowest sales growth in three years. Revenue grew by 11.8% in the third quarter, year on year, to $12.9bn. It expects even lower growth of 11.5% in the fourth quarter. Media reports of the company’s woes as it struggles with slowing subscriptions read like a Hollywood movie plot, with both the head of film and the head of content summarily dismissed from their positions and the announcement of 1,000 job cuts. Despite massively increasing its spending on content, Netflix is no longer producing a string of hits.
GDP expanded in China by 4.5% during the third quarter, year on year, an improvement on the 4.3% recorded in the second quarter. China’s exports boom is offsetting weak domestic demand.
The
riots in France
helped push the yield on French ten-year government bonds above 5% for the first time since 2002, as investors bet that budgetary reforms would be delayed. Carrefour, a big supermarket chain, cut its annual profit forecast and blamed the violence, which it thinks will deter shoppers. Insurance losses from the weekend’s unrest are expected to reach €1bn ($1.1bn), exceeding the €700m in losses incurred over a week of rioting in 2023.
The developers of the PHP programming language
issued a fix
that they urged users to download immediately, after an OpenAI-led consortium discovered two critical vulnerabilities. PHP shores up a large part of the internet, running in the background of websites, hosting platforms and control panels. Some governments, including in Finland and the Netherlands, took some websites offline while they worked on the issue. America’s National Security Agency recommended that systems be taken offline if users couldn’t apply the mitigations. The fix will have alerted criminals to the vulnerability of servers.
Britain’s annual inflation rate jumped to 3.5% in September. Markets are now all but certain that the Bank of England will raise interest rates at its meeting in November.
The British government at last approved the development of the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, the first big endorsement of a fossil-fuel project under Andy Burnham as prime minister. The governing Labour Party has pledged to deliver a net-zero carbon emissions policy. Greens are furious, but Mr Burnham said it would protect jobs. Unions hailed the decision. The government is now under pressure to approve the Rosebank oil project, which environmentalists also vehemently oppose.
UniCredit, Italy’s second-largest bank, won approval from the European Central Bank to take over Commerzbank, a big German lender. Having secured 48% of Commerzbank’s shares, UniCredit thinks it will take control of the bank by the end of the year.
The IPO of Jio Platforms, Mukesh Ambani’s telecoms firm, was fully subscribed just two hours after it opened. The flotation is expected to raise $3.2bn, making it India’s biggest-ever listing. The shares start trading on October 28th.

epub_14.title: The agony of liberal Europe
epub_14.text:
The agony of liberal Europe
Leaders
| Our cover
The agony of liberal Europe
Centrist rulers have fallen dangerously short—and are now paying the price
Oct 22nd 2026
“The first steps into the Unrest seem straightforward enough—anger at the fall of real wages, at capitalist aggression, at the unwillingness of Parliament; anger fomented by agitators...reason wars with instinct.” Few of those who mobbed French cities this week would recognise those words. But many would agree with George Dangerfield, the British-American journalist who wrote them. The demonstrators were consumed by rage. Rage at the failure of the state and against the floundering centrist politicians who govern. Rage at high prices and economic dysfunction. And for some, rage against the idea of centrist politics at all.
Dangerfield wrote about “the strange death of liberal England” in the years before the first world war. Some predict a similarly grim fate for liberal Europe today. Arson, mob violence, looting and mass protests show how much citizens despair of their leaders. France has a long tradition of the manif, but the violence unleashed by hooded and masked rioters across the country over the past weekend was
unusually severe
. Protests also flared in Belgium, Italy and Portugal. In looming elections, first in Spain next month, then in France and Poland next year, voters are poised to punish moderate parties—and in Italy the far right is outflanking the populist Giorgia Meloni, who has governed from the centre. In the wings wait more charismatic figures from the extremes, including Marine Le Pen in France and Alice Weidel in Germany.
Many in America and in Europe say the centre has only itself to blame. Donald Trump crows that Europe is on fire because its leaders spurned his advice, left their borders open and let millions of immigrants rush in each year, from Afghanistan, Algeria and Syria. Those on the MAGA right, such as Elon Musk, say growing Muslim populations pose the greatest threat. Some talk, apocalyptically and absurdly, of “civilisational erasure” or civil war. Even in Germany the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said this week that high rates of migration and a failure to integrate the foreign-born are partly behind the sudden, violent upheaval. So has Hungary’s newish prime minister, Peter Magyar.
Their analysis is either craven or self-serving. Undoubtedly, many European voters also wish to curb immigration and asylum. But when it comes to the violent protests, the diagnosis is plain wrong. Instead the problems facing Europe’s centrists are more complex—and less easy to fix.
Even if some young protesters in France wear Algerian football shirts or chant pro-Palestinian slogans, the upheaval in Europe today is not about race or religion. Over 500,000 people marched in France on Saturday and they were largely unmasked and white. They were fired up, as in other countries, by the cost of living and poor public services. They want more fuel subsidies, more spending on schools, more handouts. Perhaps the largest group are aligned with the populist-left Jean-Luc Mélenchon, an ageing rabble-rouser and one-time Trotskyist, more akin to Bernie Sanders than an emir of ISIS.
Real violence did follow. But blame that on other factors, none to do with race. Mobs struck at public buildings, police cars and more. They also smashed and grabbed from luxury retailers, like Louis Vuitton, and small stores run by immigrants. The police failed to keep order, having earlier been accused of brutality against student protesters. And much of the violence was incited and orchestrated by anarchists, who have a revolutionary political agenda. Typical among them is a man arrested after the burning of a 19th-century town hall in Limoges, a white French citizen in his mid-30s.
Although the critics are wrong, Europe’s centrists do face real problems—and France shows how serious they are. The first is the fiscal bind that makes effective political action so hard. When Emmanuel Macron, the president, faced huge protests by the gilets jaunes in 2018-19, he could deploy billions of euros to placate them. Today, that is no longer possible. France is spending too much and growing too slowly—by just over 1% a year under Mr Macron.
This autumn, lawmakers will struggle to pass a budget that cuts the deficit by a feeble 0.4 percentage points, to an unsustainable 5% of GDP. And still the government may fall. France is so overborrowed, and markets have so little faith in its politicians, that spreads of French government bonds over German ones have soared to levels last seen during the euro crisis.
Instead of rising to this challenge, the centrists seem out of ideas. The Economist once cheered Mr Macron as a bold new standard-bearer for radical centrism. Today, while centrists huddle together for protection, all the energy is at the extremes. Surveys say over 80% of the French are pessimistic about their future, especially about their economy. Mr Merz is deeply unpopular and may be forced from office. His anti-migrant sniping reflects his inability to find the words and ideas to see off Ms Weidel and her party, the Alternative for Germany.
No wonder the centrists face an electoral walloping. Polls show that Pedro Sánchez, the centre-left prime minister in Spain, will probably be turfed out soon to be replaced by a coalition of the centre- and populist right. In France the riots—and the myth that immigrants were to blame—may lift Ms Le Pen of the populist-right National Rally into the presidency in May. Polls show that the violence boosted her this week. While Mr Macron jetted off on a trip to the Gulf, Ms Le Pen gave a presidential-sounding speech calling for public order.
The violence in France should jolt head-in-the-sand centrists to confront the consequences of failure. If their countries descend into strife, they will lose power. If they lose power, the European Union will choke, as the rest of the world races ahead. If bond markets seize up, financial contagion could spread. If EU countries indulge Vladimir Putin of Russia, he will only become more aggressive. Dangerfield was writing about a time when most people were ignorant of the catastrophe that lay ahead. Today’s liberals have no such excuse.

epub_15.title: Saudi Arabia and the UAE are sowing chaos
epub_15.text:
Saudi Arabia and the UAE are sowing chaos
Leaders
| The rivalry wrecking a region
Saudi Arabia and the UAE are sowing chaos
Gulf powers should stop fuelling carnage in their backyard
Oct 22nd 2026
Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) could once pose as oases of stability. Now the two Gulf powers are under siege. A hostile Iran has a chokehold over the Strait of Hormuz, through which much of their commerce flows. The Houthis, an Iran-backed militia in Yemen, are lobbing missiles at Saudi airports and pipelines, disrupting trade and travel, and threatening Bab al-Mandab, another vital waterway. America, once the Gulf states’ most reliable ally, is now less willing to guarantee their security, leaving both countries exposed.
Given the scale of the crisis, you might think the Saudis and Emiratis would be marshalling their resources to deal with the problems close to home. Instead, they are tussling for influence farther afield, and recklessly
inflaming some of the worst wars in the world
.
The conflicts on either side of the Red Sea have complex causes. The Emiratis and Saudis did not start them, and are not the only foreign powers meddling, but they are making them bloodier and harder to end. This is clearest in Sudan, where a mass-raping genocidal militia, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), is fighting the Sudanese army for control of the country. So vile are the RSF that they
hunt down and kill doctors
, since any doctor can testify to their crimes. Yet the Emiratis arm and support the RSF. (They deny it.) The Saudis back the somewhat less brutal regular army.
In Yemen, where both the Saudis and Emiratis have battled the Houthis, their squabbles have led to an Emirati pullback and allowed the Houthis, a regional menace, to fill the vacuum. The two Gulf states also vie for influence over ports on the Red Sea. Their competing alliances risk further aggravating tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea, which are already close to (another) disastrous war.
Little of this makes sense. Granted, the ports of the Horn of Africa could be vital to regional trade, particularly as other routes are under threat. And as America becomes less dependable under President Donald Trump, it is reasonable for both Saudi Arabia and the UAE to develop networks of allies to bolster their own security. But not like this. The two Gulf states’ projections of power seem to owe more to the petulant rivalry between their respective rulers,
Muhammad bin Salman
and Muhammad bin Zayed, than to any thoughtful strategy. By arming combatants, failing to curb the laundering of war loot and making conflicts more complex, they are likely to prolong them.
The human cost is vast. The wars in Sudan and Yemen have claimed hundreds of thousands of lives, driven nearly 20m people from their homes and pushed millions to the brink of famine. That alone should be ample spur for the Gulf meddlers to change course.
Failing that, they should recognise that their foreign adventurism threatens their own interests. Chaos on either side of the Red Sea imperils trade routes even as the war with Iran buffets the Gulf economies. Also, it is hard to see how hastening the collapse of the gigantic African state in their backyard makes either Gulf power more secure. The barren UAE’s dream of using Sudan as a breadbasket is unlikely to be realised while gunmen are slaughtering Sudanese farmers.
So the Saudis and Emiratis should stop supporting the warring parties in Sudan, especially the RSF, and work together towards a ceasefire. In Yemen they should set aside their rivalry, collaborate to contain the Houthis and try to restore a ceasefire there, too.
More responsible, less incendiary foreign policies from Abu Dhabi and Riyadh would not suddenly make the region calm. But they might make its wars a bit easier to tamp down. And that would ultimately benefit nearly everyone, including the Saudis and Emiratis themselves.

epub_16.title: Either AI or public debt could crash markets. But probably not both
epub_16.text:
Either AI or public debt could crash markets. But probably not both
Leaders
| Pick your phantom
Either AI or public debt could crash markets. But probably not both
If AI stocks collapse, bond yields will fall
Oct 22nd 2026
Two SPECTRES stalk financial markets. One is the fear that surging bond yields will make the rich world’s shaky public finances unsustainable, triggering a nasty fiscal crisis. The other is the worry that the revenues from artificial intelligence needed to keep the data-centre boom going will fail to arrive.
As we report
, that would devastate credit markets and cause a big fall in stocks, too.
The good news is that only an Ichabod Crane would think that both these scenarios could strike at once. Instead, investors must decide which story is scarier. For now, The Economist is more worried about sovereign debt.
For most of the year,
concerns about governments have dominated
. Between the end of February and the start of October, the yield on 30-year US Treasuries rose by a full percentage point. The Iran war has sent inflation up and forced central banks to raise interest rates. Strong economic growth and the rush to build data centres have caused a scramble for capital in which governments have had to compete with the private sector. In Japan, Britain and especially France, investors have fretted about the ability of governments to service their debts.
In recent weeks, though, the prospect of an end to the AI boom has scared the markets more. The five-year bonds of CoreWeave, a “neocloud” that rents out data centres, trade at a 15% yield, up from 10% in July. The company’s share price has fallen by about a third in the past month. The slowing revenue growth of Anthropic, an AI-model provider, has investors worried that the cash CoreWeave and its peers need may not arrive, or at least not quickly enough to pay their creditors. Interlinked financing means that pain could spread quickly, through both the ai supply chain and the private-credit and insurance firms that hold a lot of data-centre debt.
As a result, many sovereign bonds have rallied. There has been
little relief for France
, where riots are worsening a political crisis, or
Britain
, where an upcoming budget makes investors nervous. But yields on ten-year Treasuries are down by a fifth of a point. Investors usually flee to the safety of American bonds in a downturn. Everywhere else, as data-centre investment slowed, an AI crash would ease the scramble for capital. And it would lead central banks to lower interest rates to support growth, thereby making debts easier to service.
Only in a big crash akin to the global financial crisis (GFC) of 2007-09 would the two risks collide. Governments are already sufficiently in the red that a deep recession would, by collapsing tax revenues and increasing welfare spending, make budget deficits look truly terrifying. Long-term bond yields might rise even as short-term interest rates fell—a nasty symptom of fiscal malaise that sometimes strikes emerging markets. It did not happen during the GFC, but the starting-point for debt and deficits today is higher.
Thankfully, there is no reason to expect such a deep crash. True, the history of finance shows that useful new technologies often bring about a boom and bust, and the web of financing behind AI has become complex. But the industry’s interlinkages are better understood than the alphabet-soup of housing-market securities was in 2007. Banks are safer, too. Though they are exposed to ai via their lending to private-credit firms, their balance-sheets are less fragile and better monitored. And backstopping much of the industry is the chipmaker Nvidia, which has an enormous cash pile. Most important, AI assets, though a big slice of many stock indices, are a smaller chunk of household wealth than housing.
So the best comparison for today’s AI vulnerabilities remains the dotcom bubble of the late 1990s. When it burst in 2000, cratering stocks caused only a mild recession. Bond yields came down, too, and underlying productivity growth held up. Such a scenario would hardly solve governments’ long-term budget problems, but it might forestall them. Many economies outside America are less exposed to the AI boom than they are to bond yields; growth falling by less than interest rates would make legacy debts a lighter burden. America’s deficit would grow in a recession, but so would the world’s appetite for Treasuries, because the dollar is the world’s reserve currency.
By contrast, if high interest rates triggered a sovereign-debt blow-up the consequences would be truly grave. If investors lost confidence in Treasuries, it would threaten the dollar’s valuable status as a haven. As France is discovering, trying to close big deficits under duress can lead to political instability. Governments may prefer to inflate away debt than to pay it down. That could imperil the stability on which all investment depends. A run on sovereign debt in a big advanced economy could well leave investors wishing that a dotcom-style ai bust was all they had to worry about.

epub_17.title: Europe must escape its reliance on American satellites
epub_17.text:
Europe must escape its reliance on American satellites
Leaders
| Eyes in the sky
Europe must escape its reliance on American satellites
To do so it will have to drop old habits
Oct 22nd 2026
RECENT DAYS have made clear the folly of relying too much for your national security on a capricious private citizen named Elon Musk. Mr Musk is said to have ordered the partial hobbling of his satellite-internet service inside Ukraine. That had two malign effects. It hampered Ukraine’s already limited ability to defend its cities and civilians from fast and deadly Russian drones. It also made it harder for Ukraine to strike back at Russia’s occupying forces.
If President Donald Trump objected to this egregious favour to the Kremlin, he kept quiet about it. America’s allies, in Europe and elsewhere, may reasonably ask how much they can trust the superpower. If, in the future, they need space-based communications systems to defend themselves against attack, can they be absolutely certain that America will supply them unconditionally? The problem, alas, is that no adequate
home-grown alternative exists
. Europe talks a good game of trying to achieve “autonomy in space”. But that will take time and money, and also require Europe to cut the waste, infighting and duplication that have weighed down its space efforts.
How to get there? First, Europe must have the launch capacity to put large numbers of satellites into orbit. In this, its record so far is poor. It can lift heavy payloads into space on its Ariane rockets, but nowhere near as cheaply or efficiently as Mr Musk’s company does.
Europe’s rocket programme exemplifies flaws of its space ventures. Delays in developing its heavy-lift launcher, the Ariane 6, left Europe without access to space for almost a year in 2023 and 2024. The European Space Agency (ESA), which funds the programme, is partly to blame. It fails to award contracts to the most innovative or efficient suppliers, instead favouring firms from countries that donate the most funds. The programme is also shielded from market forces, getting roughly €300m ($337m)  a year in public subsidies. Small wonder it has been trounced by SpaceX, which last year launched Falcon 9 rockets 165 times, charging private clients $70m a pop, while Ariane charges more than $90m despite those subsidies.
To fix this, the ESA is tentatively copying America’s space agency, NASA, which decades ago encouraged the growth of commercial space firms by switching from “cost-plus” contracts for developing rockets to buying fixed-price launch services, a policy that let Mr Musk’s SpaceX flourish. The agency has awarded contracts to three rocket startups. Mergers, such as the proposed tie-up of three of Europe’s biggest satellite-making businesses, could follow. But can Europe create a firm big enough to compete globally without reducing competition at home?
Europe’s second priority should be to create a rival to Mr Musk’s Starlink, and to do so without policies that drive up prices and stifle innovation. OneWeb, a firm part-owned by the British and French governments, already provides some services similar to Starlink’s. The European Union is going ahead with IRIS2, a €16bn project to deploy 348 satellites to provide secure communications to governments and armed forces. Yet even this suffers from fragmentation and duplication. Germany plans to build a swarm of 100 military-communications satellites at a cost of about €10bn, while France and Britain are investing in their own smaller programmes. It would be wiser for all to pool their demand for satellite services.
Some governments will insist on having such systems under national control. Yet their concerns could be met by building satellites to common standards, so that they are interoperable. Countries or blocs could own these, but by linking them together, all would benefit: larger fleets would mean more resilience and greater coverage. Examples of this are already in orbit, such as small radar satellites built by Iceye, a Finnish firm. It offers customers a “federated model”, in which they can choose how much to share intelligence and co-ordinate where their satellites focus. Such an approach should encourage like-minded middle powers beyond Europe, such as Canada, Japan and South Korea, to co-operate too.
Europe need not stop there. The more it builds up its own space capabilities and shares them with America, the more convincingly it can show that an alliance of democracies is valuable. If so, despite Mr Trump’s instincts, America would have much to lose by holding its allies to ransom.

epub_18.title: Indonesia’s populist president is losing his charm
epub_18.text:
Indonesia’s populist president is losing his charm
Leaders
| The perils of Prabowo
Indonesia’s populist president is losing his charm
Prabowo Subianto’s erratic policies are holding back his country
Oct 22nd 2026
At the first anniversary of his inauguration two years ago this week, 81% of Indonesians told pollsters that they approved of Prabowo Subianto, a former general who is their eighth president. Now only 45% do. Many Western leaders would kill for that number, but in Indonesia’s deferential culture it marks the steepest fall in support for a president since the return of democracy in 1998. How has it all gone so wrong?
First, investor confidence has collapsed. The Indonesian stock market has plunged by 40% so far this year, making it the world’s worst-performing. On October 16th MSCI, a financial-analytics company, threatened to dump Indonesia into its lowest grade of market, along with such shrapnel-scarred places as Lebanon and Ukraine. Mr Prabowo’s government, it says, has not done enough to end pump-and-dump schemes and insider trading. The currency is at its weakest for two decades. Flows of foreign direct investment (FDI), which soared under Mr Prabowo’s predecessor, Joko Widodo (known as Jokowi), as he courted Chinese miners, have been disappointing. FDI ought to be roaring, as it is in nearby Vietnam and Malaysia, on the back of the AI boom and strong global trade. But Mr Prabowo’s erratic rule is making Indonesia a
tricky place to do business
.
Second, Mr Prabowo has done little to cure underlying economic maladies. A broken labour market has become worse on his watch, with falling middle-class real wages, a huge black market and high levels of graduate unemployment. A growth target of 8%, always ambitious, is far out of reach. Mr Prabowo’s main initiatives have proved wasteful (a $13bn-a-year free-school-meals programme) or complicated and unnecessary (plans for 80,000 state-run village co-operatives). Such gimmicks used to be popular; recent polling shows that voters, having sampled them, are no longer so impressed.
If Mr Prabowo cannot get the economy right, he risks alienating political elites—a third problem. Already, party bosses are considering
moves against him
. Mr Prabowo won in 2025 thanks only to the endorsement of his predecessor and former rival. However, Jokowi and the general now appear to be at loggerheads. Some officers linked to Mr Prabowo are seeking the removal of his vice-president, who is Jokowi’s son. Indonesia’s other two living ex-presidents are said to be manoeuvring, too. The political stability of Mr Prabowo’s first two years in office may not last.
Mr Prabowo can still count on the backing of the army and the police. He used to command Indonesia’s special forces and was alleged to have made dissidents disappear in the 1990s, an accusation that he furiously denies. Some fear he will be tempted to use dirty tricks to suppress dissent again. Hints of this are already visible. In the weeks leading up to planned demonstrations on the second anniversary of his inauguration, on October 20th, police and soldiers allegedly bribed activists to stay off the streets. Assailants beat up one of the protest’s main organisers. Police say they are investigating but have yet to identify any culprits.
Writing a guest column in The Economist in June, Mr Prabowo declared that he welcomed criticism and that Indonesians deserved better than the 5% growth of previous years. He is right to aspire to more. Indonesia, the world’s fourth-most-populous country, has almost 290m people, immense resources, a huge market and boundless potential.
Unfortunately, the main obstacle to it fulfilling that potential is Mr Prabowo himself. Indeed, expectations are now so low that even minor policy improvements could lift investors’ confidence. Steadier stock and currency markets could alleviate some of the political pressure, too. But for Indonesia to hit its stride, Mr Prabowo must recognise that his populist approach has run out of road.
■

epub_20.title: How effective is effective altruism?
epub_20.text:
How effective is effective altruism?
Letters
| A selection of correspondence
How effective is effective altruism?
Also this week, gun laws, rock concerts, human oversight of AI, public debt
Oct 22nd 2026
Letters are welcome via email to
letters@economist.com
F
ind out more
about how we process your letter
The doctrine of
effective altruism
tells charities to spend their money to produce the largest possible benefits (“The century’s biggest idea”, October 3rd). But a much bigger idea says that governments, too, should be doing just that.
This idea is rapidly taking root. In Britain it is what the Treasury’s Green Book now adheres to. So when departments ask for money they have to estimate the benefits that the spending will produce and show how that compares with the cost to the taxpayer. And the benefits have to include not just increases in income but all those non-monetary things that make our lives worthwhile; health, safe streets, a job and so on. All of these non-monetary things are to be evaluated in units of life satisfaction, before they are translated back into their monetary equivalents.
In this way Britain is leading the world, by including all well-being benefits and applying this test to all expenditures, current as well as capital. This is a huge movement towards more rational government.  As a recent report from the London School of Economics shows, this approach, if followed through in decision-making, would require major shifts in priorities. Let us hope these can be reflected in the next spending review.
Professor Lord Richard LayardCo-directorWell-Being ProgrammeCentre for Economic PerformanceLondon School of Economics
Example number one for the “strangeness” of effective altruists in your reckoning is that some “see the moral distinction between humans and other animals as weak”. But that’s not a strange idea at all. It is a viewpoint grounded in science and articulated by everyone from Charles Darwin and Jeremy Bentham to Jane Goodall and Richard Dawkins, who refer to other animals as our evolutionary cousins.
According to Our World in Data, humans farm and slaughter roughly 220bn vertebrate animals every year (90bn land animals and another 130bn farmed fish). That’s more animals raised and slaughtered for food each year than the total number of humans who have ever lived.
Pointing out the immorality of this reality does not require any “complex, even bizarre moral calculations.” It just requires the ability to apply scientific facts to moral reasoning.
Bruce FriedrichWashington, DC
Will MacAskill defends effective altruism without apparently noticing how far his moral reasoning depends on his own standpoint (By Invitation, October 10th). The very idea of a tithe presumes an ability to pay, which depends on one’s existing circumstances, and the whole enterprise rests on the worldview afforded by its adherents’ predicament and education. It is no accident that people such as Mr MacAskill sit at the forefront: Oxford-trained, with the time and, comparatively speaking, the money to contemplate the plight of others.
Living in Africa has opened my eyes to the Elastoplast effect of sporadic injections of money, which can lift even large numbers of indigent people for a time, but with little or no lasting effect.
On a microscopic scale, I give every day to a man who sleeps in a bus shelter. The effect is superficial and transitory. He is back every night until the police move him on, because structural unemployment and political stasis leave him with no prospect of work. Effective altruists say that large-scale giving can have high expected value, but where poverty is politically and economically induced, well-meaning giving makes no substantive long-term difference.
Without change at that level, nothing the effective altruists dream up will endure.
D.A.L. COLDWELLProfessor of managementUniversity of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg
More letters on this topic can be found at:
economist.com/lettersaltruism
America’s gun violence will continue, you say, until voters follow Australians and Britons “
and decide they have had enough
” (“Under the gun”, October 10th). The truth is messier. From 2005 to 2008, nearly a decade after Britain banned most handguns, I was a detective superintendent in Lambeth, south London, where young gang members favoured machine pistols, firing them from passing cars. Local officers and the wider Metropolitan Police worked with community groups to stop the shootings. In December 2025, in Sydney where I now live, two gunmen killed 15 people at Bondi Beach.  The older gunman held a firearms licence and owned six guns lawfully.
Lambeth showed me the limits of a ban, and Bondi has shown Australians the limits of a licence. Strict laws have made both countries safer, yet each leaves a gap that falls to the police and the communities they serve, which is why Malcolm Gladwell’s point about the size of European police forces is worth taking seriously. Crime fell in central London when almost a third more officers were put on its streets after the bombings of July 2005. In Philadelphia a randomised trial  found that foot patrols on the most dangerous corners cut violent crime by almost a quarter, though the gains vanished when the officers left.
Neither case isolated shootings, yet both show what visible policing adds to the law. America, with far more guns than either country, needs both.
Jonathan TottmanSydney
How should the law
handle intent when robots act beyond their users’ control
(“Unsuitable”, October 10th)? Consider the drunk driver. Getting blackout drunk  doesn’t remove responsibility. The law traces culpability back to an earlier decision by an agent capable of making it; the pre-drunk self deciding to put the future self in that position. Why should autonomous systems be any different? A machine can’t bear moral responsibility. It sits with the human who exercises judgment in deciding to delegate authority to it.
Liam TalbotBristol
Your warning about relying on liability law to govern AI has a contractual dimension. OpenAI’s standard services agreement generally caps its contractual liability at the customer’s preceding 12 months’ fees, with exceptions including gross negligence, wilful misconduct and indemnification. Such caps can limit what an adopter recovers from its supplier even while the adopter faces claims from third parties.
A small employer may control how it uses a model while having little power to inspect or repair it. Making the employer liable may encourage caution, but it need not give the developer the same incentive to remove a defect.
Risk allocation should reflect who can prevent the particular harm, as well as who signs the purchase order. The bill can travel downstream. The power to fix the model may stay upstream.
Rohan SharmaUS delegate and technical expert for the International Organisation for Standardisation ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42 (AI standards)Temecula, California
Pop and rock stars who demand that fans
put away their phones at concerts
are not considering the price of a ticket (“Crowd control”, September 19th). Musicians are charging extraordinary prices for the privilege of seeing them perform. Last year I paid more than $300 to see Sir Paul McCartney in Las Vegas. For that money I want to leave with more than a T-shirt and a programme (another $50 each). I want photo and video memories of what I experienced, captured on my phone and available to me long after the T-shirt has worn out.
The Grateful Dead understood that recordings could extend the experience rather than diminish it, famously allowing, and even encouraging, fans to tape their concerts. Today’s artists should recognise the value of allowing fans to do the same. If I’m paying hundreds of dollars to be there, I’d like to decide how much of the experience to preserve.
Jason RussellLehi, Utah
Regarding the
looming government-debt crisis
(“Will bonds blow up?”, October 10th), politicians will not treat voters like grown-ups until voters start behaving like grown-ups. Voters consistently want leaders who offer them candies and sweets, without understanding that this will only lead to the dentist’s drill.
Vera HutzuliakMississauga, Canada

epub_22.title: Ignore the doomsayers. American democracy is in good shape
epub_22.text:
Ignore the doomsayers. American democracy is in good shape
By Invitation
| Integrity intact
Ignore the doomsayers. American democracy is in good shape
Its resilience rests not on politicians’ restraint but on the robustness of institutional arrangements, writes Frances Lee
Oct 22nd 2026
AMERICA’S TWO main parties do not agree on much, but they share a slogan. “We’ve got to be too big to rig,” Kamala Harris told an audience recently. Days later Donald Trump called for a midterm win “too big to rig” because “they rig elections in this country.” Both parties urge their own supporters to vote while warning that the other side cheats. Scholars and journalists, meanwhile, have settled on a diagnosis: democratic backsliding.
Many voters themselves are anxious. Looking towards the
midterms on November 3rd
, only 49% of respondents expect a free and fair election. Under Mr Trump’s influence Republicans are especially cynical. Democrats worry about election interference from his administration. Minority voters fear harassment from Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents at polling stations.
Anxieties notwithstanding, American elections are healthier than the backsliding narrative allows. Indeed, there was also considerable anxiety in advance of both the 2022 and 2024 elections. Then, as now, Americans worried about election interference, voter fraud and political violence. But in the end turnout was high by historical standards and the vast majority of Americans expressed confidence in the outcomes.
American democracy rests on durable institutions capable of checking concentrated power. Midterm elections are important in this regard. The “midterm law”—that the president’s party loses seats midway through his term—has held in 20 of the 22 votes since 1938. Mr Trump’s first term followed the pattern: Republicans lost their majority in the House of Representatives in 2018.
Notably, the president’s party loses seats in midterms even when most Americans approve of the president’s performance. The penalty grows when the president is unpopular and the economy weak.
Mr Trump’s approval rating
languishes in the mid-30s. In September consumer confidence fell to its lowest level since 2014, partly owing to high fuel prices. Across midterms since 1992 the president’s party has lost an average of 25 House seats. The current Republican majority disappears with a net loss of three.
In an effort to forestall losses, Mr Trump induced Republican-controlled states to redraw their electoral maps. The resulting gerrymanders probably netted some Republican seats, albeit fewer than they had hoped. But here again American institutions retain safeguards against a president’s effort at electoral deck-stacking. A president can demand new maps only in states where his party holds the pen, and Democrats in California answered a gerrymander in Texas with
one of their own
. The Cook Political Report projects a net Republican gain of four seats from redistricting, not nearly enough to protect the party’s House majority.
Mr Trump floated and later disavowed the idea of postponing or cancelling the midterms. Regardless, that scenario was always wildly implausible. Election day is fixed by federal statute, and the constitution sets the date when office-holders’ terms end. The decentralised administration of elections across thousands of local jurisdictions denies the president any easy lever to manipulate outcomes. Mr Trump’s attempt to turn the postal service into such a lever against mail-in ballots was thwarted by the courts.
More likely than interference with the election is that unsuccessful office-seekers will refuse to concede, claiming their opponents cheated. Nothing is more basic to democratic legitimacy than the loser’s consent. Many feared that Mr Trump’s refusal to concede in 2020 would spread across the political system. It has not. Bright Line Watch, a research group, examined all 884 congressional races in 2020 and 2022. The overwhelming majority of losing candidates publicly acknowledged defeat. Explicit refusals were concentrated among first-time candidates who had lost by wide margins. And there were fewer such refusals in 2022 than in 2020. Candidates with political careers to protect still concede. When they do, complaints of election “rigging” lose their force.
None of this is cause for complacency. My research with Geoffrey Layman and Christina Wolbrecht finds that party activists, long regarded as guardians of democratic norms, are now no more committed to losers’ consent than ordinary citizens. Any deterioration in basic democratic values is worrying.
Nevertheless, the record of American elections since 2020 has been encouraging. Election administration has improved. Although many career administrators resigned amid increased harassment after 2020, the voters’ experience actually got better. In both 2022 and 2024 the share of people waiting more than 30 minutes to cast their ballot was lower than in 2020, and the long-documented racial gap narrowed: by 2024 black, white, Hispanic and Asian voters reported comparable waiting times.
Overall, the evidence points to a resilient democracy. That resilience rests not on politicians’ restraint but on institutional arrangements that are difficult to manipulate: fixed election dates, decentralised administration and officials independently elected in their own constituencies, with their own interests to protect.
James Madison defended the House’s two-year terms as giving Congress “an immediate dependence on, and an intimate sympathy with, the people”. That dependence will be on display in November. Democrats are favoured to win a House majority. The Senate, which looked safely Republican last year, is now in play. If control of either chamber changes hands, Mr Trump will have to bargain with Congress to fund his priorities and face its oversight for the rest of his term. Midterm elections are a routine check the constitution imposes on every president. Whatever else has weakened, that guardrail holds.
■
Frances E. Lee is a professor of politics and public affairs at Princeton and the author of “A Case for Congress”, “The Limits of Party” (with James M. Curry) and “In Covid’s Wake” (with Stephen Macedo).

epub_23.title: A former ally asks why Donald Trump abandoned his own legacy
epub_23.text:
A former ally asks why Donald Trump abandoned his own legacy
By Invitation
| Midterm melancholy
A former ally asks why Donald Trump abandoned his own legacy
The president is undermining the few advantages Republicans still have, writes Marc Short
Oct 22nd 2026
MIDTERM ELECTIONS are a referendum on the party in power, and Republicans took power promising to defeat inflation, restore a roaring economy and usher in a new American golden age. But they have not delivered, and on November 3rd voters will punish them at the ballot box.
The first Trump administration brought a new style but largely embraced traditional free-market policies: lowering taxes, cutting regulations and encouraging the government to leave the American people alone and let them prosper. The result—over the first three years of the administration, before covid-19 struck—was almost 7m new jobs, a $6,000 average increase in the income of middle-class families and an unemployment rate of 3.5%, a 50-year low. Had it not been for the pandemic, Donald Trump may have won re-election in 2020 on the strength of the economy. I was the White House director of legislative affairs in the first Trump administration, leading our congressional outreach, and I will always be proud of our conservative record.
When he returned to the White House in January 2025, however, Mr Trump embraced some of his most protectionist and populist economic instincts. Needless trade wars with Canada and other allies have pummelled American farmers, including in key swing states. Six of the Senate swing seats alone account for more than a fifth of America’s $880bn a year in goods-and-services trade with Canada. But all Americans have suffered from the uncertainty and higher prices brought on by the president’s on-again, off-again tariff policies.
Meanwhile, Mr Trump has shaken business confidence by embracing a litany of other interventionist policies, including securing stakes and even “golden shares” in private companies. The economic results will be even worse if he follows through on promises to expand unsustainable entitlement programmes, order banks to cap credit-card interest rates or impose price controls.
Beyond the economic risks, these policies have frustrated and alienated voters who expected the Republican Party to defend free markets and small government, and to “drain the swamp” following the corruption that swirled around the Biden administration, from the president’s inner circle to his pardon selections (including his own son, Hunter). Between real economic consequences, Democrat-lite rhetoric and administration officials from top to bottom bathing in the swamp rather than draining it, Republican control of the House and possibly the Senate is now in question.
Some voices in the Trump coalition argue that tariffs and a populist agenda are necessary to win elections. The evidence suggests otherwise. Today only 28% of voters approve of the president’s handling of the economy. Yet when his first administration embraced conservative economic policies, 63% did.
Independent conservative voices were widely denounced by Mr Trump’s loudest supporters for even suggesting that the second administration’s tariffs and other trade policies—the largest tax hike in decades, had they come fully into effect—would hurt the economy and the Republicans’ electoral chances. They now stand vindicated. The president is already setting low expectations ahead of the midterms and the knives are out among his closest political advisers.
Mr Trump appointed the justices who overturned Roe v Wade, the 1973 Supreme Court ruling that established a constitutional right to abortion, and pro-lifers rejoiced when Planned Parenthood, a nationwide reproductive-health-care organisation, was defunded. But Congress failed to extend the measure beyond one year, and Planned Parenthood’s taxpayer funding has returned. The president continues to side with Planned Parenthood and the abortion industry against pro-life states that want to restrict access to the chemical abortion pill. Pro-lifers are growing more disenchanted with the Trump administration by the day.
Conservative critics raised the alarm and the administration ignored us—gleefully so at times. Congress ceded its power to the executive and chose not to act.
The one saving grace for Republican candidates may be the Democratic Party’s swift pivot to the socialist left. Republican candidates are rightly criticising these radical and sometimes antisemitic candidates: look no further than Michigan, where the Democratic Senate candidate views Israel’s government as no less evil than Hamas; or New York, where another congressional contender participated in rallies at which protesters celebrated Israeli deaths. Yet their messaging falls flat when the president is offering up $5,000 “Trump dividend” cheques if Republicans win in November and promises to muscle into more private companies. The administration has already taken stakes in 34 companies, most prominently Intel and most recently two critical-minerals groups, Elmet and Hertha Metals.
Mr Trump returned to the White House by contrasting his first-term economy with the high prices and malaise wrought by the Biden administration’s inflationary, anti-growth policies. Then he abandoned his own legacy. The results have been predictable.
■
Marc Short is the chairman of Advancing American Freedom, a campaign group. He was chief of staff to Vice-President Mike Pence from 2019 to 2021 and White House director of legislative affairs from 2017 to 2018.

epub_25.title: Emirati-Saudi rivalry is spurring bloodshed on a horrific scale
epub_25.text:
Emirati-Saudi rivalry is spurring bloodshed on a horrific scale
Briefing
| The petty feud wrecking a region
Emirati-Saudi rivalry is spurring bloodshed on a horrific scale
The rift is prolonging and deepening deadly wars in Sudan, Yemen and elsewhere
Oct 22nd 2026
TO THE EAST of the Arabian peninsula, along the shores of the Persian Gulf, war is simmering, in the form of America’s on-again-off-again conflict with Iran. Iranian missiles have rained down on Arabian cities and infrastructure and continue to menace shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, the peninsula’s economic lifeline. But it is to the west and south, in the countries along the shores of the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, that fighting is really raging.
Yemen’s 12-year-old civil war is spilling beyond its borders, with rocket attacks on ships in the Red Sea and on oil terminals and airports in Saudi Arabia. On the far side of the Red Sea, the civil war in Sudan has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives and forced some 11m of the country’s 50m people from their homes. Farther south, yet another civil war, in Ethiopia, threatens to become a regional one, as forces from Eritrea join the fighting. These wars, in turn, aggravate divisions in neighbouring countries such as Libya and Somalia. It is a vast zone of devastation (see map), with destruction and killing on a scale far exceeding that of the war on Iran, or even the conflicts in Gaza or Ukraine.
The Arabian peninsula’s two biggest powers, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, tried to avert the war in Iran, fearing—rightly, it turns out—that they would get caught in the crossfire. But instead of trying to quell the wars to their south and west, they have fuelled them, taking sides and funnelling support to favoured factions. Extraordinarily, given their similar geopolitical interests, Saudi Arabia and the UAE sometimes support opposing forces in the same conflict, intensifying and entrenching wars that were already grotesquely bloody. Even when they are theoretically on the same side, as in Yemen, the pair often fail to co-operate, helping draw out the misery and bloodshed. Not even the existential threat posed by the war in Iran, which has throttled their oil exports and shredded America’s security umbrella, has convinced the two countries to put their differences aside. Instead, their petty rivalry is abetting the demolition of a vast region of 250m people.
The conflicts in question are vicious. In Yemen, as in Sudan, hundreds of thousands have died and millions have been displaced. The civil war in Ethiopia is on an only slightly smaller scale. All three have involved famine, massacres and other atrocities. Not all this bloodshed stems from Emirati and Saudi meddling by any stretch; all three conflicts reflect long-standing divisions within the countries concerned. Nor are the two Gulf monarchies the only meddlers: Egypt, Israel and Turkey, among others, have eagerly stuck their oars in. Yet the Saudi and especially the Emirati involvement stands out as destabilising and short-sighted.
Saudi Arabia and the UAE could scarcely have more in common. They are neighbours, sharing the same language, religion and culture. They are both wealthy, absolute monarchies whose fortunes depend on the steady export of oil and the steady military support of America. They are both trying to diversify their economies away from hydrocarbons. They both face the same geopolitical threat, a hostile Iran, and the same domestic quandary, keeping their citizens happy without democracy.
Muhammad bin Salman, the crown prince and de facto ruler of Saudi Arabia, and Muhammad bin Zayed, the emir of Abu Dhabi and president of the UAE, also have a lot in common. They are both younger siblings, not initially raised in the expectation that they would rule. They both cast themselves as modernisers, bringing development to their countries. They both fancy themselves as statesmen, wielding influence in their region and beyond.
Perhaps that is why MBS and MBZ, as they are often known, used to get on so well. In 2017, when MBS staged a palace coup at the age of 31 to become ruler of Saudi Arabia in all but name, he had help from MBZ, who had largely taken control of the UAE after his older brother, Khalifa, suffered a debilitating stroke in 2014. The Emiratis worked to promote MBS in America, where many officials had their doubts about the young, impulsive crown prince. Diplomats described the relationship between MBZ and MBS as that of mentor and protégé, or elder and younger brother. They worked together to impose their will on the region, sending troops to Yemen in 2015 and blockading Qatar in 2017.
The mentorship did not last. Cracks began to appear in 2019, when the UAE withdrew some troops from Yemen. More disagreements followed. The Emiratis established ties with Israel in 2020, whereas the Saudis did not. In 2021 they argued over trade barriers, production quotas at the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and a Saudi push for firms to move their regional headquarters to Riyadh, at the expense of the Emirates.
Some of these disagreements endure. Take oil. The Saudis need prices above $90 a barrel to balance the budget and pay for costly schemes to
diversify the economy
. They want OPEC to impose strict production caps to keep prices high. The UAE, in contrast, can balance its budget at around $50 a barrel. It would prefer to sell more oil now, even at lower prices, lest its reserves become worthless in the future. After years of bickering about quotas, the UAE finally left OPEC in April.
Saudi Arabia’s diversification effort has also brought it into competition with the UAE. Both seek to be regional hubs for finance, trade and travel, and big forces in AI and alternative energy. The Emiratis have a decades-long head start, however, and they are keen to keep their edge.
But there is at least as much injured pride as there is substance to the royal rivalry. Saudi Arabia sees itself as the pre-eminent power among the Gulf monarchies. It is the most populous of the six, with more citizens (20m) than the other five combined and by far the biggest economy. This attitude grates on the Emiratis, who have come to see themselves as the Gulf’s real success story: their economy is more diversified, their army more professional and their society more open.
Though court politics are opaque, personal animosity appears to play a part in the Saudi-Emirati rift. Diplomats say the two rulers often go months without speaking. They make a point of avoiding each other’s capitals. MBZ skipped a summit with China’s president in Riyadh in 2022. MBS returned the snub a month later when Arab leaders gathered in Abu Dhabi. In recent years the Emirati leader has visited Azerbaijan more often than Saudi Arabia.
Perhaps the most churlish element of their competition is foreign policy.
A decade ago Saudi Arabia and the UAE were allies fighting the Houthis, a Shia militia that had seized much of Yemen in 2014. They backed different factions in the anti-Houthi camp: the UAE aligned itself with separatists who seek an independent south Yemen, whereas the Saudis backed Islah, an offshoot of the Muslim Brotherhood, and tribal groupings in the north. But they managed to find common cause.
In December, though, the separatists launched an offensive against their supposed allies. The Saudis worried that they might attempt to secede. They eventually pushed the separatists back and forced the UAE to withdraw its troops from Yemen. Now they find themselves battling the Houthis without the UAE, although in recent weeks the Emiratis have hinted that they may rejoin the fight. The Houthis, meanwhile, have been advancing against their divided opponents. This week they killed more than 70 recruits to the Saudi-backed forces in a rocket attack on a training camp. They have also encircled the city of Taiz, trapping some 600,000 civilians with little food or medicine.
Even worse is the damage inflicted on Sudan, where the UAE’s adventurism and Saudi intransigence are prolonging a catastrophic conflict. The number of people killed will never be known, but reports from Darfur, an especially war-torn region, give a sense of the appalling toll. During their siege and eventual capture of the city of el-Fasher last year, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the militia backed by the UAE, slaughtered thousands of civilians. Fighters posted gloating videos of killings on social media. They then dumped the bodies in mass graves to cover up the scale of their crimes and began hunting the
few remaining doctors
in the city lest they reveal what they had seen and heard while treating survivors.
It is hard to square such horror with the Gulf countries’ stated interests in Sudan. The UAE, a rich but small country worried about its reliance on oil, sees the Horn of Africa as a potential economic hinterland. It has made investments all along the Red Sea, including in Djibouti, Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Somaliland. Before the war, the UAE was drawn by Sudan’s ports, precious metals and agricultural land (the UAE imports about 90% of its food).
Saudi Arabia is concerned mainly about instability in Sudan, less than 200 kilometres across the Red Sea at its closest point. It has also invested in agriculture and is keen to preserve trade through Port Sudan. The UAE’s growing role in what it considered its backyard made it nervous.
These concerns have grown more pronounced in recent months as the Iran war has disrupted trade through the Strait of Hormuz. But disagreements between the two Gulf countries shaped the war in Sudan from the very beginning. Initially both supported Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Muhammad Hamdan Dagalo, the two generals who overthrew Sudan’s short-lived civilian government in 2021. The princes, perhaps worried that a successful democratic experiment in Sudan might give their own people ideas, seemed to prefer the military regime.
Yet when the two strongmen began fighting each other in 2023 Saudi Arabia supported the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), led by Mr Burhan. Meanwhile the UAE, concerned about the influence of Islamists in the ranks of the SAF, threw its weight behind Mr Dagalo’s RSF (although it does not publicly admit doing so). That turn of events was not without irony: in 2015 thousands of RSF fighters battled the Houthis in Yemen on behalf of Saudi Arabia. The Saudi payment for the deployment is thought to have helped fund the RSF’s battle against the SAF.
The conflict in Sudan might not have lasted so long were it not for the rift between the two Gulf princes. At the outbreak of the war, America and Saudi Arabia convened talks in the Saudi city of Jeddah to broker a ceasefire. Saudi diplomats, infuriated by the Emirati support for the RSF, refused to invite the UAE to the talks. After being excluded, the UAE redoubled its backing for the RSF, bringing it early successes on the battlefield and encouraging Mr Dagalo to keep fighting.
Since the beginning of the war in Iran, a similarly pernicious dynamic has played out in the other direction. The disruption to traffic in the Strait of Hormuz has sharpened Saudi Arabia’s focus on shoring up stability in the Red Sea and preventing the break-up of Sudan—an outcome that has looked increasingly possible since the RSF declared a parallel government in the Darfur region last year. The Saudi position has shifted from mediating a ceasefire between the SAF and the RSF to supporting the SAF outright, says Kholood Khair of Confluence Advisory, a Sudanese think-tank. Saudi support has probably helped the SAF capture some territory from the RSF in recent months and may explain the army’s intransigent refusal to consider a ceasefire or even talks with the RSF.
The UAE, meanwhile, may also be helping to foment conflict in Ethiopia. A four-year-old peace agreement between the national government and rebels in the northern region of Tigray broke down in September. The rebels are thought to be getting help from Eritrea, Ethiopia’s northern neighbour, whose troops have been spotted on Ethiopian territory. Abiy Ahmed, Ethiopia’s prime minister, would like his landlocked country to regain access to the Red Sea via the ports of Eritrea (which was part of Ethiopia until 1993). There are concerns that he may use Eritrea’s incursion as a justification for an invasion, sparking a full-blown war between the two sides.
If Mr Abiy does so, it will be thanks in part to the steadfast support of the UAE. Since he came to power in 2018, it has sent billions of dollars in financial aid, investment and weapons. In September alone dozens of flights from the UAE landed in Ethiopia, thought to be carrying supplies for the campaign in Tigray.
Eritrea, meanwhile, has been trying to secure Saudi Arabia’s backing. Issaias Afwerki, Eritrea’s dictator, has held several rounds of talks with Saudi officials. The Saudis have thus far demurred. But the RSF is now being accused of using Ethiopian territory to launch attacks in Sudan. That has angered the SAF, which might back Eritrea if Ethiopia attacks, potentially merging the two wars. In contrast, if MBS and MBZ were to reconcile, they might be able to exert pressure on the warring parties to settle their differences.
An equally unfortunate dynamic appears to be in motion in Somalia. The UAE’s close ties to Somaliland, a breakaway province, and other regions run by secessionists have caused a rift with the beleaguered national government, which is courting Saudi Arabia as a counterweight. In the meantime, there are reports of strengthening links between the Houthis and the jihadists of al-Shabab, who are battling both national and provincial forces in Somalia. The Emiratis’ short-sighted factionalism, in other words, is certainly not helping to end Somalia’s civil war and may in fact be exacerbating it.
Each individual decision that embroiled the UAE and Saudi Arabia in these many conflicts and then gradually pitted them against one another may have seemed rational enough at the time. But the results clearly do not serve either country’s interests. The region on their doorstep is poorer, more unstable and more violent than when their interventions began. It presents fewer opportunities for investment and more potential for unwelcome spillovers, of refugees or violence. Their meddling generates ill-will between the pair at a time when their overriding concern should be co-operating to counter the menace of Iran. And it generates untold misery for the 250m people around whom the region’s wars are intensifying.

epub_27.title: Indonesia’s experiment with populism is wavering
epub_27.text:
Indonesia’s experiment with populism is wavering
Asia
| Politics of the street
Indonesia’s experiment with populism is wavering
How will Prabowo Subianto respond to crashing approval ratings?
Oct 22nd 2026
HAFIDZ HERNANDA was riding down a quiet street in Jakarta, Indonesia’s capital, close to midnight on October 4th when another motorcyclist kicked his bike, knocking him to the ground. Two more men joined the attack as the assailant beat Mr Hafidz and threatened to kill him. Afterwards they took his phone and bag, robbery seemingly an afterthought. The police say they are investigating, but no suspects have been identified.
The assault was notable because Mr Hafidz has become one of the highest-profile organisers against President Prabowo Subianto, leading two protests by students against
his policies
earlier this year. On the night of the assault he was riding back to his home near the University of Indonesia from a meeting with other student activists at a roadside eatery. There, they had been planning a demonstration against Mr Prabowo on October 20th, the second anniversary of his inauguration.
It was a protest that the administration desperately sought to prevent from going ahead. In the days after the attack on Mr Hafidz, army and police officers pleaded with students to stay at home. One activist says he was offered a bribe if he could persuade students not to hit the streets. On the morning of the anniversary, police said they had deployed 9,500 officers to keep demonstrators in line. If that was intended to intimidate them, it seems to have worked. Only a few hundred hardy students gathered in central Jakarta to demand that Mr Prabowo do something about high prices and what they call a long list of failures of
his administration
.
Mr Prabowo, whose father-in-law, the dictator Suharto, lost power amid mass demonstrations in 1998, has long had a fear of the street. That anxiety was reinforced in August 2025 when protests by students and workers against corruption and police brutality led to days of unrest and calls for broader political reforms. At the time, Mr Prabowo called a press conference where he gave in to some of their demands. He later watered down his promises after the protests died down.
But that was when Mr Prabowo still enjoyed unprecedented popularity, with 81% of those surveyed in November 2025 telling pollsters that they approved of the job he was doing. Since then, his approval ratings have seen record declines. In a survey released on October 16th, only 45% said they were satisfied with his performance. That figure would be the envy of many Western leaders, but in Indonesia—where, for cultural reasons, many respondents are shy about being too damning in responses to pollsters—it is near historic lows.
Those who disapprove of Mr Prabowo’s performance mostly cite higher prices for necessities, not his heavy-handed approach to politics, as the reason for their dissatisfaction. America’s war against Iran has driven up the cost of importing fuel, while
a strong El Niño
is driving agricultural yields down. The prices of staples have soared. Bird’s-eye chillies, which give Indonesian food its kick, have risen by 76.5% compared with a year ago. The prices of chickens, eggs and rice are all up, too. But the drivers of inflation, the war and the weather, are out of Mr Prabowo’s control.
That leaves the president in a bind. He could double down on the expensive populist programmes that have become his hallmark in office, like his “free nutritious meals” scheme and a network of 80,000 state-run village co-operatives. The former had been curtailed this year so as to fund expensive petrol subsidies popular with voters. Mr Prabowo might try to win back his former supporters by ramping the free meals programme up again. But surveys also suggest that Mr Prabowo’s signature programmes are less popular than before.
New handouts may therefore follow. On October 13th the president’s influential younger brother, Hashim Djojohadikusumo, proposed that every citizen be given a free mobile phone. Linked to a free bank account, the phones would bring Indonesia’s unbanked into the formal financial system, he argued. It would also, no doubt, endear Mr Prabowo to many voters.
Another possibility is that a less popular Mr Prabowo will crack down on dissent and political opposition. There is no clear evidence that Mr Hafidz’s assault was directed by his administration, but that has not stopped activists from implying that it was. The possibility is hard to dismiss, given Mr Prabowo’s past. As a special-forces commander under Suharto, Mr Prabowo kidnapped dozens of student activists in 1997 and 1998. He admits doing so and says he returned them all unharmed. But some were never heard from again.
The street is not the only source of opposition to the president. Foreign investors and local tycoons are turning against him, too. The
main stock-market index
sank by nearly 12% on October 16th and is down by 40% so far this year, making it the world’s worst performer—and indeed, in the two years since his inauguration. Foreign capital is fleeing what was once a promising emerging market. Investors blame regulatory uncertainty and a lack of transparency. Local tycoons, particularly those who are ethnically Chinese, say they fear shakedowns by Mr Prabowo’s lieutenants. They have been stashing money abroad rather than investing it at home.
The turmoil has united political-party bosses quietly eyeing moves against the president. The most concerning for Mr Prabowo must be the signs of a rift with his predecessor, Joko Widodo. The two were once rivals but teamed up in the 2024 election, when Gibran Rakabuming Raka, Mr Widodo’s son, joined Mr Prabowo’s presidential ticket as his running mate. That gave them a landslide victory. A falling-out between the two would make any prospect of winning a second term at the next election, in 2029, a fantasy. Kevin O’Rourke of “Reformasi Weekly”, a newsletter, says that if Mr Prabowo’s poll numbers remain so low, he may not risk facing the voters.
Instead, he could amend the constitution to end direct presidential elections. Parliament would select the president and vice-president, as was the case until 2004, letting Mr Prabowo avoid a referendum on his performance and win a second term through backdoor deals. But to do so would surely spark the kind of street protests he seems so desperate to avoid.
■
