epub_28.title: Tackling stray dogs in Bhutan
epub_28.text:
Tackling stray dogs in Bhutan
Asia
| Rabid result
Tackling stray dogs in Bhutan
A lively campaign in a small country shows what to do
Oct 22nd 2026
CROSS FROM India into Bhutan at Jomotshangkha and little seems to change. The same hills stretch across the border, roadside shops sell mostly identical wares and similar-looking dogs laze on the streets. Yet the observant visitor may notice one difference: the dogs on Bhutan’s side have notched ears.
Those marks signify sterilisation and vaccination against rabies. The tiny Himalayan kingdom has sterilised its entire stray-dog population. With mass vaccination and free treatment for people who’ve been bitten, this has helped eliminate human rabies carried by dogs, making Bhutan just one of three countries to do so. The disease, a global scourge, is especially deadly in South Asia. In India rabies kills some 5,700 people a year, by one estimate. Bhutan’s last human death from it was in 2023.
Like its much bigger neighbours, Bhutan has long grappled with stray mutts. In the 1980s marksmen used dart-guns from the UN’s World Health Organisation to shoot dogs in public. In some places dogs were fed raw meat laced with strychnine. The campaign appalled Bhutan’s people, most of whom are Buddhist. Nor did it work: dog numbers kept rising.
From 2009 the government switched to a gentler approach. Dogs were caught, neutered, vaccinated and released. But implementation was patchy. Over nine years some 92,000 animals were treated, but vaccination rates never got close to the 70% needed to break transmission. It took a royal decree to give the campaign bite as well as bark. In 2021 the king ordered “a professional, humane and compassionate sterilisation of the entire free-roaming dog population”. Some 9,000 members of De-suung, a national volunteer corps, helped count the dogs, keep records and stir up communities. In under two years vaccinations hit 90%.
Other Asian countries should take note. The scale of the problem in places like Bangladesh and India,  which host millions of stray dogs, many of them rabid, may seem daunting. But local governments could follow Bhutan’s example, pooling resources and tackling the problem one area at a time.

epub_29.title: America’s attack on the International Criminal Court is a headache for Japan
epub_29.text:
America’s attack on the International Criminal Court is a headache for Japan
Asia
| Regrets, she’s got a few
America’s attack on the International Criminal Court is a headache for Japan
It’s hard to support international law when your main ally wants to destroy it
Oct 22nd 2026
AKANE TOMOKO was on holiday back home in Japan when she learned that Russia wanted to arrest her. At the time, in 2023, Ms Akane was a judge at the International Criminal Court (ICC), which had recently issued an arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin. Russia was retaliating. But she wasn’t too fussed, she recalled in a book last year, after she had become the court’s president. What really worried her was a more existential danger: that sanctions might be imposed by America, which, like Russia, has never recognised the ICC’s jurisdiction. Several judges had already been put under American sanctions earlier that year. The worst-case scenario would be sanctions on the court itself, she wrote. “The ICC would essentially be shut down.”
That scenario is now coming true. On October 9th Marco Rubio, America’s secretary of state, announced the latest stage of a campaign to “dismantle the ICC, brick by brick”. The Trump administration says the ICC is threatening American sovereignty because it claims the power to investigate and prosecute American citizens for war crimes or crimes against humanity committed on ICC member states’ territory. The sanctions freeze ICC assets in America and block American firms and banks from engaging with the court. They will take effect after 180 days, a period during which Mr Rubio expects member states to rein in the court.
This puts Japan in a quandary. It is the largest funder of the ICC, contributing 15% of its budget. And for decades Japan has made the international rule of law a pillar of its foreign policy. But Japan also depends on America for its security; so the government was muted in its initial response when Ms Akane herself was put under sanction in August. Takaichi Sanae, the prime minister, said the sanctions were taihen zannen, “very regrettable”; but she pointedly did not call for their withdrawal.
Her careful wording sparked a backlash. Nakatani Gen, a former defence minister from Ms Takaichi’s party who now heads a cross-party group focused on human rights, accused her of being “docile and not saying what needs to be said at a crucial time”. In Nagoya, where Ms Akane taught law in 2005-08, her former students have gathered more than 174,000 signatures in her support. “It’s not idealism for Japan, it’s security,” says Shamoto Yosuke, one of them. “Japan cannot rely on military power alone to protect itself. That is why we need an international order based on rules, not just power.”
Since then Ms Takaichi has been bolder, calling the sanctions incompatible with Japanese policy. She raised the issue with Mr Trump in New York in September. After the latest sanctions, Japan signed a joint statement in support of the court with other ICC members, including all G7 countries bar America. Some suggest that Japan could discuss ICC reform over matters of jurisdiction to appease Mr Trump. But talk is unlikely to change his administration’s position. A better use of the 180 days, suggests Christopher Lamont of Tokyo International University, would be to plan how to keep the court running: by setting up funding that isn’t exposed to the American financial system, for instance.
This, though, could anger America further. Japan does not want to choose between two components of its security, one based on international law and the other on American protection. Regrettably, it is being pushed to do so.

epub_30.title: India is pouring money and concrete into its border with China
epub_30.text:
India is pouring money and concrete into its border with China
Asia
| The road to deterrence
India is pouring money and concrete into its border with China
Can roads and villages secure a state that China claims?
Oct 22nd 2026
JUST 10km from India’s north-eastern border with China, the village of Zemithang lies in the heart of territory claimed by the Chinese. Everyday life feels unmistakably Indian. Locals chat in Hindi, listen to Bollywood songs and fly Indian flags. But occasionally there is an unwanted Chinese presence. “My phone keeps changing to Beijing time [two and a half hours ahead], because I lose my Indian network and pick up the Chinese one,” says a local official. His complaint captures the challenge facing India as it tries to transform its remote frontier, and match a massive infrastructure roll-out on the other side.
India is pouring concrete and money into Zemithang and other parts of Arunachal Pradesh (AP) to strengthen its hold over the Himalayan state. Home to fewer than 2m people, it is claimed by China, which calls it Zangnan, or southern Tibet. The state was also the main theatre of the only war between the two countries. In 1962 Chinese soldiers descended through the mountains, overran Indian forces and occupied parts of it. They eventually withdrew, but the defeat has ensured that relations have been edgy ever since.
Today the frontier is far calmer. The two armies face each other across the “line of actual control”, a disputed border that runs through spectacular mountains and valleys (see map). Barring a few scuffles, there has been no clash in AP since 1975. Even during hand-to-hand fighting in 2020 between Indian and Chinese troops in Galwan, 1,500km to the west, the border in AP remained quiet. But this is an ugly stability, says Ajai Shukla, a security analyst based in Delhi. The road to the border on the Indian side is lined with military camps: an estimated 90,000-120,000 troops are deployed in the region. In August local political groups alleged there had been Chinese intrusions near Taksing, in eastern AP, though India’s government dismissed the reports as rumours.
The fiercest contest is over infrastructure. For decades Indian officials eschewed building roads in AP, fearing it would give an invading Chinese army an easier route south. That is now considered a mistake: poor connectivity hindered India’s ability to supply its own troops and kept its citizens isolated. Meanwhile China built an extensive network of roads on its side, as well as hundreds of “dual-use” villages that combine civilian settlements with military infrastructure.
India is rushing to make amends. “Until the clashes in Galwan, India assumed that the relationship with China would improve in a linear fashion. That incident was a real wake-up call,” says Jabin Jacob of Shiv Nadar University. These days India regards connectivity as essential to deterrence. Much of the work is led by the defence ministry’s road-building arm, which has constructed hundreds of kilometres of roads in the region, including the Sela Tunnel, which keeps Tawang, the biggest town in the area, accessible even during winter.
The building drive extends far beyond roads. AP’s rivers have huge hydropower potential. To harness it, India is planning several dams, including its biggest-ever on the Upper Siang river. Securing the border also involves breathing more life into the settlements near it. Indian officials have become increasingly alarmed by satellite images revealing the rapid expansion of Chinese border villages. In 2023 the Indian government launched the Vibrant Villages Programme. Around 27bn rupees ($286m) has been set aside for projects in the state, 6% of the state’s GDP.
The aim is to stem migration from the region, draw people in, and improve administration. Much of the focus is on construction. But the army is also helping to turn the area into a tourist attraction (for Indians only), offering visitors access to border posts and history lessons on the 1962 war. At Bum La pass, at around 4,600 metres, soldiers accompany tourist groups right up to the frontier and lead chants of “Bharat Mata ki Jai” (”Victory to Mother India”) while facing the Chinese side.
All this is welcomed. The state has always been one of India’s poorer and more isolated corners, but in 2024-25 (the latest year for which data are available) its economy grew by 10%, the third-fastest rate in the country. Still, residents crave more development and of better quality. Locals fret that funding takes too long to arrive and gets tangled in bureaucracy.
Such complaints reflect the chasm between China and India that shapes their rivalry. China enjoys greater economic and military resources and also the advantage of unfettered state capacity. It is said to have forcibly relocated people to border villages. The Indians, meanwhile, must contend with local concerns—such as opposition to the construction of dams.

epub_31.title: Indians’ rights have been chipped away for decades
epub_31.text:
Indians’ rights have been chipped away for decades
Asia
| Ashoka
Indians’ rights have been chipped away for decades
But interfering with the sanctity of elections is a step too far
Oct 22nd 2026
THE CONSTITUTION of India is filled with all sorts of noble ideas. The preamble promises every citizen justice, liberty and equality, to say nothing of dignity. The body lays out a dizzying array of institutions designed to secure those rights. And then, almost as soon as the ink had dried on the document, India’s new leaders started having second thoughts. The first amendment to the constitution imposed “reasonable restrictions” on the right to
free speech
. The 24th made explicit that Parliament can alter even the parts about fundamental rights. Things reached a nadir with the 42nd amendment, passed in 1976 during a state of emergency imposed by Indira Gandhi, when, not satisfied with further curtailing Indians’ rights, Parliament also created something called “fundamental duties”.
The Emergency eventually ended. But the chipping away of rights did not. Successive governments have kneecapped or subverted independent institutions. Narendra Modi has continued this cross-party tradition since coming to power in 2014. Under his rule investigative agencies are seen by many as the enforcement arm of his Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), Parliament has frequently resembled a rubber stamp, and the courts have become curiously uninterested in upholding individual liberty. Indians, for the most part, have turned a blind eye. For the vast majority, there are more pressing concerns.
Yet there is one right Indians take with deadly seriousness. That is the right to vote. Every five years they march to the polls to express approval or frustration in vast elections that are widely considered free and fair. In the interim politicians rule with imperiousness, pretend that voters don’t exist and help themselves to public money. Fine. So long as citizens believe they have the power to punish their rulers come election day, they will put up with a lot. This is the essence of India’s social contract.
The sense that it is being violated is why the latest protests against Mr Modi’s government have touched a nerve. Some 130m of the country’s nearly 1bn registered voters have been struck off electoral lists in a “special intensive revision” that the government says is necessary to “purify” the rolls of duplicates and the dead. Critics say it has
disenfranchised
millions of citizens, perhaps tens of millions. Both of these things may well be true. Last month the Indian Express, a newspaper, revealed that two of the three commissioners of the supposedly independent Election Commission of India had objected at least 14 times to decisions taken under its chief, Gyanesh Kumar. The commission denied this. But protesters have spent much of October on the streets demanding his resignation, painting him as a BJP stooge.
Well before the special revision the BJP had in state after state used sleazy political tactics and its control of institutions to break up rival parties and lure away their lawmakers. Voters accepted that, just as they once accepted armed men routinely capturing polling booths and stuffing ballots in the more lawless parts of the country. And just as they still accept rampant vote-buying, both legal (cash handouts from the state) and illegal (cash handouts from candidates). All of this is seen as part of the game. Under dispute now is the much more fundamental question of whether the game itself is fixed.
India’s political class should consider itself lucky. In next-door China, the Communist Party has to do something much more difficult than winning elections. China’s social contract requires the state to consistently raise living standards, the quality of life and national power in exchange for which citizens keep their noses out of politics. All Indian politicians have to do is to feign interest in their constituents once every five years. Yet instead of accepting this sweetheart deal, Mr Modi’s government is doubling down by suppressing protests that are attempting to enforce it.
Anyone who has ever set foot in an Indian kitchen will be familiar with the pressure cooker, a terrifying contraption that lets out an almighty shriek to vent its accumulated steam at predictable intervals, not unlike an election cycle. If that usual outlet is blocked, however, one of two things can happen. A safety valve breaks, letting loose a paroxysm of scalding steam everywhere. Or the pressure grows—and grows and grows—until there is a catastrophic structural failure. It is to prevent precisely such an explosion that India’s founders added safety valves to the constitution. To block them all is not just dangerous. It is foolish.

epub_33.title: China’s universities are rich. But they're getting squeezed
epub_33.text:
China’s universities are rich. But they're getting squeezed
China
| Stressed universities
China’s universities are rich. But they're getting squeezed
Researchers can’t escape a bleak economy
Oct 22nd 2026
In its competition with China, America sometimes commits self-sabotage. Under Donald Trump, cuts in federal support for universities have been particularly damaging. To convey their anguish, some American scientists have drawn attention to the advantage that their country’s strategic rival may gain from these retrenchments. China has been handed the future “on a silver platter”, complained one academic from Harvard University last year.
In China there is plenty of funding for academics who are engaged in cutting-edge research in fields favoured by the Communist Party such as artificial intelligence and robotics. But the Harvard academic may be surprised to learn that on many campuses, the mood among staff is sullen. Eager though the party is to promote scientific endeavour, it is becoming more selective about who gets the state’s cash. In April the education ministry said that it had revoked 12,200 degree programmes in recent years, mainly in soft subjects such as “business management”, replacing many with majors in AI and other sciences that are the party’s priorities.
But departments involved in subjects such as physics and chemistry are also feeling the pinch. This decade’s spending by central and local governments on science and technology has grown annually at just 3.5%, slumping from 10% in the late 2010s. Such outlays cover everything from museums to social sciences, but government spending on natural-science departments is also growing more slowly. Some university budgets are being cut. In September Peking University in Beijing was one of several to issue new orders to “practise thrift and tighten belts”. At some institutions researchers’ pay and perks are being reduced.
Since the 1990s China’s universities have expanded rapidly and the living conditions of academic staff have become far more comfortable. The international stature of the country’s universities has also soared. In 2017 just two of them were among the world’s top 100, according to Times Higher Education, a British magazine. This year eight were, including Tsinghua University and Peking University which ranked 11th and 13th globally—the highest of any in Asia.
To Chinese academics who have long been used to good times, the belt-tightening has come as a painful shock. Even some of the country’s 75 elite universities, which are funded by the central government, are being squeezed. Their median budget grew 6.8% this year, but one in five suffered cuts. Some have more than halved the number and value of scholarships for postgraduate programmes.
China’s weaker economy is in part to blame. Other than top-tier ones, many universities depend heavily on financing from local governments whose budgets are being crimped by a prolonged slump in the property market. Local authorities are responsible for 95% of the country’s 2,900 universities. Documents reviewed by The Economist show that even in Shenzhen and Hangzhou, both big hubs of party-backed tech, universities have had their budgets cut by more than 5% this year.
The economy is still growing at 4.5%. But it cannot create enough new jobs to absorb record numbers of graduates: youth unemployment is 19%. So more are staying on campus. The annual intake of doctoral students has nearly doubled since 2019 to 200,000. Those who remain in academia have to compete for shrinking shares of government money. Post-doctoral work has become insecure and, as one academic puts it, requirements for promotion are turning “inhumane”.
Academics often need a grant to move up the ladder. Since 2021 applications to the main grant programme of the National Natural Science Foundation of China—the principal source of central-government funding for sciences—have risen by 80% to 200,000 (see chart). But the amount disbursed has climbed by only 3%. Success rates for applications fell from 22% in 2013 to 12% last year. This year the foundation has boosted handouts to young researchers by 50%—in part, maybe, to assuage their discontent.
Restoring happiness will be difficult. Increasingly, universities are adopting Western styles of employment, with academics often having to labour for years before being granted a permanent job, says Qiang Zha of York University. Some complain that, because of tighter budgets, universities are hiring junior staff to bolster research with no intention of giving them a permanent place. Getting a job or promotion in academia is now such a struggle that many quit. Shenzhen Middle School employs more than 100 staff with PhDs.
As the party’s main mouthpiece, People’s Daily, pointed out last month, China’s universities are not “running out of money”. In aggregate, at least, they are getting more: spending on university research rose by 11% last year, to 341bn yuan ($47bn), according to official figures. But companies, including non-state ones, are providing a growing share of that cash. In 2024, the most recent year for which data exist, they supplied half of new funding for research at universities. But they have little interest in supporting scholarship that is unlikely to nurture the talent and technologies that will help them commercially. And they prefer well-funded big-name universities.
There may be some benefit in tight-fistedness. When China’s universities were rapidly expanding, promotion was often linked to the quantity of material published rather than quality, says Yu Xie of Princeton, who also runs a centre at Peking University. Now money-conscious universities have to be more discerning and produce more breakthroughs.
But, as one academic notes, the pressure to publish papers creates an incentive for fraud. “Paper mills” advertise their services on popular e-commerce sites such as Taobao. Some researchers have been caught paying bribes to get their work published. Online sleuths (including dropouts from doctoral study) have been ferreting out academic malfeasance in order to topple professors from their posts. A few provincial governments are investigating a practice whereby academics pay companies to fund their research to meet grant quotas for promotion. In a small government survey, one-fifth of respondents admitted to the practice.
Junior academics mostly grind away at their research with poor prospects for long-term employment. Some, however, will climb to the top of the academic pile. As it does in the country’s export sector, ferocious competition can help produce champion ideas.
■

epub_34.title: China wants to revive the spirit of the Long March
epub_34.text:
China wants to revive the spirit of the Long March
China
| The Long March
China wants to revive the spirit of the Long March
That means keeping in lockstep with Xi Jinping
Oct 22nd 2026
It is a story of “perseverance, solidarity and hope”. So claims an English-language documentary released by China’s state media this month to mark the 90th anniversary of the official end of the Long March: the famously gruelling retreat by embattled Communists during China’s civil war. The two foreign presenters of the series retrace small sections of the thousands of miles the Communist Party covered, spouting platitudes along the way. “Not only did we see history, we also saw the future,” says one, marvelling at the skyscrapers and data centres that have sprouted in the once-remote regions the Red Army marched through. “There will always be people marching on the road to hope,” sighs the other, in the last episode.
Some may find this more than a little mushy. Luckily China released a second and more interesting documentary on the Long March this month, intended for domestic audiences. Called “The Great Expedition”, it was co-produced by China’s armed forces and broadcast to much fanfare on state television. It also celebrates China’s modernisation since the dark days of the 1930s. But it makes this point with muscular footage of tanks, missiles and helicopters. And the documentary’s takeaway is less guff about hope and more about the need for absolute loyalty to the party and its leader.
A central focus of “The Great Expedition” is Mao Zedong and his clashes with other Communists along the Long March, like Bo Gu, a Soviet-trained revolutionary, Otto Braun, a German adviser, and Zhang Guotao, a rival general. They had various disagreements with Mao over military strategy. But as the documentary relates with some relish, Mao was proved correct again and again. Bo and Braun were stripped of their command early in 1935; a little later Zhang dared to set up his own Central Committee (the party’s
governing body
) and led his troops in a different direction from the one suggested by Mao. Zhang was humiliated after a catastrophic battle; the documentary camera pans out over the graves of his soldiers.
On social media, one enthusiastic reviewer summarised the key message: “When you’re unsure what to do, look to Mao; when you encounter difficulties, look to him again.” The implication for today’s party members is pretty clear. Footage of Mao’s successor, Xi Jinping, appears in the first few minutes of every episode. The documentary should, according to state media, “guide and inspire the entire party and the entire army…to unite more closely around the Central Committee with comrade Xi Jinping at its core”.
Many of the party’s 100m members will watch “The Great Expedition”, if they know what is good for them. It has been put on a party app called Xuexi Qiangguo, which means both “Study the Strong Country” and “Study Xi to Make the Country Strong”. Party members’ usage of the app is tracked; they must log in daily. Soldiers, especially, should be keen viewers. Scores of generals have been purged in recent years for disloyalty. As Mr Xi has said: “Each generation has its own Long March.” Everyone should stay in step on his.

epub_35.title: China’s party elite gathers with purges and promotions in mind
epub_35.text:
China’s party elite gathers with purges and promotions in mind
China
| The fifth plenum
China’s party elite gathers with purges and promotions in mind
Xi seeks new ways to curb corruption before a leadership shake-up
Oct 22nd 2026
“Off-sites” at hotels are among the more sorrowful features of modern working life. Who does not dread the awkward conversation over the breakfast buffet, the unexpected grilling from the boss during a presentation or the struggle to stay awake through the post-lunch carb crash? Spare a thought, then, for the 300 or so members of the Chinese Communist Party’s Central Committee who will soon attend one of the most brutal gatherings of the genre. The Soviet-style Jingxi Hotel in Beijing, where it takes place roughly once a year, is run by the armed forces. Mobile phones are thought to be banned, as are alcohol and cigarettes. Participants have to assume that every word is recorded by note-takers or bugs.
The “fifth plenum”, to be held from October 26th to 29th, will be especially fraught. It comes about one year before a quinquennial congress that is expected to give Xi Jinping a fourth term as the party’s leader. That means that he and other party bigwigs will be scrutinising potential candidates for promotion next year to the top decision-making bodies: the Politburo and its (now seven-strong) Standing Committee. What’s more, the theme of this year’s plenum is “full ​and rigorous party self-governance”—in other words, combating the corruption and indiscipline that continue to frustrate Mr Xi. So attendees’ personal conduct will be examined even more closely than usual.
Mr Xi might also spring a surprise, perhaps by floating proposals to adopt a new title such as party chairman (held by Mao Zedong). A plenum in 2016, also a year before a congress, established Mr Xi as the party’s “core leader”. That paved the way for him to scrap term limits on the presidency. And a year before a congress in 2022 another plenum further elevated his authority by granting his political doctrine equal status to those of Mao, Communist China’s founder, and Deng Xiaoping, the architect of reforms that began in 1979.
The plenum’s precise mechanics are secret. But based on limited official accounts of previous ones, it will start with Mr Xi delivering a report from the Politburo on its work over the preceding year. Next he will make a speech explaining the main item on the plenum’s agenda, in this case a “decision” on party self-governance. Participants are then expected to divide into about ten groups to discuss the report and the proposed decision. These breakout sessions usually include one each for military delegates, regional leaders and the chiefs of state-owned enterprises.
In the past the smaller meetings have sometimes involved fierce debate over ideology or policy. Not so under Mr Xi. Each delegate is expected to express approval of the party chief’s leadership, the Politburo’s report and the decision. But they must try to do so in pithy, creative terms while heeding Mr Xi’s increasingly dire warnings against self-promotion, flattery or performative parroting of party slogans. If they strike the right balance they might hope to get their remarks included in the note-takers’ summary of discussions, which is thought to be sent to top leaders at the end of each day. Better still is to catch the eye of Mr Xi, who usually drops into group talks in person along with other Standing Committee members.
On the last day the delegates reconvene and vote (unanimously, unless they are intent on career suicide) to confirm the expulsion of purged Central Committee members and to appoint replacements. That could reveal fresh victims of Mr Xi’s purges, which have already ensnared some 20 full members of this Central Committee, including three in the Politburo. Some of the committee’s members have already been replaced, leaving eight empty seats. Another 15 could be expelled, reckons the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI), a think-tank in New York.
There could be signs that others are in trouble if they do not attend or are not promoted. And there may be new appointments to the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces (although that normally happens at a congress). The commission currently has just two members—Mr Xi and a general—following a purge of the other five.
Participants then vote (unanimously again) to approve the decision on party governance. It is expected to reinforce anti-corruption work with measures including closer oversight of government spending, enhanced use of big data and more accountability for officials whose subordinates break the party’s rules. It might also bolster the power of bodies that investigate errant officials. In a speech published (with omissions) on October 15th, Mr Xi said the party needed to “confine power to a cage of institutions”. He cited threats including “nice guys” who ignore problems, “two-faced” officials who secretly hold liberal views, and a “revolving door” between business and government.
Mr Xi’s goal appears to be to win support among the elite for his next five-year term and his quest to revitalise the party. If so, he is also revealing the limits of his powers to implement change, suggest Neil Thomas, Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang of ASPI. In a recent paper they compare Mr Xi to a Leninist Logan Roy, a patriarchal character in the TV series “Succession”. Like Logan, Mr Xi “presides over an enormous enterprise, exercises commanding authority and remains perpetually disappointed by the people expected to carry out his wishes”. In Mr Xi’s view, they add, there is only one model of diligence to emulate: that of his own younger self.

epub_36.title: Does China really prize AI speed over safety?
epub_36.text:
Does China really prize AI speed over safety?
China
| Chaguan
Does China really prize AI speed over safety?
In full command of its own cyberspace, China wants the same for AI
Oct 22nd 2026
“Guard the golden three seconds, guard your wallet.” In recent weeks a video of an avuncular policeman, Guo Tao, delivering this message—a warning about how to handle fraudsters on the phone—has spread widely in China. All it takes is a simple greeting for criminals to capture one’s voice and then use artificial intelligence to synthesise it for duping friends and relatives. So, as Mr Guo says, it is best to stay silent for three seconds when called from unknown numbers, to see if a real person speaks. Not bad advice. It also relates to one of the tech world’s most pressing questions: what does China think about the risks posed by AI?
Many observers believe China does not care much about the dangers. Donald Trump is one. “China will be doing absolutely nothing to stand in the way of AI,” he claimed last month, explaining his own disdain for regulation. Indeed, surveys point to overwhelming Chinese optimism about AI. In a poll by Gallup, 93% of respondents in China said it would mostly help their country, versus just 36% in America. Calls for China to work with America to slow down frontier models have been brushed aside in Beijing. “Fearmongering” serves no one, says China’s foreign ministry.
In fact, China spends an awful lot of time thinking about AI safety. Telephone fraud is just the tip of an iceberg of anxieties. China’s concerns run from criminal activity, labour displacement and national security to, yes, the loss-of-control scenarios causing sleepless nights in Silicon Valley.
This should not be surprising. The Communist Party, which obsesses about danger in almost every domain of life, has fought for years to bring cyberspace under control. Is a regime that views the internet as an existential challenge suddenly about to let AI rip? If, as in the Trump administration, one defines regulation as intrinsically a form of slowdown, then China is, in effect, slowing AI—though it would never say so. “China already has the most stringent AI rules anywhere in the world,” says Kendra Schaefer of Trivium, a consultancy based in Beijing.
The foundational document is China’s framework for the governance of AI safety. A second update came out in September. It lists 54 risks under three categories: “inherent” (models behaving in unintended ways), “application” (use by criminals) and “secondary” (social alienation). It also proposes ways to eliminate or, at least, mitigate these threats. One is to require checkpoints at which humans (remember those?) must review and, if necessary, halt AI agents before they roam too widely.
Some of the framework’s earlier ideas are already in force—for instance, AI-generated content such as audio and video must be clearly labelled. Others are likely to form the basis of new rules. Draft measures call for service providers to shut down any feature with serious problems immediately. On October 16th China also proposed curbs on exports of its most advanced AI technologies.
As AI has grown more powerful, China has paid more attention to doomsday possibilities. The original version of its safety framework, issued in 2024, made just one glancing reference to loss of control. In the newest version, that topic comes up more than a dozen times. Even so, it is possible to discern a philosophical gap. Whereas some in America fear that AI models will eventually surpass human intelligence and take control of their own evolution, the more common view in China is that AI is a transformative technology that can be harnessed and directed, not something that will slip human grasp.
Xi Jinping compares AI to the steam engine, electricity and the internet—technologies that were epoch-shaping but did not pose dangers that required a co-ordinated slowdown. With China still trailing America at the frontier of AI, Mr Xi is all the less inclined to agree to apply the brakes. As China sees it, such an agreement looks both unnecessary and self-serving for Americans.
Unsurprisingly, Chinese officials devote much bandwidth to ideology. They want to ensure that models do not contradict the party on important matters, and that new tools do not undermine its control. Yet there are more banal concerns, too, reflecting the soft paternalism of the Chinese state. Hence Mr Guo’s three golden seconds on the phone and a ban on offering virtual lovers or, for that matter, virtual relatives to minors.
China’s yen for rules may have an unintended effect. In America, where the government has a much lighter touch, companies have stepped into the breach, evaluating their own models and asking for more guardrails. In China firms are often more passive, waiting for directions from the party and government before applying controls. A review by Concordia AI, a consultancy in Beijing, of ten Chinese firms with recently released models found that just five had published safety evaluations. That suggests possible perils if models develop faster than regulators expect.
China’s rules will also fail to impress those who view its open-weight models as unavoidably dangerous. Critics fret that such models, unlike the closed ones dominant in America, can be abused more readily. Yet many in Chinese AI argue the benefits outweigh that hazard: they note that China’s open models have helped defend computer systems from rogue attacks launched by American closed models, as when OpenAI tools breached Hugging Face, an AI platform. In any case, China is already working on tougher rules to govern open models. Insiders say that new releases face exacting safety reviews before being offered to the public.
By most measures China’s AI models are a few months, or more, behind America’s in their performance. That is a big gap for such a fast-evolving technology. But do not accuse China of lagging behind America in its management of risks. When it comes to rules, controls, limits and warnings, China is in its element.

epub_38.title: Republicans’ identity crisis in Texas
epub_38.text:
Republicans’ identity crisis in Texas
United States
| Midterms maths
Republicans’ identity crisis in Texas
The old campaign messages aren’t working and the new ones are risky
Oct 22nd 2026
REPUBLICANS IN AMERICA’S biggest red state don’t usually have to play defence. But less than two weeks before election day, they are panicking.
Ken Paxton
, the scandal-plagued Senate candidate, is trailing James Talarico in the polls. Since early September, national Republicans have poured about $200m into ads in a bid to save his campaign—and their Senate majority. Greg Abbott, Texas’s three-term governor, has won past elections by double digits, but this year is being forced to fend off a Democratic challenger, Gina Hinojosa, outspending her six-to-one over the summer. “We’re worried about Texas,” Donald Trump admitted early this month.
Mr Paxton is a uniquely bad candidate, dogged by investigations and marital infidelity. But he is not Republicans’ only problem in Texas.
Latinos
in South Texas, who swung to Mr Trump in 2024, now appear to be drifting left; soccer moms in the suburbs of Dallas and Houston are tired of the president’s rancour. After more than two decades of unbroken rule, Texas Republicans are struggling to find a winning message—old campaign lines aren’t working and the party is trying to whip up the base by questioning if foreigners belong. Even if the party hangs on to power in Texas on November 3rd, its grip is loosening.
Like Republican candidates elsewhere, those in Texas are being dragged down by Mr Trump. The president’s statewide approval rating is -18, according to
The Economist’s tracker
. Mr Paxton told donors in September that Mr Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas sank his numbers, according to a leaked recording. Mr Abbott was conspicuously absent from a Trump rally in San Antonio on October 7th.
Texas’s political identity has long been secure enough to withstand a national leftward tilt. Now Republicans’ Lone Star arguments are losing force. For years, calls for border security united Texas Republicans and won over many independents. The party can now boast that the problem has been fixed—border encounters in August were 94% below the average month under Joe Biden. The issue is also less salient. For the first time in a decade, voters rank the cost of living above immigration as the “biggest issue facing the state”.
The ferocity of Washington’s deportation
crackdown
doesn’t help. “Stephen Miller and the guys calling shots in DC have taken immigration policy from being a net positive for Texas Republicans and made it neutral or negative,” says Bill Miller, a Republican lobbyist in the state. After a federal agent killed a man in Houston in July, Mr Paxton offered no condolences.
When the going gets tough, Texas Republicans tend to fall back on bragging about the “Texas miracle”, the economic boom unleashed by low taxes and light regulation. In the five years to 2025, at least 184 companies moved to Austin, Dallas and Houston. When Google announced a $40bn investment last November, Mr Abbott declared the state the “headquarter of headquarters” and promised to make it the “epicentre of AI development”.
Those words now haunt him. This year Texans, like Americans elsewhere, turned against data centres, forcing Mr Abbott to ask the legislature to repeal the tax breaks that helped lure them. Ms Hinojosa, his challenger, pounced on the hypocrisy. Campaigning in towns such as Amarillo and Granbury, where Democrats rarely win, she casts herself as a populist. “Greg Abbott is selling you out,” an ad reads. The governor’s other big policy priority, universal school vouchers, is also unpopular among Republicans in small towns, where public schools are a top employer.
“The classic arguments have run out of steam and a new order hasn’t been born yet,” says James Henson, an Austin pollster. To fill the void, some Republicans are testing a new message that they hope will resonate in November and beyond: “keeping Texas, Texas”. The meaning of that slogan has recently come into focus, as politicians wage war on foreign influences they say threaten Texas from within.
First it was Muslims. Last year Mr Abbott tried to block a mosque in Plano from building a community he dubbed “Sharia city” and designated America’s biggest Muslim civil-rights group a terrorist organisation. Mr Paxton tried, unsuccessfully, to bar Muslim schools from school vouchers. In the Republican primary Mr Paxton beat John Cornyn, the incumbent senator, with the help of an endorsement of Mr Trump and a new line of attack, with ads accusing Mr Cornyn of having a “special place in his heart for radical Islam”.
Then it was legal immigrants. In January, Mr Abbott froze H-1B visa applications at state agencies and universities. Four months later Mr Paxton opened investigations into 30 firms he accused of using “ghost offices” to allow “foreign nationals to invade Texas”. In September Bo French, a Republican running for railroad commissioner (a job that actually involves regulating oil and gas), posted a photo of students celebrating a University of Texas football victory on X—nearly all of whom had brown skin. “The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined,” he wrote. Old-guard Republicans whom the party has ostracised, including Karl Rove and Mr Cornyn, called the post racist. Texas’s top brass didn’t condemn it.
The fight over who belongs in Texas is most heated in the suburbs. There, dizzying growth has transformed Republican strongholds into political battlegrounds that decide statewide elections. Between 2020 and 2025, the Dallas metro area grew faster than any other in America. The Muslim population grew with it, building cultural centres the size of Walmarts, and the share of people who identify as Hindu roughly tripled. In Frisco, a wealthy northern suburb where a quarter of residents are now Asian, city council meetings turned into political theatre. In public sessions this spring, speakers  likened a proposed mosque to a Nazi recruitment centre and called Indians “job stealers”.
The effort fell flat. When a mayoral candidate in Frisco ran on the nativist message in June, he lost by 16 points. “The problems are manufactured in Frisco, and in a lot of other places too,” says Bill Woodard, a former city councillor. The fearmongering, he argues, jars with people’s positive experience of their neighbours. Burt Thakur, the council’s first Indian-American member and a former Trump voter, agrees. “It’s the consultant class doing what they do best,” he says, “which is cleave on during election times and try to figure out how to get out the vote.” Polls from the University of Texas show that social issues don’t resonate when petrol prices are high.
Mr Abbott is still expected to be re-elected and Mr Paxton may eke out a win, too—he is reviving a tactic that has worked for Republicans before, saying Mr Talarico, who once said “God is non-binary”, is for “they/them, not you”. But, as national Republicans search for a post-Trump direction, the bitterly fought campaigns in Texas offer a warning. “Texas is the design shop for the future of the party,” says Ross Hunt, a Republican strategist in Dallas. Some Texas Republicans seem to relish the divisive zeal that is Mr Trump’s speciality, but they haven’t convinced voters—beyond the 7% who vote in their primary—that they care about them and their problems. “If we can see that attitude get punished a little bit,” Mr Hunt says, “I don’t think anyone will shed a tear.”
■

epub_39.title: The midterms’ fundraising figures tell a surprising story
epub_39.text:
The midterms’ fundraising figures tell a surprising story
United States
| A green wave
The midterms’ fundraising figures tell a surprising story
The money that matters most is flowing one way
Oct 22nd 2026
REPUBLICANS WERE supposed to have two big advantages in this year’s congressional elections: maps and money. Neither appears to be protecting them from a midterm bloodbath. Despite
winning
this cycle’s House gerrymandering war and benefiting from a red-hued Senate battleground, polls suggest that Republicans currently trail in both chambers. And new fundraising data should dent conservative hopes that the party’s candidates could close these deficits by swamping their opponents with advertising in the campaign’s final weeks.
Third-quarter financial reports show a “green wave” of Democratic money alongside the blue wave seen in polling. Excluding self-funding, Republican Senate candidates raised just $65m from July to September, compared with a whopping $276m for their opponents. Democrats had a smaller but still commanding advantage in House fundraising of $226m to $130m.
Republicans have offset these shortfalls with a big lead in spending by independent “super PACs”, which are not subject to donation limits. Elon Musk alone gave more than $200m to such groups in the third quarter. In total, Republican-aligned super PACs have outspent Democratic ones on Senate ads by $750m to $317m. However, these groups pay around three times more than campaigns do for advertising, making Democrats’ edge in direct fundraising far more valuable. As a result, according to the Wesleyan Media Project database, there were only 20% more Senate ads favouring Republicans than Democrats during the first half of October.
Moreover, money is not just a cause of campaigns’ success but also a measure of it. The more candidates raise from individuals (whose donations are capped at $3,500) in their states, the likelier they are to have large numbers of enthusiastic supporters. Nominee quality cannot be estimated from contribution ratios alone: incumbents generally out-raise challengers, and both parties enjoy big fundraising advantages in their electoral strongholds. But when candidates’ contribution shares are much larger than you would expect based on these factors, they often go on to overperform on election day.
By this measure, Democrats have large fundraising leads in almost every competitive Senate race. The most extreme case is Kansas, which has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932. The Economist’s
forecast model
reckons that in this year’s political environment, a standard Democrat trying to unseat a Republican incumbent in Kansas should get around one-third of instate individual donations. Instead, Adam Hamilton, a pastor and first-time candidate, has received a stunning 92%.
In two other Senate races the nominees changed during the summer, so no fundraising data were available on the new candidates until recently. In Maine Democrats replaced Graham Platner, who was accused of sexual assault, with Troy Jackson, a former state legislator.
In South Carolina, following the death of Lindsey Graham, the incumbent, Republicans nominated his sister Darline, a political novice. Democrats did remarkably well in these races: each of their candidates received around 85% of instate contributions.
The only competitive Senate race where a Republican had a clear fundraising edge was Minnesota. Michele Tafoya, a former sportscaster, has received 54% of instate donations in her contest against Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic lieutenant governor—19 points above the benchmark for a light-blue state in what looks like a deep-blue year. Sure enough, Minnesota also looks competitive in polls.
This year’s Democratic fundraising advantages are nothing new. During the past four congressional election cycles, the party’s Senate candidates have on average run 12 percentage points ahead of our model’s benchmarks. Yet Trump-era fundraising data have still reliably identified states where a party went on to beat expectations. This cycle, following the money adds credence to polling showing Kansas and Minnesota as two of the least likely battleground states in recent memory.

epub_40.title: Why Gen-Z conservatives love Richard Nixon
epub_40.text:
Why Gen-Z conservatives love Richard Nixon
United States
| Nixon now
Why Gen-Z conservatives love Richard Nixon
The disgraced president’s revival highlights a generational split among conservatives
Oct 22nd 2026
To looksmaxxing and gymmaxxing now add Nixonmaxxing, an activity to stretch your thinking if not enhance it. Slickly edited videos featuring America’s 37th president, often set to hip-hop beats, have gone viral in recent months. Influencers are donning baseball caps and tote bags embroidered with slogans like “Pretty Girls for Nixon” and “Nixon Now More Than Ever”. Attendance at the Richard Nixon Presidential Library in California is up 30% on last year.
The strange revival of the disgraced late president owes much to the media-savvy millennials running the Richard Nixon Foundation, a non-profit that helps manage the presidential library and, in a newer development, pumps out bite-sized videos.  Covering everything from his musings on America’s relationship with Russia to his thoughts on his rivalry with John F. Kennedy, the clips have racked up millions of views. “Love seeing these old Nixon videos resurface”, reads one comment. “They really show the younger generations what a political genius he really was.” Your correspondent, a forlorn Nelson Rockefellermaxxer, recently spent hours scrolling through content to figure out what’s behind the newfound love for Tricky Dick.
Few are hyping up detente or Nixon’s creation of the Environmental Protection Agency. In Gen-Z speak, the enthusiasm is mostly down to vibes. The most popular clips capture Nixon’s bare-knuckle politics and refusal to give up. Some young conservatives see in Nixon an analogue to Donald Trump: two presidents marked by their antagonistic relationships with the press and hounded by investigators. “The Right’s rediscovery of Richard Nixon is not about particular policies,” wrote Chris Rufo, a millennial conservative, on X recently; it’s about “the attitude, and the narrative of the self-made man who won 49 states on behalf of the Silent Majority, and was taken down in a Deep State coup.”
The Trump administration seems to have a similar view. The Department of Justice is reviewing whether the special prosecutor’s office that investigated the Watergate break-in committed misconduct. “If Watergate happened tomorrow it would be like a 12-hour news story,” quipped J.D. Vance, the vice-president, during a talk at the Nixon library in June. “The idea that it would have taken down a presidency is crazy.”
In embracing Nixon, young right-wingers are also rejecting their elders’ worship of Ronald Reagan. The Gipper’s faith in free markets and internationalism is at odds with the MAGA worldview. “Reagan is the baby-boomer god,” says Curt Mills of the American Conservative, a magazine. “And the subtext of so much of what the New Right and younger conservatives think is that old people destroyed this country, and if Reagan is their god, then it must be a false god.”
Alas for keepers of the Nixon flame, he remains one of most unpopular presidents in the country’s history. A burst of Nixonmaxxing is unlikely to fix his reputation anytime soon. Then again, he has been written off before.

epub_41.title: The curious, predictable case of the fake poll
epub_41.text:
The curious, predictable case of the fake poll
United States
| Fake numbers
The curious, predictable case of the fake poll
Incentives for fraudulent surveys are high and oversight lax
Oct 22nd 2026
By late June, Mallory McMorrow’s campaign to be Michigan’s next senator was probably already doomed. The Democrat was squeezed between Abdul El-Sayed, a dynamic leftist, and Haley Stevens, an establishment-backed centrist, in a heated primary. When a poll was published showing she had the support of only 9% of registered voters, it seemed to be a death knell. Reporters asked when she would drop out, which she did on July 5th. It now seems that poll was fake.
An investigation published on October 20th by FiftyPlusOne, a data-journalism outfit, found that a group called Wedgewood Polls had fabricated its results. The discovery follows another in August, when the Los Angeles Times spotted a forged poll on the city’s mayoral candidates. FiftyPlusOne has also criticised a pollster for manipulating figures to serve its client. The spate of bad polls undermines an industry already widely distrusted.
Wedgewood published 15 public polls ahead of the midterm elections. Then FiftyPlusOne—led by G. Elliott Morris, a former journalist at The Economist—received a tip that the data were fake. Mr Morris and his colleagues confirmed the forgery by comparing Wedgewood’s figures with data from a provider the firm had supposedly employed. Mismatched identification numbers gave the scammers away. When FiftyPlusOne requested a comment from Wedgewood, the firm claimed it had forged the polls to “demonstrate the vulnerabilities” of the industry.
Whatever Wedgewood’s motive, there are many reasons to fake polls. One is to earn easy money by selling fraudulent services to campaigns and political groups, which tend to spend heavily on public-opinion research; another is to manipulate prediction markets, where billions are bet on elections. Fake polls can also be used to influence elections themselves, for example by making candidates seem unviable. Ms McMorrow claims that donations dried up after the fraudulent poll was published.
With so much cash coursing through elections in America, the incentives to fake polls are greater than in other democracies. However, oversight is weaker. In Brazil, South Korea and France, for instance, pollsters must submit information to national authorities that monitor their work. In August the Brazilian Superior Electoral Court upheld a R$53,000 ($10,600) fine for a polling firm that had released insufficient information about a poll, despite there being no suggestion that its results were misleading. America’s wild-west approach has benefits—the industry is more dynamic and understanding of public opinion is deep. But the country’s pollsters already faced public scepticism. The latest fiasco won’t help.
■

epub_42.title: How to share the wealth from AI? Alaska offers lessons
epub_42.text:
How to share the wealth from AI? Alaska offers lessons
United States
| Divisive dividends
How to share the wealth from AI? Alaska offers lessons
Divvying up the proceeds of a boom is harder than it looks
Oct 22nd 2026
OCTOBER IS EVENTFUL in Alaska. Its vast landscapes erupt in a riot of colour, daylight becomes precious and beefy bears rush to fatten themselves before winter. It is also the month Alaskans get a payday. Each October the state government disburses dividends from the investment earnings of its oil revenues. The amount varies, but this October each resident who has lived in the state at least one full calendar year will receive $1,200.
For half a century Alaska has run an experiment in how to use revenues from its abundant oil resources for the public good. Now, as American lawmakers grapple with whether and how to share the wealth that artificial intelligence might create, the state’s experience has new relevance. Proposals to put stakes in AI companies into a public fund, and use the proceeds to pay dividends or finance public services, echo Alaska’s approach. But Alaska’s Permanent Fund and its dividend offer both a model and a cautionary tale.
The state’s good fortune dates back to 1968, when roughnecks drilling at Prudhoe Bay, on Alaska’s North Slope, struck oil. Less than a decade later Alaskans voted to create the Permanent Fund, an investment vehicle for a portion of annual mineral royalties. The idea, says Mike Dunleavy, the Republican governor, “was to ensure that finite resources such as oil mining could be converted into infinite revenue for the people of Alaska”. In 1980 the legislature created an independent state-run corporation to manage the Permanent Fund’s investments. Two years later Alaska began paying the dividend. Today the fund is worth $90bn, or roughly $122,000 per Alaskan.
The remaining mineral royalties, along with oil production taxes, are used to finance public services. For a long time the riches seemed inexhaustible. A single lease sale in 1969 raised more than five times the state’s annual budget. In 1980 Alaskan lawmakers repealed the state’s personal income tax. They have since shunned other broad-based levies on residents. This makes Alaska unique among American petro-states. Others, such as Texas and New Mexico,  continue to collect sales or income taxes to finance their spending.
Alaska’s utter dependence on the black stuff has left it hostage to fluctuations in the oil price. In 2018, after several lean years, lawmakers decided to use Permanent Fund earnings to help bankroll the state government for the first time. Now annual draws from the fund account for roughly two-thirds of the state’s budget. Lawmakers must haggle over how to divide the oil money between dividends and public services. Brett Watson, an economist at the University of Alaska Anchorage, says Alaska’s budgeting has become “zero sum”.
Mr Dunleavy was elected in 2018 after promising to restore a long-standing formula linking dividends to the fund’s investment earnings, which would have given Alaskans annual payments of more than $3,000. But lawmakers had stopped following the formula two years earlier, amid a budget crisis. In office, Mr Dunleavy has had to face up to the maths; the average dividend during his tenure has been roughly $1,500. “Every legislator who gets elected saying, ‘I promise you a $3,000 dividend’, once they get down to Juneau, and they look at that budget, they realise you cannot do that,” explains Gary Stevens, the Republican state Senate president.
Under Mr Dunleavy, lawmakers have also cut spending on services, both to balance the books and to preserve money for dividends. Deprived of state dollars, cities and boroughs are operating on shoestring budgets. “Many local governments…just close when they run out of money,” says Nils Andreassen of the Alaska Municipal League, a non-profit. Lawmakers have long hoped the dividend would help keep residents; some now worry that worsening services will drive them away. The state’s net migration has been negative in each year since 2013.
The war with Iran offers a band-aid: higher oil prices are propping up the state budget. Bernadette Wilson, a Republican candidate for governor, is calling for bigger dividend cheques; her opponent, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a former Democratic state legislator, favours fiscal reform.
When it comes to AI wealth, the debate is only beginning. Bernie Sanders, a senator from Vermont, wants big AI firms to hand over 50% of their shares to a sovereign wealth fund, which would pay Americans at least $1,000 a year and eventually support health care and other services. The bosses of OpenAI and Anthropic favour donating a more modest 5% stake to a public fund. OpenAI also backs higher taxes on capital gains and corporate income.
An AI fund would not initially face the same fiscal pressures as Alaska’s Permanent Fund: America, after all, still collects federal income taxes. But Alaska’s predicament shows the dangers of relying too heavily on a single source of revenue, and how easily dividends can become a political football. Donald Trump is already dangling a “Trump dividend”, unrelated to AI, if Republicans win the midterms. Just vote for the party’s candidates, he implored recently, “and you will each have $5,000”.

epub_43.title: City-hall socialists try to make populism pragmatic
epub_43.text:
City-hall socialists try to make populism pragmatic
United States
| Mayors of America, unite!
City-hall socialists try to make populism pragmatic
Can leftist mayors be both radicals and realists?
Oct 22nd 2026
ON A SWELTERING October Sunday in Los Angeles Nithya Raman, a city-council member running for mayor, laid out her vision for America’s second-largest city. Ms Raman (pictured) is affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Yet the dream she described to Angelenos was not of “ending capitalist oligarchy”, part of the DSA’s platform, but of competence. “City government has made solving problems look impossible for so long, people are starting to believe it is impossible,” she lamented, before rhapsodising about homelessness audits and cutting red tape. Her slogan, far from being revolutionary, is simply: “A city that works”.
Donald Trump has long derided cities run by Democrats as crime-ridden hellscapes; it would seem a political gift that a growing number are either already led, or will soon be led, by Democratic Socialists, whom the president calls “crazed lunatics and radicals”. But even as Republicans try to use socialism to undermine Democrats’ appeal, a new crop of pragmatic city socialists insist they will do the opposite.
Zohran Mamdani of New York is the most famous of this group—even Mr Trump has proved unable to resist the magnetic mayor, holding a chummy press conference with him in September that enraged Republican strategists. But along with Mr Mamdani there is Katie Wilson, elected last year to be mayor of Seattle, as well as Janeese Lewis George, the Democratic nominee all but sure to be the mayor of Washington, DC. In LA Ms Raman is in a fierce campaign against the incumbent Democratic mayor, Karen Bass. These four are all millennials either aligned with, or members of, the DSA. All four have also, either of their own volition or pushed by external factors, inched to the centre.
A pragmatic socialist may seem like an oxymoron, but America has a tradition of them. Mr Mamdani and Ms Wilson have spoken admiringly of the “sewer socialists” of 20th-century Milwaukee, who downplayed revolutionary rhetoric while trying to improve sanitation and parks. Today’s leftists have rebranded this strategy as “sidewalk socialism” or “pothole politics”. Ms Raman, for example, is fixated on repairing broken streetlights, a symbol of LA’s dysfunction. Unlike DSA members in Congress, who specialise in bold, inconsequential positions, socialist mayors must contend with their cities’ problems.
This does not mean abandoning populism. Mr Mamdani is rolling out a tax on pieds-à-terre—earlier this year he posted a video celebrating the prospect of a new levy on the $238m penthouse of Ken Griffin, a hedge fund boss. But more basic concerns are the priority.
Take public safety. Even progressive voters doubt the logic of abolishing the police, as the DSA has suggested. Ms Lewis George once wanted to cut police funding; now she highlights her career as a prosecutor and promises to “support law enforcement”. Mr Mamdani kept his predecessor’s competent police commissioner, Jessica Tisch, and continues to stand by her despite her status as a DSA bête noire. “He knows that allowing crime and disorder to spiral out of control would take New Yorkers’ focus away from his affordability message,” explains John Ketcham of the Manhattan Institute, a conservative think-tank.
On housing, the four speak as ardently about slashing red tape as they do about squeezing landlords. Mr Mamdani’s efforts have earned the praise of local developers. In LA Ms Raman is an urban planner who embraced the YIMBY movement while serving on the city council. She wants to reform a “mansion tax” she once championed, as it has helped depress development. Her about-face impressed Dave Rand, a land-use lawyer who represents developers. “I don’t want an ideologue,” he notes. “I want someone who’s going to adjust to the facts on the ground.”
In Seattle, Ms Wilson campaigned on new taxes on capital gains and vacant properties. But her proposed budget would plug the deficit, cut city jobs and increase police spending. The business lobby cheered. Democratic socialists “may have values that are anti-capitalist”, says Joe Nguyen, of the Seattle Metro Chamber, “but they exist in a capitalist regime”. Ms Wilson is forthright about her evolution from activist to politician. “I’ve had to do a lot of work this year building relationships with the business community that I didn’t necessarily need to have, or cultivate, as an organiser,” she admits. “As the mayor, everyone’s problems are my problems.”
A less charitable interpretation is that leftist mayoral candidates are better at promising than governing. Mr Mamdani made fast, free buses a centre of his campaign. One year on, he’s focusing on the fast. Ms Lewis George’s ambitious plans for Washington are running into the reality of the city’s dismal finances, flagging economy and limits under federal law.
If these shifts come as a relief to business leaders, they can outrage the base. This month The Stranger, a newspaper in Seattle, asked: “Is mayor Katie Wilson still a socialist?” Israel and Palestine have little to do with municipal governance, but Mr Mamdani’s criticisms of the war in Gaza energised progressive voters during his campaign. When he attended a vigil for the Israeli victims of the October 7th attacks, protesters heckled the mayor and called him a “traitor”.
Some members of the DSA’s chapter in LA reckon Ms Raman is insufficiently anti-Israel, too, and are suspicious of her support for market-rate housing. During a recent meeting at a church in Hollywood, every other DSA candidate on the ballot got louder cheers. A young woman next to The Economist placed a blank canvassing sign-up form under her pew. “I’m not interested in campaigning for Democrats,” she explained. A century ago Milwaukee’s sewer socialists were derided by other leftists for their “bourgeois” worries. But the concerns were real. And those other leftists remained on the fringe.

epub_44.title: Donald Trump should love the new documentary about Elizabeth Holmes
epub_44.text:
Donald Trump should love the new documentary about Elizabeth Holmes
United States
| Lexington
Donald Trump should love the new documentary about Elizabeth Holmes
But when will other Americans get tired of hearing that truth is a slippery thing?
Oct 22nd 2026
“What is the reality?” asks the disgraced entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes near the start of Nathan Fielder’s new documentary, “You Can See Everything”, about the 34 days he spent with her before she reported to serve a prison sentence for fraud in 2023. And the audience member thinks, Oh no, here we go again.
Or, at least, so thinks that audience member who has grown weary of this endless post-modern era, of being reminded that objective truth is elusive, that one’s purchase on reality is determined by whichever narrative one chooses to believe. By the end of this ingenious, absorbing film, Mr Fielder and his co-director, Lance Oppenheim, have not only questioned whether Ms Holmes is truly guilty of defrauding investors by claiming, as the founder of the blood-testing company Theranos, to have revolutionised the detection of dozens of illnesses. They have raised doubts about the motives of her romantic partner, the integrity of the New York Times and even their own portrayal of Ms Holmes. You can’t see everything. So how can you trust anything?
Americans absorbed this lesson long ago. They might not all have read Michel Foucault on how power shapes truth, or Jean Baudrillard on how modern media erase the boundaries between authenticity and artifice. (Lexington hasn’t got around to it, either.) But they have watched plenty of reality television and become sophisticated enough about the plasticity of truth to have elected their first post-modern president, not once but twice. Or is it three times? Narratives differ.
It is paradoxical, though characteristic of the self-sabotaging academy, that an intellectual movement meant to subvert traditional power structures has helped a right-wing American politician magnify the power of the presidency. But from his days lying about the number of storeys in his buildings to his success as a reality-television star to his years in the Oval Office, Donald Trump has exhibited an intuitive mastery of this corrosive post-Enlightenment realism about reality. His basic rule of business and politics has been to trust nothing and no one. “I’m a non-trusting person,” he told CBS News back in 1990.
Mr Trump has succeeded partly by relying on radical scepticism of facts proclaimed not just by other politicians but by the news media, the pollsters, the courts and the scientists. He knows that reflexive cynicism is trailed everywhere by its idiot twin, gaping gullibility about conspiracy theories with only the flimsiest connection to any fact. Election deniers, climate-change deniers and anti-vaxxers are flourishing in America’s years of epistemic crisis. Even the flat-earthers are having a bit of a moment, if the polls are to be believed, which of course they’re not.
To be fair, Ms Holmes, for one, has reason to be annoyed, or jaded, about the nature of narrative, at least as it is constructed by the news media. She was widely celebrated, including in rigorously fact-checked publications, before she was widely demonised. The head-snapping reversal came after reporting by the Wall Street Journal revealed that the seemingly miraculous “Edison” device developed by Theranos was not able to perform the many tests Ms Holmes claimed, and she was eventually found guilty.
It is on this point that Mr Fielder’s documentary is a bit too clever for anyone’s good, except perhaps Ms Holmes’s. She comes across as a nice lady, if a bit strange. One would need a heart of stone not to feel sorry for her and her family as she leaves her toddler and infant behind with her partner, Billy Evans, to begin serving more than 11 years for bilking the likes of Rupert Murdoch and the heirs to the Walmart fortune. Mr Fielder asks penetrating questions, and he is a master of the awkward silence. But Ms Holmes proves his equal, meeting his stillness with stillness and his hooded stare with wide, seemingly guileless blue eyes that at times mist with tears. She believes she has never told a lie, she says, and (unlike the president) she is a trusting person who is “always being real”. Mr Fielder lingers over the possibility that her “fraud” hinged on an epic miscommunication. When she claimed the Edison device “can” work, she meant it could work, once science caught up with it. She did not intend to deceive anyone. “She just thinks differently,” explains Mr Evans. Ms Holmes laments that “the world believes in a reality about me that isn’t true.”
The post-modernists are right. Power does shape the perception of truth and narrative can mould reality. Ms Holmes’s ascent demonstrated that. And, as Mr Trump has claimed, even the courts can be rigged, and juries can deliver mistaken verdicts. Yet the jury in Ms Holmes’s case does not seem to have decided blithely.
After a trial of almost four months, the jury acquitted her on four counts and deadlocked on three, while convicting her on four. It sifted through a mountain of witness testimony and documentary evidence, including that Ms Holmes, as she admitted, personally affixed the logos of pharmaceutical companies to favourable reports on Edison, even though they had reached no such conclusions. To gesture, on the basis of word games, at the idea the jury might have got it wrong is not, as some movie critics have put it, a “bold, perhaps impossible, quest for truth” or a “battle for the essence of truth”. It is, instead, a shrug at the impossibility of apprehending the truth—an act not of idealistic struggle but of surrender, if not nihilism.
Maybe it is silly to get wound up about this. The movie is thought-provoking and funny. But America is about to have another election. If it does not go his way Mr Trump can be expected to reject the results, and maybe even to try to reverse them. He has done that before. Will Americans follow the model of Mr Fielder and so many others, and throw up their hands, uncertain of what the facts truly are? The world may be about to find out.
