epub_46.title: Can Lula, now the underdog, pull off one last trick?
epub_46.text:
Can Lula, now the underdog, pull off one last trick?
The Americas
| Brazil’s election
Can Lula, now the underdog, pull off one last trick?
The polls are tightening with just days to go
Oct 22nd 2026
THE PRESIDENTIAL
run-off
on October 25th is shaping up to be the tightest since Brazil returned to democracy in 1985. The election pits
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva
, the 80-year-old left-wing incumbent, against
Flávio Bolsonaro
, the 45-year-old son of Jair, a former president. No candidate who lost the first round has ever gone on to win the second. But though Lula, as the incumbent is known, trailed Flávio in the first vote on October 4th (Lula got 45%; his rival 47%), he is refusing to go down without a fight. Can he pull off an upset?
Since his loss in the first round, Lula has taken dramatic action. Once a technophobe who declined even to use a mobile phone, he has lately begun posting selfie-videos on Instagram. He has come out in support of lowering the age of criminal responsibility for serious crimes, a policy that was previously anathema to the left. And he has pushed Congress to pass a wildly popular measure that will reduce the work week from 44 hours to 40 hours without pay cuts. His campaign has rallied hundreds of thousands of supporters in marches across big cities, replete with celebrity performances.
He is also making big spending pledges. He has promised to forgive federal tax debts racked up by sole traders such as barbers, manicurists or plumbers, and to hand out $1,000 to 1m of them. He has pledged to make public transport free at weekends. This comes on top of a recent increase in the government’s flagship cash transfer to poor families, the abolition of income taxes for lower-middle-class Brazilians and a decision to outlaw gambling firms (who were paying lots in tax). These new measures all combined could cost the government a total of $58bn by the end of 2027 (over 2% of GDP), according to the Independent Fiscal Institution, a research outfit linked to Brazil’s Senate.
The promises are having an effect. Lula is making up ground on Mr Bolsonaro, particularly among women. Some of the latest polls show them neck and neck in the race (with the caveat that pollsters in Brazil have repeatedly failed to fully capture right-wing sentiment, including before the first round on October 4th, when the polls had Lula  ahead). In the week after October 10th betting firms almost doubled Lula’s odds of victory, though they still put him behind his rival.
Mr Bolsonaro is hitting back. He ended up voting in favour of the shorter work week, having previously disparaged it. In a presidential debate on October 18th he alleged that crime had exploded during Lula’s third term (in fact it has fallen). Of the four right-wing candidates knocked out in the first round, who between them received 8% of votes, three have backed Mr Bolsonaro. Despite the narrowing polls, Le Millénaire, an election forecaster based in Paris, puts his odds of victory at 82%.
A trip to Minas Gerais, the country’s second-most populous state, shows the hill Lula has to climb. It is a microcosm of Brazil: its arid north borders the country’s poor north-east, Lula’s heartland. To its south and west, agribusiness and industry reign supreme and voters lean right. No president has ever won without taking Minas. Though Lula carried the state in 2022, he lost it by five percentage points to Mr Bolsonaro on October 4th.
In Monte Sião, a town of 25,000 people, some 2,000 tiny firms churn out knitwear from the ground floors of the owners’ houses. Residents complain about the rising cost of living. In the backroom of a small firm, five seamstresses are adding the finishing touches to dresses. “We pay so much in taxes, taxes, taxes,” complains one. “We have no money left over at the end of the month—we earn just to survive.” Her colleague chimes in: “It’s called the Workers’ Party, but the worker gets nothing!” Their boss blames crushing interest rates for pushing up his debt.
Fatigue with Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT), which has been in power for 18 of the past 24 years, is common in these parts. In Poços de Caldas, a town nearby that is known for its thermal baths and abundant deposits of rare earths, voters are disheartened. “Lula said he would give everyone picanha (rump steak), but today even eggs cost a lot,” says a 45-year-old bricklayer, referring to a promise Lula made on the campaign trail in 2022, that he would make all Brazilians rich enough to eat top cuts of beef. After voting for Lula in the past, he says he will cast a blank vote. In a down-at-heel suburb, Carlos Moisés, a 64-year-old barber, is sweeping the floor of his shop. A lifelong PT voter, he will vote for Flávio, explaining that he is drowning in taxes. “I know the Bolsonaro family isn’t all that great. But we got tired, you understand?”
The PT was built on support from trade unionists, Catholic priests and academics. It has struggled to adapt to a more evangelical Brazil, with workers who are increasingly self-employed. Since 2010 the number of registered sole traders has rocketed from under 1m to 15m. That sector now accounts for almost a fifth of formal jobs. These people commonly earn too much to receive government support but also too little to live comfortably. For years, PT mandarins derided them as “CEOs of one-person companies”. Lula’s pledge to forgive some of their debts is a late attempt to win them over.
Dotted around the green landscape are Pentecostal temples, some preaching a doctrine celebrating wealth. “The growth of Pentecostalism has helped spread conservative values in poorer neighbourhoods,” says Lucas Pavanato, a 28-year-old in São Paulo who has just won a seat in Congress for Mr Bolsonaro’s party. “Left-wing ideology puts all the blame on social structures, whereas religion places responsibility on the individual to improve their life.” Among evangelicals, Lula trails Mr Bolsonaro by 33 percentage points.
Mr Pavanato’s success demonstrates the right’s social-media prowess. In the legislative election held on October 4th he got the second-largest number of votes in the country—just behind Nikolas Ferreira, an ardent evangelical Christian and social-media whizz who has over 30m followers. Brazilians use social media more heavily than people almost anywhere else, and many get their news from such platforms.
Before the first round of the presidential ballot Mr Bolsonaro’s campaign spent at least $2m boosting his content online. Lula’s campaign spent barely $500,000. It handed out lots of stickers with his face on them. Lately his team have been accusing social-media platforms of improperly limiting their campaign-messages’ reach. With only days of campaigning remaining, Lula’s team must fervently hope that the old ways may still prove to be the best.

epub_47.title: Latin America is embracing Israel
epub_47.text:
Latin America is embracing Israel
The Americas
| Bibi’s buddies abroad
Latin America is embracing Israel
New right-wing leaders are rushing to upgrade ties
Oct 22nd 2026
“Something remarkable is happening in Latin America”, grinned Binyamin Netanyahu, Israel’s embattled prime minister, on October 14th. “It’s all coming back! The great friendship.” He was speaking following the opening of Colombia’s new embassy in Jerusalem. Colombia has become the fourth—and so far the most populous—Latin American country to recognise the holy city as Israel’s capital. It is unlikely to be the last.
Israel has grown more isolated as a result of the war in Gaza. Yet conservative leaders in Latin America—many of them newly elected—are dramatically stepping up ties. Javier Milei, Argentina’s president, is the keenest. Earlier this year he told The Economist he thought Mr Netanyahu was a “superstar”. He himself has claimed, oddly, to be the “most Zionist president in the world”. In April Mr Milei announced the “Isaac Accords”, a vague framework for closer engagement between Israel and the region. A new direct flight between Buenos Aires and Tel Aviv launches next month.
Flávio Bolsonaro, the frontrunner in Brazil’s presidential election, has vowed to relocate his country’s embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem if he wins on October 25th. He expressed his “full support” for Israeli settlers during a recent visit to the West Bank; both he and Mr Milei have prayed before the Western Wall. As well as moving its embassy, Colombia in August became the only country other than the United States to say it supported Israel’s claim to the Golan Heights. “We have never paid so much attention to our relationship with Israel,” says Sandra Borda of the University of the Andes in Bogotá.
Rodrigo Paz in Bolivia, José Antonio Kast in Chile and Nasry Asfura in Honduras have all bolstered diplomatic ties that their predecessors had downgraded in response to the bloodshed in Gaza. Delcy Rodríguez, the interim president of Venezuela, has softened the chavista regime’s longstanding hostility towards Israel. After big earthquakes near Caracas in June she accepted Israel’s offer to send rescue teams and resumed consular ties. “Latin America is becoming a blue continent,” says Marcos Peckel of the Confederation of Jewish Communities in Colombia, referring to Israel’s blue-and-white flag.
Some of the region’s leaders are motivated by strong personal convictions. Mr Milei is known to study the Torah with a rabbi. When The Economist visited his office in August, a Hebrew text sat on his desk. In a speech to Israel’s parliament in 2025, he vowed to “defend Western culture”. Yet political calculations are plainly central, too. Moving closer to Israel is one way for the new right in Latin America to curry favour with America’s Republican Party, and with Donald Trump.
The political costs are relatively low, says Christopher Sabatini of Chatham House, a think-tank in London. A survey by Pew, a pollster, finds that a little over half of Argentines, Brazilians, Colombians and Peruvians have an unfavourable view of Israel—much lower than the 69% reported in Britain and 78% in Spain. In most of Latin America, questions related to Israel and Palestine matter far less to voters than fighting crime and boosting the economy.
The region also has a swift-growing constituency that encourages outspoken support for Israel: evangelical Christians. Many believe the Jewish return to Israel fulfils biblical prophecy. Born-again Christians have been effective in getting right-wing leaders into power. Before Colombia’s election evangelical voters held prayer vigils for Abelardo de la Espriella, the eventual winner, who was once an atheist but is now a fervent Catholic. Evangelicals also mobilised behind Mr Bolsonaro in the first round of Brazil’s election.
Many of the region’s leaders took office promising to take a tough line on drug gangs. Governments are counting on weapons and advice from Israel to give their plans a boost. In 2022 Ecuador, which has a murder rate three times the Latin American average, said it would spend around $65m buying Israeli armoured vehicles. The violence in Ecuador has its roots in neighbouring Colombia, where Mr de la Espriella has recently been bombing armed groups. But the armed forces need Israeli intelligence and drone technology to act effectively, says General Alberto José Mejía, who led Colombia’s military services in 2015-18.
In 2024 Gustavo Petro, the president at the time, severed ties with Israel and halted purchases of arms and other equipment that Colombia’s army had long relied on. The country’s weapons stocks were depleted, says General Mejía. Colombia’s various rebel groups now rally more than 28,000 fighters, almost double the figure when Mr Petro took office in 2022. “The Israeli defence complex will have a field day with this government,” says a Colombian intelligence expert.
Will the love-in with Israel endure? America’s midterms, in November, are relevant. If Republicans come out wounded, leaders in Latin America may grow a bit less inclined to follow Mr Trump’s lead. In Chile, a friendlier policy towards Israel has prompted a backlash (it has a large Palestinian community). Supporters of Colombia’s formerly pro-Palestinian policies are also aghast. Israel’s own election, on October 27th, adds uncertainty. But for now, at least, Latin America and Israel are enjoying their tightest bond in years.

epub_48.title: Rastafarians in Jamaica want more rights
epub_48.text:
Rastafarians in Jamaica want more rights
The Americas
| Herbal remedies
Rastafarians in Jamaica want more rights
The government is keen to atone for past abuses
Oct 22nd 2026
SISTER NANNY is easy to spot. Sporting a red, gold and green dress—with a matching headpiece—the Rastafari campaigner is outlining an idea she thinks will help marginalised members of her faith. Jamaica takes advantage of the world’s interest in Rastas to “attract visitors” to the country, she notes. Yet those same people continue to suffer stigma. She thinks the Jamaican government should share proceeds with the community, whenever it profits from their culture.
Dreadlocks, cannabis, reggae: think of Jamaica and aspects of Rastafari culture commonly leap to mind. On the island, however, the religious movement has often been maligned. Rastafari beliefs originated in poor Jamaican neighbourhoods in the 1930s. They revolve around a single God, Jah, said to reside within each person. Haile Selassie I, the Ethiopian emperor crowned in 1930, is seen by some as the second coming of Christ (Selassie politely discouraged the idea).
From the beginning, authorities took a tough line. Many Rastafari were arrested for possessing cannabis, which they view as a sacrament. Schools and prisons forced them to shave their dreadlocks, which violates a vow. Violence erupted in 1963, following an altercation at a petrol station in the city of Montego Bay. Security forces detained Rastas all across Jamaica; some were killed.
In 2017 the Jamaican government formally apologised for the “Coral Gardens incident”, as it became known. This year it has gone further, formally handing the deeds to land in Montego Bay to a campaign group that Sister Nanny helps organise, as restitution. The land will be used for a Rastafari care home.
The move fits into a broader trend of pro-Rastafari policymaking in the Caribbean. In 2015 Jamaica somewhat liberalised its drug laws, explicitly permitting Rastas to grow and use cannabis for religious purposes. St Vincent & the Grenadines passed a similar rule in 2018; Barbados the following year. When Antigua & Barbuda joined them in 2023, the prime minister, Gaston Browne, acknowledged that his country had once tried to “destroy” the faith. This year St Kitts & Nevis formally recognised Rastafarianism as a religion, which grants it stronger legal protections.
Rastafari in Jamaica say discrimination has decreased, but not disappeared. “The police still harass Rastafari…for having herb,” says Ras Iyah V, chairman of the Westmoreland Hemp and Ganja Farmers’ Association. The movement is pleased with the progress, but it is pushing for more. Sister Nanny’s group has begun advocating for Rastas to get intellectual property rights that might protect “the colours, the language, the food...Anyone who wants to appropriate our culture, then they should pay”. The promise is that funds raised in this way would be used to build schools and more care homes.
Talks with Jamaica’s government continue. A lack of unity hampers the fight. In 2023 several distinct groups formed Rastafari Mansions and Organisations, an umbrella body, to help co-ordinate advocacy. Coherence remains a challenge, says Sister Nanny. “There is no one voice yet.”

epub_50.title: Everything is going wrong for Muhammad bin Salman
epub_50.text:
Everything is going wrong for Muhammad bin Salman
Middle East & Africa
| Saudi bets gone bad
Everything is going wrong for Muhammad bin Salman
This is his annus horribilis
Oct 22nd 2026
IN ANY OTHER year, Muhammad bin Salman would be getting ready for his star turn. October 26th was supposed to have been the start of the Future Investment Initiative (FII), an annual summit in the Saudi capital that is sometimes dubbed “Davos in the desert”. The crown prince usually spends the week glad-handing heads of state, titans of finance and other dignitaries, all of them eager to do business with his kingdom.
Not this year. The Houthis, an Iran-backed militia in Yemen,
have spent weeks
firing missiles and drones at Riyadh. The airport is still, in effect, shut after a series of deadly attacks. Many Western governments have warned their citizens not to travel to the kingdom. Executives were nervous that hotels or other venues could be targets. After days of deliberation, organisers decided on October 19th to postpone the event until next year.
As he
rose to power
a decade ago, Prince Muhammad made a few big gambles. He wagered that he could defeat the Houthis; that he could reshape the Saudi economy; and that Donald Trump would prove a reliable ally. All of them have gone awry at once. The decision to cancel FII is emblematic of Prince Muhammad’s annus horribilis. He faces a set of interlocking crises, none of which has a ready solution.
The Saudis failed to defeat the Houthis, but they had hoped a ceasefire agreed on in 2022 would contain the threat. Instead the truce began to unravel this summer because of America’s broader war with Iran. The Houthis have seized additional territory in Yemen and battered Saudi Arabia. People close to the crown prince see only bad options. The kingdom can send ground troops into a bloody war; continue a campaign of air strikes that is unlikely to succeed; or make a deal that helps cement the Houthis’ rule in Yemen.
A long conflict will derail the prince’s economic programme, which was sputtering even before 2026. Big projects were being shelved amid a strain on public finances. Wages have not kept pace with inflation. Annual foreign direct investment is only about one-third of the crown prince’s $100bn target. A year ago the IMF expected the Saudi economy to grow by 4% in 2026; now it expects a 3.3% contraction.
Whether it rebounds in 2027 will depend on whether peace breaks out in the Middle East—and that will depend largely on Mr Trump. The kingdom thought it had influence over him. It wooed him by promising to invest implausible sums in America. It also made tawdry deals with the first family, paying Trump-owned golf courses to host Saudi-funded tournaments and investing $2bn with Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law. None of that stopped Mr Trump from embarking on a disastrous war. “He’s not loyal to anyone for long,” says one well-connected Saudi.
There are no reliable public-opinion polls in the kingdom, but it is fair to say most Saudis trust their government. Some have found recent weeks unnerving, nonetheless: the war in Yemen has caused real disruption. Yet since October 10th, when a Houthi missile killed 13 people at Riyadh’s airport, Prince Muhammad has been largely invisible. It fell to ministers to visit victims and offer reassuring messages.
A few Western commentators have begun to ask whether this crisis-filled year poses an existential threat to the crown prince’s rule. The view among diplomats in Riyadh is that such talk is overblown. “He was in a much tougher place seven or eight years ago,” says one Western envoy.
Back then the prince was a newly appointed heir, still consolidating his rule. The war in Yemen was already a quagmire, the blockade of Qatar was upsetting America, and much of the world was horrified when Jamal Khashoggi, a Saudi journalist, was murdered inside the kingdom’s consulate in Istanbul. Prince Muhammad’s grip on power is far more secure today: he has sidelined rivals and centralised power unlike any Saudi ruler since King Abdulaziz, the founder of the modern state. Though he certainly has his detractors, none could plausibly organise a putsch.
Nor is he facing much criticism from allies. The response to the recent escalation in Yemen has been telling: even long-time critics of the war are now willing to acknowledge that the kingdom has little choice but to fight. “I do understand that this is a different moment than 2018 or 2020. They are facing these Houthi advances and Houthi rocket attacks,” says Chris Murphy, a Democratic senator who met the crown prince in Riyadh this month. “We should recognise that.”
Seen in another light, though, this is a more challenging moment for Prince Muhammad. Because the woes of his early years were mostly self-inflicted, they were easier to fix. By 2021 he was steering Saudi foreign policy in a more pragmatic direction. He ended the blockade of Qatar and sought a deal with the Houthis. Even the Biden administration, which took office promising to make the crown prince a “pariah”, grudgingly praised his new direction.
This year is harder. The biggest decision is out of Prince Muhammad’s hands. He has urged Mr Trump not to escalate the war with Iran. If the president ignores him and resumes bombing after the midterm elections in November, Saudi officials worry the kingdom will take blows from all sides: the Houthis to the south, Iraqi militias to the north and Iran itself to the east. They have a big country to protect—four times the size of France—and not many air-defence interceptors left to do it.
In his first decade, the crown prince made laudable strides towards liberalising Saudi society. Women can drive. Female labour-force participation has almost doubled. Concerts and cinemas are now widespread in a country where fun was long verboten. A few well-off foreigners can even enjoy a legal tipple. But the core of the Saudi state has changed little. Its economy still depends on oil money, its army is still built to protect the regime rather than wage war, and its foreign policy still relies on America as an indispensable protector.
Perhaps eventually those things will change as well. The Mecca pact, a mutual-defence agreement with Pakistan and Turkey, is an effort to find new allies that could supplant a now unreliable America. But those changes will take time. In his second decade, the test for Saudi Arabia’s ruler will be to change the foundations, not just the façade.

epub_51.title: A deeply divided Israel prepares to vote
epub_51.text:
A deeply divided Israel prepares to vote
Middle East & Africa
| The more things change
A deeply divided Israel prepares to vote
Old political alliances are fraying but the outcome is still deeply uncertain
Oct 22nd 2026
On the morning of October 7th 2023 Hamas fighters drove through the Israeli town of Sderot, less than a mile from Gaza, shooting at civilians. For Israelis, the small city became a symbol of the extent to which their nation’s defences had failed. In the last election, in 2022, over three-quarters of its voters plumped for parties that joined the coalition government of Binyamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister. But nine days before the country’s next election, Gadi Eisenkot and Naftali Bennett, the leaders of the two big centre-right parties and Mr Netanyahu’s main challengers, were there to hold him to account.
Three years after the massacres of October 7th, Mr Netanyahu’s rivals are determined to make the election a reckoning for that day and the wars and bloodshed that have followed. “Whoever promises total victory is hoodwinking the public,” Mr Eisenkot said on his visit, in reference to Mr Netanyahu’s wartime slogan. “He has nothing to offer.” Those listening murmured in assent, but many more in Sderot still back the prime minister and his allies. Travelling around Israel, it is clear that the country is deeply divided. No party is set to win over 20% of the vote. Political alliances are shifting. Mr Netanyahu and his allies have no obvious route to power but his squabbling foes may not be able to form a coalition either.
Sderot is a hardscrabble “development town” in the Negev where in the 1950s Jewish immigrants from elsewhere in the Middle East, the mizrahim, were sent to live. Resentment towards what many there see as an elite dominated by Ashkenazi (European) Jews still lingers, fuelling votes for Mr Netanyahu’s Likud and its allies.
Sderot and towns like it are plastered with pictures of Mr Eisenkot with the slogan “A prime minister dialna”, an evocative word in Moroccan Arabic that means “of us”. If he wins, he will become the first prime minister descended from the mizrahi wave of immigration. Many Israelis would prefer him or Mr Bennett to lead the country. But the prime minister has beaten the polls and expectations time and again.
Twenty minutes down the road from Sderot is Netivot, another coalition stronghold. Most of the customers at a popular couscous joint reckon Mr Eisenkot is in the clutches of “the left”. Three contractors eating lunch all voted Likud in the past. But only one, Kfir Almassi, says he’s “sticking with Bibi”. The other two are disappointed with the inconclusive outcome of the Gaza war. “Bibi is too left-wing for me,” says another, Nave Cohen. He plans to vote for the Jewish Power party. Its leader, Itamar Ben-Gvir, currently the national-security minister, promises to make the population of Gaza “voluntarily migrate” if he remains part of the government. The third, Yaniv Magen, plans to vote for Yisrael Beiteinu, an opposition party led by Avigdor Lieberman, a nationalist who has sworn to remove Mr Netanyahu but, like others in the opposition, refuses to join a government supported by Arab-Israeli parties.
And yet splits among religious and right-wing voters threaten the prime minister’s grip on power. Netivot is a stronghold of Shas, the mizrahi ultra-Orthodox party led by Arye Deri, Mr Netanyahu’s oldest political ally. But a new Haredi party has sprung up there. It is unlikely to cross the electoral threshold of 3.25% but it could still deny Shas, and thus the Netanyahu bloc, a seat.
Another new party, the Haredi Public, is challenging the established ultra-Orthodox parties. These have long been close partners of Likud and the recipients of lavish public funding for religious schools that fail to teach subjects such as maths and science. The Haredi Public represents young ultra-Orthodox Jews who want their children to have the skills to join the workforce and even enlist in the Israel Defence Forces. “We probably won’t cross the threshold,” admits one activist at a packed rally in Jerusalem. “But we’re founding a movement to change our community and that’s more important.” Mr Netanyahu, worried that they, too, will cost his coalition seats, has tried—unsuccessfully—to persuade the Haredi Public to withdraw.
Meanwhile in the coffee-shops of Tel Aviv, Israel’s liberal bubble, secular Israelis feel the pressure to vote tactically. Some like The Democrats, a merger of the two struggling parties of the Zionist left, but reckon Mr Eisenkot’s Yashar is more likely to beat Mr Netanyahu, even if it is more right-wing than they would prefer.
Many who care about Israel’s treatment of the Palestinians feel politically homeless. “Neither The Democrats or Mr Eisenkot are addressing the conflict with the Palestinians,” says Sarah Ben-Yaakov. She’s leaning towards Ra’am, an Islamist party which in 2021 became the first independent Arab party to join a ruling coalition.
It is increasingly clear that the Arab parties could be the deciding factor in this election. In Kfar Qasim, an Arab town east of Tel Aviv, a large Likud billboard looms, warning of the danger of Mr Eisenkot joining Arab partners. “They put the sign there to make us despair of any chance to influence events and not vote,” says Issa Amer, an engineering student.
In 2022 only 53% of Arabs voted; general turnout was 71%. Pollsters expect many more Arabs will vote this time. The Arab parties could win more than their current ten seats. They might take seats from Mr Netanyahu’s bloc. But given the opposition’s qualms,  they could make it harder for Mr Eisenkot to replace him.

epub_52.title: Russia is escalating its information war in Africa
epub_52.text:
Russia is escalating its information war in Africa
Middle East & Africa
| Propaganda extravaganza
Russia is escalating its information war in Africa
The Kremlin is betting it can sway public opinion on the continent
Oct 22nd 2026
ON OCTOBER 28TH African leaders will gather in Moscow for the third Russia-Africa summit since 2019. For Vladimir Putin the event is part of a concerted effort to persuade the global south that Russia is fighting on behalf of what he calls the “global majority” against “neocolonialism”. The bid has gathered pace since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. At the most recent summit in 2023 a spokeswoman claimed that “
Russian men
give their lives at the front so that people from the African continent are free.”
Many African leaders will scoff at such sentiments. But Mr Putin believes that the continent provides fertile ground for seeding Russia’s poisonous ideas. In February Sergei Lavrov, the foreign minister, said 90% of the Russian officials expelled from Europe had been reassigned to the continent. Russia has stepped up attempts to sway African hearts and minds through cultural diplomacy, the Orthodox Church, higher education, professional groups, media ventures and disinformation. As with its more muscular military interventions on the continent, it is hard to assess the success of this cognitive warfare. But Russia benefits from lingering sympathies for the Soviet Union as well as legitimate African criticisms of richer countries.
Russian efforts are like matryoshka dolls: there is more to them than meets the eye. Take cultural diplomacy. In September Russia said it would expand the number of “Russia Houses”, cultural institutions that operate under the ministry of foreign affairs, in Africa from 16 to 24. Critics, such as Ivan Klyszcz of the International Centre for Defence and Security, an Estonian think-tank, call them “nodes in Russian propaganda networks”. The films they show support Kremlin narratives: “Battle for Africa”, a documentary about how Russia came to the aid of Sahelian countries defying French “neocolonialism”, or “Why I Moved To Russia”, about Americans who supposedly fled wokeism at home. Ukraine alleges that the houses are used to recruit Africans to fight against it in the war. Governments in Europe are debating whether to close them in their countries for spreading propaganda.
The newest Russia House opened in São Tomé and Príncipe—a tiny former Portuguese colony that was a Soviet satellite in the cold war—in September in a former physiotherapy practice on the capital’s main road. An AI-generated collage with smiling São Tomeans and the Soviet slogan amizade dos povos (“friendship of peoples”) greets visitors at the entrance. Posters of authors, monarchs, sports stars and cosmonauts “tell the Russian story”, explains Inna Afanaseva, who runs the centre. A framed photo of Mr Putin stares down at students learning Russian.
A growing number of African students are moving to Russia: the latest tally, at 37,000 or so, is roughly five times greater than in 2010, in part because of an increase in scholarships. It recently surpassed the peak during the cold war, when the Soviet Union educated a generation of African elites, including the current presidents of Angola, Ghana and Namibia.
Russia Houses host meetings of professionals who studied in the Soviet Union, part of an effort to reactivate old relationships. They also convene gatherings for the Orthodox Church. The Kremlin has supported the church’s expansion in Africa, which is home to many conservative Christians, to position Russia as a haven for traditional values, in contrast to a supposedly decadent West.
Russia promotes media outlets on the continent. RT, a state-run service, has struck content-sharing deals with outlets such as Afrique Media from Cameroon. African Initiative, launched in 2023, claims to be an independent news agency but has close links to former members of the Wagner Group, a state-funded Russian mercenary outfit, and Russian intelligence, according to a report published by the French government last year. The report alleges that the outfit is behind false stories that blame America for spreading dengue fever in Burkina Faso and has probably spread the claim that France supports the jihadists who plague the Sahel.
Like many Russian efforts it works in tandem with African creators. Gandhi Malien Web TV, which is supported by African Initiative, has a talk show with a Malian presenter and a Russian journalist. In Burkina Faso “L’Heure Russe” is presented by MC Ruskof, a Russo-Burkinabe rapper.
Russian media are seeking influence over African journalism. RT and other state-funded outlets have held at least 20 training events for African journalists from at least 29 countries since July 2025. These courses include practical tips. But the material is tendentious. Ukrainian prisoners of war are labelled “neo-Nazis”. The massacre in Bucha at the start of the Ukraine war is used as an example of “fake news” that needs to be fact-checked.
Other falsehoods are pushed by a mix of online and offline campaigns. This year Forbidden Stories, a coalition of journalists, reported that a Russian-backed influence network known as “the Company” paid reporters throughout the global south for fake stories which ran in local media. To take one example, the campaign sought to undermine the Lobito corridor, an American- and EU-funded infrastructure project in Angola.
Russia also creates fake journalists. In a report published in August, Code for Africa, an NGO, and Graphika, a firm, identified as many as 35 ghost “reporters” with fake profiles. Their “articles” were published in real media outlets, whose content was picked up by others, creating a cycle of “information-laundering”. AI was often used to create personas and write stories and translate them into local languages.
Similar ghosts are appearing in other areas, says Justin Arenstein of Code for Africa. He notes the creation of fake academic research by fake academics that is uploaded onto preprint repositories, as well as fake think-tanks publishing reports that lend credibility to Russian narratives.
The impact of Russia’s efforts is hard to gauge. Few Africans watch RT or visit the website of African Initiative. Polls suggest that Russia is on average seen as a less positive influence on Africa than America, China or former colonial powers. That may reflect the fact that Russia has less to offer economically. Russia’s recruitment of African soldiers is a reminder of its war’s real costs, including to Africans.
Yet it would be wrong to take comfort from that. Mr Arenstein compares the impact of Russia’s campaign to termites eroding the structures of African societies. The Kremlin, he says, is unusual among disinformation merchants in that it deliberately tries to weaken social cohesion, rather than only promoting its own agenda. After all, the more fragile the country, the more Russia can exploit it.

epub_53.title: Joseph Kabila moves against his successor in Congo
epub_53.text:
Joseph Kabila moves against his successor in Congo
Middle East & Africa
| Rebel, rebel
Joseph Kabila moves against his successor in Congo
By seeking to unseat Félix Tshisekedi as president, he could upend politics
Oct 22nd 2026
Back in 1974 Kinshasa, the capital of what is now the Democratic Republic of Congo, hosted a lavish boxing match known as the “Rumble in the Jungle”. Today the city is gripped by a different heavyweight clash. In one corner is Félix Tshisekedi, the president. In the other is Joseph Kabila (pictured), an ex-president, who on October 12th stunned the country by announcing that he would lead a rebel coalition against his successor “by all means, including the use of force”.
Mr Kabila’s move threatens to worsen the conflict in the war-riven east. It also complicates Mr Tshisekedi’s bid to change the constitution to stay in power past the end of his second term in 2028. If either man can land a knockout blow it will shape the future of Africa’s second-largest country—of great interest to America, given its quest for critical minerals.
The feud has a long history. The latest chapter began in 2019, when Mr Tshisekedi was declared the winner of an election with more rigging than a giant sailboat. In the aftermath he struck a power-sharing deal with Mr Kabila that recognised the former president’s majority in parliament. That pact was torn up acrimoniously in 2020. Kabila loyalists were purged and Mr Kabila ultimately went into self-imposed exile, where he complained privately to other African leaders about what he saw as a power grab by an illegitimate successor.
Events in Kinshasa were inflamed by the conflagration in the east. In 2021 M23, a Rwandan-backed force, resurfaced after a dormant eight years, taking Goma and Bukavu, two regional capitals, in early 2025. To Mr Kabila, who was born in the east, the conflict was a reaction to his successor’s “tyrannical regime”. To Mr Tshisekedi, who won re-election less dubiously in 2023, the war was an invasion by Rwanda. When Mr Kabila moved to Goma in 2025, Mr Tshisekedi saw confirmation that his successor was a Rwandan stooge. In September 2025 Congo sentenced Mr Kabila to death in absentia for treason.
Over the next year Mr Kabila and M23 denied any links. “Kabila is not our boss,” Corneille Nangaa, the head of the group’s political arm, told The Economist in May. But he is now. Mr Kabila’s coalition includes M23. He wants to use the rebellion in the east to bring change to Kinshasa.
Will he succeed? NGOs in Goma are watching for troop movements south to the mineral-rich Katanga region. Yet M23’s fighters are more reluctant to expand the battlefield than their political peers. Rwanda has shown no sign of wanting to broaden the conflict either. It may have endorsed the elevation of Mr Kabila because it makes the conflict across the border look more of an intra-Congolese fight. Uganda, another player, wants to preserve a deal that lets it station its forces in the north-east of Congo. America, which put sanctions on Mr Kabila this year for his links to M23, is unlikely to welcome any effort to destabilise the regime of Mr Tshisekedi, with whom it has struck mineral deals.
Other Congolese opposition figures may prove decisive. An unwieldy coalition known as C64 (after the 64th article of the constitution rather than the popular 1980s computer) opposes Mr Tshisekedi’s power grab. Some previously called for Mr Kabila to be included in a “national dialogue”. But supporting him will be harder now.
Mr Kabila’s best hope might be that Mr Tshisekedi is so spooked that he becomes more paranoid and autocratic. That could prompt strategic errors—some in Kinshasa say the death sentence for Mr Kabila is an example of such a mistake—and prompt a backlash by political elites. Mr Tshisekedi is already under pressure. On October 14th Belgian authorities raided his relatives’ houses in connection with an investigation into money-laundering.
That would amount to Mr Kabila adopting the political equivalent of the “rope-a-dope” strategy used by Muhammad Ali in 1974. By leaning on the ropes to absorb blows, Ali let his opponent, George Foreman, punch his way to exhaustion. Then he delivered a knockout blow. “It’s not bragging if you can back it up,” Ali apparently said. Congo is waiting to see whether Mr Kabila can back it up, too.

epub_55.title: France’s devastation and its aftermath
epub_55.text:
France’s devastation and its aftermath
Europe
| Riots and politics
France’s devastation and its aftermath
The violence will benefit the extremes
Oct 22nd 2026
In Limoges the clock tower and roof of the 19th-century town hall collapsed after it was set alight. In Marseille casseurs, or hooligans, broke into the town hall. In Bordeaux hooded looters smashed the glass windows at Louis Vuitton and nearby shops, grabbing handbags, trainers and other stash. Pyres of electric scooters burned on street corners. Plumes of black smoke billowed in the air. Across the country over 2,000 people were arrested. “This evening we are all feeling anger, and shame,” declared President Emmanuel Macron in a televised address, before jetting off for a trip to the Gulf.
France is no stranger to upheaval. But even in a country hardened to street revolts, the events of October 17th were shocking. What set off this outburst of destruction? Mr Macron faced months of violent demonstrations by gilets jaunes (yellow jackets) in 2018-19. Yet the combination of devastation on the streets and powerlessness by the authorities was worse. It encapsulated a paralysis at the heart of government, a collapse in confidence in centrist politics, and lays the ground for greater division: voters at next spring’s presidential election could face a choice between the populist-right Marine Le Pen and the populist-left Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
The chaos was the result of a combustible mix on the streets—and an inadequate police presence. Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, conceded that the police had “lost control”, and a parliamentary inquiry has been opened. Those on the streets fell into three groups. The first were the half-million students, teachers and unionists who protested peacefully against underinvestment in education and the cost of living. “The casseurs are discrediting our movement,” complained Pauline, a 20-year-old university student, who said she was demonstrating against “everything”, from overcrowded lecture halls and high petrol prices to police repression. The unpopular president was also on her list. “Macron, t’es mort” (Macron, you’re dead) read graffiti near a smashed-up bus shelter, next to “ACAB”, or “all cops are bastards”.
A second group, the casseurs, have a history of infiltrating demos. Dressed in black and full-hooded, often wearing ski goggles and face masks, they looked to pick a fight. In France there are 600-800 members of such ultra-left groups, often anti-capitalist anarchists, said a parliamentary report in 2023. They are agile, covert and deft at evading the police. Of 48 “black blocs” (a group of casseurs) arrested after protests in 2023, 85% were men and 75% aged under 33. Most are well educated and not poor, noted the report. They seek “to create trouble in order to overturn the system”, said Mr Nuñez, then head of the Paris police.
The third group were opportunistic looters. Messages shared on TikTok guided youngsters to smashed-up shopfronts. In Bordeaux one young man casually swung stolen goods inside a shopping basket; others ripped looted Nike trainers from their boxes and ran. Within hours stolen goods were put on sale online—“jumper stolen during the demos” read one description—before the websites took them down. Some 3,000 shops and businesses were looted or vandalised.
Intelligence services had forecast a turnout of 200,000; the number was over twice that. Some 60,000 police officers were deployed, about a third less than during the worst days of the gilets jaunes protests. During earlier protests police were accused of brutality. This time shopkeepers were enraged that they were left to fend for themselves. Calm returned after Sébastien Lecornu, the prime minister, authorised partial curfews in Bordeaux, Paris, Marseille and other cities. Soldiers will help keep guard for the next protests, planned for October 24th.
The underlying tension is linked to the election, which is polarising politics. After nearly a decade in office, the centrist Mr Macron is constitutionally barred from running again. Many protesting students have no memory of life under a different leader. France wants change, but is deeply divided about what should come next.
Supporters of Mr Mélenchon, who joined the demo in Paris, saw the protests as a show of strength for their champion. Beforehand 69% of the French told a poll they backed the protesters, rising to 92% among his supporters. Backing for his Unsubmissive France (LFI) party is strong among the young and in the ethnically diverse banlieues, or suburbs, where schools are in the worst shape. A poll taken after the riots showed his base had held strong. Mr Lecornu, who blames the LFI for “exploiting” the protests, warned that the extreme left is using the violence as a “warm-up round” for the election. Mr Mélenchon blames the government for the disorder.
The real beneficiary, though, is Ms Le Pen. She got a small bump in the polls, which now give her 34-38% in the first round of the presidential election; Mr Mélenchon is on 15-20%. On October 18th she gave a presidential-style address, blaming the violence on “politicised casseurs” and “criminals from the banlieue”. Ms Le Pen regards the protests as evidence that Mr Mélenchon is unfit for office and that Mr Macron cannot control the country. One poll finds she would win a run-off against Mr Mélenchon by 68% to 32%.
Debate is shifting to law and order, which plays into her hands. Donald Trump claimed that France is being “burnt to the ground” by migrants.  But nearly all of the demonstrators are French, with white people as well represented as any other ethnicity. A government minister hinted at a racial element, but just among looters, blaming “a criminal fraction from the banlieue”.
This is fertile ground for foreign interference too. NewsGuard, an American disinformation monitor, found that 14 fake reports, often pointing the finger at migrants, were linked to a Russian influence operation. An AI-generated image of the Palestinian flag atop the Eiffel Tower was viewed 3.7m times. Mr Macron said there was indeed “foreign manipulation”, not of the events themselves, but about the narrative of what  happened.
The violence risks distracting France from the public debate it needs: about what sort of welfare system it can afford and how to generate the wealth required to sustain it. The public finances are in a dire state and the bond markets are jittery. Yet the centre is split, and lacks a compelling candidate. And the leading politicians vow to lower the retirement age, thus depriving themselves of future savings on the single biggest item of public spending.
Part of France understands this. The silent constituency was out again in the terrace cafés the day after the riots; a waiter in Bordeaux called the violence “scandalous”. But radicals are masterful at drowning out such voices. Unless the centre can find a persuasive way to tell a responsible story, about the need for order in the public finances and on the streets, voters will end up with no choice but the extremes.

epub_56.title: Unruly protests have shaken Albania, Italy and beyond
epub_56.text:
Unruly protests have shaken Albania, Italy and beyond
Europe
| A bit of the old ultra-violence
Unruly protests have shaken Albania, Italy and beyond
Radicals are turning demos into riots—and usually hurting their causes
Oct 22nd 2026
In several European countries, leftists inspired by weeks of protests in France have launched mass demonstrations of their own. But as in France, such protests are likely to benefit the right if they turn violent. The clearest case is Italy, where in October secondary-school students began imitating their French peers and occupying classrooms in protest against underfunding. Those have grown into broad demos over the cost of living, backed by left-wing parties and unions.
Things changed on October 17th, when several marches were hijacked by black-clad gangs. Riots erupted in Turin and Bologna, and fires were set in Milan’s Piazza del Duomo. Shops were looted, dozens of police injured and hundreds arrested. An October 17th Movement has emerged on Telegram and Instagram, calling for protests every Saturday until the government falls. A march is planned in Rome on October 24th, and many expect violence.
The rioters lack obvious leaders but have an unofficial soundtrack: Fabri Fibra’s “In Italia 2024”, a doom-laden anthem of social exclusion and rebellion. “We’re only at the beginning,” says Marracash, a rapper from Barona, a poor neighbourhood in Milan. The immigrant backgrounds of many rioters have provided ammunition for Matteo Salvini, head of the populist-right Lega party, to call for barring the Italian-born children of immigrants from acquiring citizenship if convicted of crimes.
Italy will hold a general election next year. Giorgia Meloni, the populist-right prime minister, has challenged the progressive Democratic Party and Five Star Movement to condemn the violence. By backing the legitimate demonstrations, they risk seeming to condone the rioting. Fear of disorder will probably benefit the right, says Raffaele Marchetti of the Luiss University in Rome. On October 20th Ms Meloni’s cabinet allowed preventive detention of minors, and gave policing powers to 500 soldiers in Milan. Yet the riots may benefit not her, but her rivals on the right. Roberto Vannacci, a far-right former general, and his opposition National Future party have said the police should use rubber bullets and dogs to disperse protesters.
Demos elsewhere also pit left against right. Spaniards have been protesting over housing costs since September, backed by Pedro Sánchez, the Socialist prime minister. Big protests over the cost of living have broken out in Portugal and Greece. On October 17th a few hundred far-left activists clashed with police in Brussels.
But the most violent demonstrations outside France and Italy are in Albania, and have a different background. Albanians have been protesting against the government of Edi Rama, the prime minister, since May 31st. For months the demonstrations were peaceful; prompted by a plan by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, to build a beach resort in a nature reserve, they were dubbed the Flamingo Revolution. But since October 13th a violent wing of the movement has attacked ministries, courts, banks and shops.
The Flamingo protests were always about more than resort development. Despite economic progress in recent years, Albania is one of the poorest countries in Europe and corruption levels are high. Mr Rama claims the riots are encouraged by Russia and Iran. He refuses to resign, and promises huge bonuses to police to take back the streets. One academic, who requested anonymity for fear of retaliation, said the protesters’ belief that they could force the prime minister out had been misplaced, but that his hard-line response had destroyed his legitimacy: “I don’t think there is any coming back from this.”
Most protesters despise the opposition leader, who was himself driven out as president by protests in 1997. But this week’s riots could mark the beginning of Mr Rama’s end. The riots in Albania, France, Italy and elsewhere do have one thing in common. Citizens are demanding things that governments, whether because of corruption or fiscal reality, cannot provide.

epub_57.title: Europe’s dependence on America in space is hard to escape
epub_57.text:
Europe’s dependence on America in space is hard to escape
Europe
| In space, no one can hear EU scream
Europe’s dependence on America in space is hard to escape
To reach autonomy in rockets and satellites, the continent needs more thrust
Oct 22nd 2026
THE STRONGEST signals that America is turning against Ukraine have come, this month, from outer space. Ukrainian drones’ connections to Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite-internet service, cut out at speeds above 160kph. Russian ballistic missiles smacked into Kyiv without the usual warnings from American spy satellites. Ukraine’s European allies reacted with deep foreboding. European defence chiefs can offer Ukraine only partial substitutes for American intelligence and communications networks. And they worry about their own dependence on America’s space-based capabilities, about whether these will stay available if Russia attacks and about how quickly they can develop their own alternatives.
All this is hastening efforts to develop alternatives. The day after Ukraine said restrictions had been placed on Starlink, shares in its closest European competitor, Eutelsat, surged by 23%. The European Union then moved to speed up the glacial pace of regulatory approval for merging the satellite-making businesses of three large European aerospace companies, hoping to create one big enough to compete with Mr Musk’s SpaceX. And on October 19th four of the region’s largest telecommunications firms said they wanted to partner with a satellite company
to compete with Starlink
.
Yet Europe
has a long way to go
before it can hope to achieve “autonomy in space”, as the jargon has it. In three crucial areas, it depends on America. The first is satellite-internet service for civilians and the armed forces. The second is space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) and early warning for defence. And the third is launch capacity: the rockets and spaceports needed to put a large number of satellites into orbit.
For decades, the space gap between Europe and America was widest in defence. America kept Europe dependent in part by letting its allies freeload on programmes such as SBIRS, an $18bn missile-warning constellation. But America also opposed Europe’s efforts to develop its own capabilities. It initially tried to block Galileo, a satellite navigation system, on the grounds that it would compete with America’s own
GPS
satellites, and could be used by its enemies.
Now, however, the biggest gap is in satellite internet, where America has rocketed ahead. Europe’s closest answer to Starlink is OneWeb, whose parent company, Eutelsat, is partly owned by the French and British governments. (Britain bailed the firm out after it collapsed in 2020, and both countries injected more capital last year.) OneWeb was founded in 2012, three years before Starlink, but was rapidly eclipsed by it: as a division of SpaceX, Mr Musk’s world-beating rocket company, Starlink had plenty of cash to fuel its massive expansion (see chart). The entry of other private firms may widen America’s lead. Amazon’s Leo aims to offer satellite internet later this year.
OneWeb has a number of terminals in Ukraine, some paid for by Germany, and is used by several European armed forces, including the French and British navies. It is also deployed on some aerial and naval drones. But it is not a direct replacement for Starlink. OneWeb has about 600 satellites; Starlink has more than 10,000. The European system cannot carry as much data or serve as many users in any one area. And because its satellites are in a much higher orbit, users need bigger terminals, the cheapest of which cost around $9,000—roughly 45 times more than a basic Starlink terminal. Kaja Kallas, the EU’s top diplomat, acknowledged this before meeting Mr Zelensky on October 16th: “Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine and unfortunately in the short term Europe can’t replace this capability.”
The EU plans to spend €15bn ($17bn) on IRIS2, a constellation of 348 communications satellites to be used by its members’ governments and armed forces. But the first will be launched only in 2029. Germany, meanwhile, plans its own network of 100 military-communications satellites at a cost of around €10bn. That has led to concerns of duplication and fragmentation.
There is more encouraging news when it comes to the second area of concern, space-based ISR, mainly thanks to private European newcomers that produce small surveillance satellites much faster than legacy firms such as Airbus. Admiral Anders Sundeman, the head of Sweden’s space force, says that if asked a year ago how long it would take to launch his country’s first spy satellite, he would have estimated 2030. “We launched it instead this year,” he says (though the launch happened on an American Falcon 9 ride-share flight). It was made by Iceye, a Finnish startup that has figured out how to shrink radar satellites that were once as big as a car down to the size of a washing machine. Iceye has put 80 into orbit and plans to double its production rate to 100 next year. Sweden has also signed a deal to buy small spy satellites from Planet Labs, an American startup that recently opened a factory in Germany.
Having lots of small, cheap satellites like these makes it easier to cope with losing a few to jamming, or to attack. That is a real risk. In mid-October a Russian satellite manoeuvred into a very close orbit with one made by Iceye that provides intelligence for Ukraine. Yet even if Ukraine’s satellite is disabled, the country has two more, along with access to intelligence from a number of European ones.
Other American capabilities will take far longer to replace. One is a ballistic-missile warning system. France and Germany are teaming up to build such satellites, but they will not come online until the early 2030s. Neither can Europe match the sensors and orbital weapons America deploys to protect friendly satellites and destroy hostile ones.
Finally, none of Europe’s plans will work if it does not have enough launch capacity to put its satellites in orbit. Arianespace, a European company owned mainly by Airbus and Safran, can fly heavy payloads into orbit. But it launches far fewer rockets than SpaceX and at much higher cost, which explains why many Iceye and OneWeb satellites were carried into space by the American firm. Even setting geopolitics aside, this dependence is worrying: there is a looming shortage of capacity as SpaceX gradually retires the Falcon 9 rocket, its workhorse.
If European countries hope to drive down the price of their rockets, they will need to commit to long-term spending plans to allow incumbents to invest, while also encouraging competition. The European Space Agency has a €900m “launcher challenge”, which pays companies if they achieve milestones such as a successful orbital launch. But once they prove they can do it, they need orders. “If you want your launcher to be as cheap as possible you need to launch it very regularly,” says Olivier Lemaitre, the secretary-general of Eurospace, a trade body. If demand remains small, he says, the industry will never achieve economies of scale. Europe’s countdown towards space autonomy will not last forever.

epub_58.title: The America-Ukraine link grows even spottier
epub_58.text:
The America-Ukraine link grows even spottier
Europe
| Signal failure
The America-Ukraine link grows even spottier
The Starlink cut-offs were a test, and worse may follow
Oct 22nd 2026
Editor’s note (October 22nd 2026): This article has been updated.
IN WASHINGTON last week’s move to cut Ukrainian drones’ connections to Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet service, might have seemed like a diplomatic warning. In Ukraine it was felt on the battlefield. In a single sortie, one unit saw $1m-worth of drones fall from the sky after limits were imposed on any that flew faster than 160kph. (By October 22nd the links were functioning again without speed limits, according to Ukrainian commanders.) No one in Donald Trump’s administration admits to making the decision. It appears to have come from a small circle around the president, Mr Musk and Steve Witkoff, the special envoy to Russia. Reports suggest Mr Musk wanted to punish Ukraine for striking Russian refineries. One official says he contacted the White House only after imposing the restrictions.
Mr Musk has a complicated relationship with Ukraine. In 2022 he used a similar mechanism to stop a naval drone attack near Crimea. He has frequently railed against President Volodymyr Zelensky. But his decision to provide satellite connectivity in the first days of the war was critical to Ukraine’s survival. One insider insists Mr Musk is sympathetic to Ukraine, “though you do get the impression that Putin sometimes gets to him first.”
For Vladimir Putin, the cut-offs capped a wonderful fortnight. On October 9th Mr Trump announced a dubious deal to buy Russian diesel. The Americans then demanded an “energy ceasefire”, but explained this meant that only Ukraine must stop hitting Russian refineries, not that Russia must stop hitting Ukrainian power plants. Reports that Mr Trump restricted intelligence-sharing, though, were misleading. A failure by American satellites to warn Ukraine of incoming ballistic missiles may have been due to Russian jamming and bad weather.
An American government source insists Mr Trump is not trying to force Ukrainian capitulation, but is the victim of “a successful Russian info-op”. The president, the source says, is panicked by terrible polling ahead of the midterms. Mr Zelensky is a convenient scapegoat. Mr Trump’s envoys, Mr Witkoff and Jared Kushner, incorrectly see Mr Putin’s motivations as economic and territorial rather than nationalistic, making them vulnerable to Russian manipulation. “Trump creates a horrible situation,” says a former official, but he is also “dependent on idiots”.
The American arm-twisting coincides with a rush to resurrect a lopsided peace deal. On October 21st Mr Witkoff went to St Petersburg, where he praised Mr Putin as a “humanitarian”. Ukrainian officials lack full details of the latest proposals, but the outline is familiar. There would be a demilitarised zone in Donbas. Russia would get American business deals, sanctions relief and political normalisation. Ukraine would get an investment package and EU membership in exchange for renouncing NATO membership. The newest sweetener for Mr Putin is an offer to restart Russian gas sales to Europe, which were due to be phased out entirely by year’s end, and to restart the Nord Stream pipeline.
This is not America’s to offer, and violates EU law. Nor does Russia seem inclined towards peace as it heads into its most destructive winter campaign yet. It will most likely stall while banking immediate concessions on sanctions. Ukraine’s negotiators fear the American envoys will front-load lucrative business deals before the war has ended. From their perspective, “why wait and lose time?” as a Ukrainian official puts it. “Time is money.”
A conversation on October 19th between Mr Zelensky and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, offered Ukraine a glimmer of hope. His renewed involvement in Ukraine suggests a fightback by the administration’s Russia hawks. But damage has been done. Mr Trump has again shown a preference for Mr Putin over Mr Zelensky. The Ukrainian president’s confrontational responses have deepened tensions.
Mr Zelensky’s turn to denouncing Mr Trump for “weak” decisions seems based on a gamble that an electoral drubbing will weaken him. That may be misplaced. The more a Democratic Congress investigates him, “the more aggressive he’ll be”, says a sympathetic congressional staffer. “This is not good for a country like Ukraine.”

epub_59.title: Germany’s young conservatives are angry with their own party
epub_59.text:
Germany’s young conservatives are angry with their own party
Europe
| Among the Johanneses
Germany’s young conservatives are angry with their own party
Members are disappointed with Friedrich Merz, but pleased with themselves
Oct 22nd 2026
SUCH IS THE power of the Junge Union (JU), the youth branch of Germany’s ruling centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), that all the party’s big beasts feel obliged to pay it homage. At last weekend’s JU congress in Bonn, each was given a prizefighter’s entrance, complete with flashing spotlights and theme music selected by the organisers. Friedrich Merz, the CDU’s embattled chancellor, will have been happy with “We stay united through the storm”. Hendrik Wüst, the premier of North Rhine-Westphalia and a potential challenger to Mr Merz, looked a little bewildered on entering to the thump of “You should know that baby you’re the best”, before delivering a dull speech. As for the congress’s slogan, “Tomorrow is loading”, it seemed either an ironic nod to information-superhighway dreams of yore or an attempt to sound vaguely digital. Either way, it was better than the toe-curling Denglish of last year’s “What the Future?!”
The JU is where Germany’s ambitious conservatives come to network, drink and complain about the Mutterpartei (mother party, ie, the CDU). They are a lively bunch, if not a diverse one: bar a smattering of women, almost everyone seems to be called Johannes. The most important is the 34-year-old Johannes Winkel, head of the JU, who has emerged as an irritant for Mr Merz. Last year Mr Winkel threatened to torpedo the government’s plan to raise pensions. In his speech this year he said the CDU was living in the past, passing off minor tweaks as ambitious “reforms” and risking extinction. The JU’s opinions matter because their group in the Bundestag has 20 MPs—which, as members point out, is larger than the 12-seat majority held by Mr Merz’s coalition. Mr Winkel has warned that last year’s insurrection will pale next to what will come if a new pension reform, designed to rein in costs, is watered down.
If these young conservatives are angry, it is because nothing hurts so much as betrayal. It was the true believers of the JU who formed the vanguard of Mr Merz’s multiple attempts to become CDU leader, the third of which succeeded in 2021. At last, they thought, a true-blooded conservative saviour to wash away the mushy centrism of the long Angela Merkel years. (One thing the JU and Mr Merz agree on is that Mrs Merkel’s 16-year reign was an embarrassment.)
But since Mr Merz won last year’s election it has been disappointment upon disappointment: borrowing binges, in-fighting and endless concessions to the Social Democrats (SPD), the junior coalition partner. At last year’s youth bash Mr Merz alienated everyone by urging the JU to cool its reformist zeal. This year he was on best behaviour, offering full support for the proposed pension reform. His speech “wasn’t a success, but it wasn’t a failure”, sniffed one delegate.
Mr Merz also showed he can press the crowd’s buttons. He earned the weekend’s biggest applause by deploring a proposed coalition in Berlin led by the
populist-left Die Linke party
, which won a recent election in the capital. Many in the CDU, and beyond, believe that party’s Berlin branch is crawling with antisemites and subversives. Yet just as the delegates’ fury peaked, Die Linke clinched an agreement with the Greens and SPD to begin coalition talks. That inspired the JU to pass a resolution, spearheaded by another Johannes, demanding “political and social ostracism” of any such government. It featured a picture of a young man in a keffiyeh and the slogan Nie wieder ist jetzt! (“Never again is now!”), a rather hysterical invocation of the Holocaust.
These days it is easier for youth delegates to rage against leftists than against the populist-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). The CDU as a whole has not gone soft on the party that has destroyed its polling lead; Mr Merz had harsh words for the AfD, too. But some CDU delegates in the parliament of Saxony-Anhalt, an eastern state where the AfD
won a near-majority
in an election last month, may soon break the party line and give the radicals the votes they need to take office there. The CDU in Saxony-Anhalt, sighs a third Johannes, is an “unguided missile”.
No wonder delegates struggled to believe that the CDU had figured out how to recover. “The party is crumbling,” confided one, adding that he is embarrassed to tell his friends he is a member. The CDU’s young guard seems to be bursting with self-confidence at precisely the moment it has lost faith in the Mutterpartei. But as one CDU grandee puts it, the JU always thrives when its elders are struggling. Kids tend to think they know best. And these ones have the numbers in parliament to prove it.

epub_60.title: How France became ungovernable at home yet unstoppable in Brussels
epub_60.text:
How France became ungovernable at home yet unstoppable in Brussels
Europe
| Charlemagne
How France became ungovernable at home yet unstoppable in Brussels
The paradox of Parisian power
Oct 22nd 2026
There are better ways to vaunt the merits of your economic model than setting fire to your capital. But tell that to the French. In recent years protests have become such a fixture of national life it is hard to see when one set of manifestations ends and the next begins. Everyone from students to pensioners seems to walk about in a perennial huff. The political class is at war with itself, wondering if an unloved president will soon make way for a populist rabble-rouser. Bond vigilantes are giving a bloody nose to the over-indebted government in Paris, demanding ever-higher yields to finance its runaway budgets. The recent
spate of violence
gives the impression of a state at once bloated and overmatched. As always, the situation looks somewhat less dire from inside France than it does to outsiders. Still, who would want to emulate the policies of a place that seems so firmly on the skids?
Moi! Moi! Moi! is the refrain from France’s neighbours in the European Union. For even as Paris reeks of tear gas, ideas promoted by French officialdom for decades have become ascendant in EU circles. Particularly on economic matters, French thinking is being copy-pasted into statute books in Brussels. France may be running out of money, political stability and public patience; it is not running out of influence. A country that plenty think ought to serve as a cautionary tale is instead being treated as a blueprint. Call it the paradox of Parisian power: even as French politicians lose the ability to govern at home, they are tightening their ideological grip on Europe.
Brussels was once a place where France’s instincts for state intervention collided with Germany’s faith in markets and (relatively) free trade—and usually lost. The EU’s institutions have long had a liberal bent that blunted France’s big-state, dirigiste preferences. The club’s rules prevented national governments from meddling in industrial matters by doling out money to favoured firms and so forth. (The French got generous farming subsidies in return.) Far from protecting national champions, the EU was usually minded to let domestic firms face competition from both within the bloc and outside. Parisian policymakers fumed at the hemming-in of the state’s capacity to do something. From the outset of his presidency a decade ago, Emmanuel Macron warned it was resulting in Europe losing its “strategic autonomy”—broadly, the ability for the continent to act independently in a world increasingly dominated by America and China. Many in the club dismissed this as a bit of Gallic eccentricity, along with the penchant for escargots and taking August off.
No longer. These days French-infused scepticism of globalisation and unfettered markets is close to being orthodoxy. Those EU rules preventing public money from being showered onto national champions are all but forgotten: subsidies once considered evidence of economic illiteracy (including by this newspaper, often) are now presented as proof of strategic sophistication. “Industrial policy” has gone from taboo to mainstream. The French idea that Europe has been naive—practising economic self-restraint while America and China brazenly pursue economic self-interest—is now commonplace. Free trade is still tolerated, but only insofar as it does not interfere with broader aims of Europe recouping some measure of economic sovereignty.
How did French ideas triumph, even as France has seemingly gone off the rails? In part, because what once looked like Parisian paranoia has come to seem like foresight. Many in the EU sniggered when Mr Macron in 2019 warned in an interview with The Economist that Europe risked being “no longer in control of its destiny”. Events proved him right. Covid-19 made globe-spanning supply chains spawned by free-trade evangelists seem less clever to some. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 underscored how relying on imports—in this case, of natural gas—brought with it unwanted dependencies (of the sort China went on to exploit with niche raw materials). And maybe, just maybe, generations of French presidents had been right to warn that America might one day prove an unreliable guarantor of European security.
Internal dynamics in the union have helped France’s cause, too. Brexit deprived the EU of a power whose raison d’être was to resist Gallic-infused thinking in Brussels. More recently Germany has made a startling pivot to support French economic interventionism, finding free trade much less appealing as Chinese firms started competing effectively with its own carmakers. Consider a slew of “Made in Europe” plans put forward by the EU’s industry commissioner, Stéphane Séjourné, a Frenchman close to Mr Macron. They advocate earmarking public spending for EU firms. Such protectionism would once have been dismissed out of hand by officials in Berlin. Now they merely want to make sure at least some allies such as Britain and Canada are included in an expanded definition of Europe. The aim is to water down French plans, not thwart them.
For those Europeans already uneasy about importing France’s Colbertist instincts, there is a more unsettling thought: Mr Macron may prove the moderate version of France’s attempt to remake the EU. Marine Le Pen, the populist currently leading the polls, would seek to recast the EU along more nationalist lines.
Will adopting French ideas end up hobbling Europe, as it seemingly has France? Not necessarily. There is a difference between a state that intervenes strategically and one that spends indiscriminately. France’s predicament offers lessons in both. Mr Macron was right to warn that Europe needs greater autonomy from foreign foes. But a country that cannot control its own finances has precious little autonomy either. France got the diagnosis right. It is a pity it made such a mess of the treatment.
