epub_62.title: Britain’s welfare state is living on borrowed time
epub_62.text:
Britain’s welfare state is living on borrowed time
Britain
| Magical thinking
Britain’s welfare state is living on borrowed time
But John Healey’s budget will feed the delusion that it is not
Oct 22nd 2026
One of the great fantasies of British politics is that the country can sustain a welfare state similar to today’s without raising taxes. It looks as if John Healey will be the latest chancellor to peddle this fiction, at his budget on October 28th. Taxes account for 32% of the cost to employ an average single Briton, three percentage points less than the rich-world average. Yet in return citizens expect a full-service welfare state, including free health care and universal pensions. Successive governments this century have funded this jammy deal only by taxing high earners hard, skimping on defence, letting public services deteriorate—and borrowing a fortune.
This strategy is running out of road. Poor growth and an ageing population, combined with increasing geopolitical turmoil, are stretching the public finances far too close to breaking point. Failure to reckon with these realities has given Britain’s past few budgets an air of perpetual crisis, with one chancellor after another scrambling to make up perennial shortfalls. Mr Healey’s budget is shaping up to be a classic of the genre, fiddling with small tax rises when in fact the whole system is flawed. Difficult decisions seem set to be postponed until a spending review next year.
The backdrop is bleak. Britain’s ten-year borrowing cost has risen to 5.4%, from 4.4% at the latest forecast by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) in March. That is partly because the Iran war has raised energy prices, but many other factors—from outsize government borrowing to surging global demand for capital—mean bond yields are unlikely to fall soon. The Resolution Foundation, a think-tank, reckons the government will need to spend £14bn ($19bn, or 0.4% of GDP) more on debt interest in the fiscal year to 2030 than previously assumed.
Mr Healey has signed up to fiscal rules ensuring day-to-day spending is fully covered by taxes in three years’ time, with debt also falling as a percentage of GDP by then. In March he was forecast to follow these rules with £24bn to spare, but the Resolution Foundation reckons only £12bn remains. (Other forecasts are sunnier.)
The chancellor has also said his budget will maintain a financial “buffer against uncertainty” and give people a “bit of breathing space”. This suggests he will dispense help with the cost of living, through targeted subsidies for energy bills, for instance, or by postponing a planned rise in fuel duty. Depending on his exact choices, expect taxes to rise modestly by 2030, probably via small-ish measures such as higher levies on banks or gamblers.
A low-drama budget would be no disaster. If Mr Healey stuck to plans made by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, in March, the deficit would fall from 4.4% of GDP in the past fiscal year to 1.8% by 2030. France, in contrast, is on track to run a deficit of 5.4% of GDP in 2026, having aimed for 5%.
But Britain should try to do more than beat the French, and abiding by the letter of the fiscal rules does not mean its public finances are in good repair. The rules themselves are eyebrow-raisingly loose, never requiring deficits or debts to actually fall. They need only be forecast to fall in three to five years—so the Treasury can always dodge hard choices by promising restraint that then fails to arrive (see chart 1). This looks likely to happen again: plans rely on real-terms cuts to many departments’ budgets that few expect to happen.
And so Britain’s debt is like a ratchet, jumping up at every crisis and never coming back down by much. Debt, excluding the Bank of England’s balance sheet, is now 92% of GDP, up from 76% before the covid-19 pandemic and 36% before the financial crisis of 2007-09. Higher bond yields have made servicing this debt painful. The government’s annual interest bill has more than doubled since the pandemic, to £109bn. That is 8% of government spending, more than the entire defence budget. When crisis next strikes, therefore, Britain may struggle to borrow its way out.
The country’s failure to pay off its debts stems from a mismatch between the state Britons want and the taxes they are willing to pay. Government spending will constitute 45% of GDP in the fiscal year to 2027, up from 39% before covid. The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS), a think-tank, points out that the last time public spending was sustained at such a high level was during the second world war.
The biggest culprit is the National Health Service. The state forks out 8.4% of GDP on health care, up from 4.9% in 2000 (see chart 2). As the population ages, and as the sector’s productivity lags behind the wider economy’s, this share will climb. The OBR reckons that health-care spending could reach 13% of GDP by the 2070s.
A growing cohort of geriatrics also needs food, accommodation and social care. In July the OBR thought spending on the state pension alone could rise from 5% of GDP by 2031 to 9% by the 2070s. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, has since said he will tweak the “triple lock”, which raises the state pension each year, to make it slightly less generous after 2030. But any savings will be swallowed by his plans for a new National Care Service.
Britain used to pay for its welfare state by spending less on defence. Threats from Russia and China mean that is no longer an option. The government has pledged to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, up from 2.7% in the fiscal year to 2028. In total, the OBR thinks that government spending excluding interest payments could rise from 40% of GDP in 2030 to 49% by the 2070s. If revenues stayed constant, Britain’s debt would balloon (see chart 3).
Should an imminent debt crisis loom, the government would take action. But the incentive to move early is weak because no one knows when this might happen. A growth spurt, perhaps fuelled by artificial intelligence, may postpone the reckoning (though it would probably also raise borrowing costs). The ageing of Britain’s population nevertheless means a reckoning is coming. When it does, one option would be drastic cuts to spending: reducing the state pension, say, or tightening eligibility for disability benefits. A brave government might even start charging patients to book a doctor’s appointment.
The alternative is rethinking the tax system. Since coming to power in 2024 Labour has been constrained by its foolish manifesto pledge not to increase income tax, national insurance, value-added tax (VAT) or corporation tax. These account for over 70% of tax revenue. Labour has already broken its promise, notably by raising the national insurance paid by employers. The total tax take is forecast to be 38% of GDP by 2030, the highest since the 1940s.
Mr Healey will be loth to break Labour’s manifesto pledge again. But if his party does not want to cut long-term spending it will have to reconsider how the government raises revenue. Some cash could come from higher taxes on the rich. The chancellor could, say, rejig capital-gains tax to skim more from unusually high investment returns. For now, however, he has reportedly rejected calls from some Labour MPs to raise capital-gains tax.
In any case, higher levies on wealth would not fund the sort of welfare state Britons have become accustomed to. For that, politicians and voters would have to accept that broad swathes of society need to start contributing more. This could involve ditching the list of products, such as many clothing and food products, which are exempt from VAT. Altogether, these exemptions cost the state £70bn a year. Or the government could raise the level of income tax paid by low and middle earners.
None of these options is politically appealing. But Britain’s fiscal reckoning might come sooner rather than later. Next year’s spending review will set departmental budgets for at least the following three. Earlier this year, when Mr Healey was defence secretary, he said it was crucial for defence spending to rise to 3% of GDP by 2030. He then resigned when the Treasury refused. The IFS reckons that meeting this target, while raising health-care spending and avoiding other real-terms cuts, would cost an extra £35bn a year by 2030.
To grasp the scale of this cost, consider that funding it would be equivalent to raising the basic rate of income tax from 20% to about 24%. If—as looks likely—Mr Healey instead fiddles at the edges on October 28th, he may get away with it for a while. Eventually, though, the bill will fall due.

epub_63.title: Britain’s least-loved hotel chain is finally splashing the cash
epub_63.text:
Britain’s least-loved hotel chain is finally splashing the cash
Britain
| Britannia waives the rules
Britain’s least-loved hotel chain is finally splashing the cash
New management, and the loss of government business, bring a change of strategy
Oct 22nd 2026
The Adelphi Hotel, an Edwardian pile in Liverpool, has hosted everyone from Winston Churchill to Roy Rogers and his horse Trigger. Among Britain’s most luxurious hotels when it opened in 1914, it boasted Turkish baths, a heated indoor pool and shooting galleries. Charles Dickens described his dinner at an earlier incarnation as “undeniably perfect”. Today the pool and spa are closed, the shooting gallery is inoperative and your correspondent’s £14.95 ($19.80) supper was scraped from a tepid buffet shortly before it closed at 8pm. The Adelphi ranks 105th of 112 Liverpool hotels on TripAdvisor.
It belongs to Britannia Hotels, Britain’s largest privately owned hotel chain, with 64 hotels and over 10,000 rooms. Britannia has finished last in 12 consecutive surveys of big hotel chains by Which? magazine. Yet many of those years coincided with healthy profits. Now Britannia is changing course. Its 88-year-old founder, Alex Langsam, has stepped back and a four-person management board plans “immediate and rolling upgrades” to rejuvenate its hotels and reputation. Why the shift?
It is a tricky time for British hotels. Wages, business rates and energy costs are rising—and customers are increasingly value-conscious. Britannia is positioned as a budget operator, with an average room price (£84 in 2025, according to Which?) higher than Travelodge’s (£69) but lower than Premier Inn’s (£94). Those chains offer consistency in standardised hotels, many purpose-built and leased. Britannia has an owner-operator model. Under Mr Langsam it accumulated an eclectic estate of grand old buildings. He once described his company as merely the “custodians for a period of time” of such heritage assets.
For years its expanding estate delivered erratic returns. Then its fortunes improved. Pre-tax profits averaged nearly £20m in the three years before covid-19, despite dismal survey ratings. This coincided with an important new customer: the government. Hoteliers could earn “much more” from housing asylum-seekers, says Philippa Goldstein of Knight Frank, a consultancy. Government spending on asylum hotels surged to more than £2bn a year after covid. Britannia’s pre-tax profits hit a record £39m in 2023; reports suggested that at least 17 of its hotels were block-booked on the government’s behalf. But as the number of asylum-seekers in hotels has fallen from over 56,000 to around 16,000, its annual profits have dipped to £27m.
One hotel, Daresbury Park (“located just off Junction 11 of the M56”), featured prominently in the 2025 Runcorn and Helsby by-election. During the campaign the Home Office announced that its asylum contract would end; the anti-immigration Reform UK won by six votes anyway. Since then Britannia has given the hotel a multi-million-pound glow-up.
On a recent visit, an £84 room was smart and the evening bar lively, especially for an out-of-town business park in Cheshire. Britannia calls Daresbury Park a “prime example” of what its investment can achieve. The hope is that its refurbished hotels will attract more paying customers as government contracts recede.
That is a work in progress. Back at the Adelphi, a dated bedroom came with a pristine new bathroom, although the shower prevented the door opening beyond half way. Several coach parties of older guests added to the throwback atmosphere. For Britannia preserves something besides old buildings: a tradition of communal British holiday-making. At coastal properties this year Britannia introduced a seaside-entertainment programme, with bingo, quizzes and live shows.
Some of Britain’s most high-profile old buildings have recently been repurposed as luxury hotels under international hospitality groups. In London the Old War Office is now a Raffles hotel; Admiralty Arch’s conversion into a Waldorf Astoria is nearly complete. Both are advertising rooms at upwards of £800 a night. A stay at the Adelphi, a Liverpool landmark owned by a British company, set The Economist back £53.40. As Mr Langsam once put it: “Our extraordinary buildings are enjoyed by ordinary people.”

epub_64.title: Britain’s elite may soon become harder to spot
epub_64.text:
Britain’s elite may soon become harder to spot
Britain
| The luminaries
Britain’s elite may soon become harder to spot
“Who’s Who”, a reference book that tracks them, is being sold
Oct 22nd 2026
“THATCHER, Baroness” liked “music, reading”. “CHAMBERLAIN, Col. Sir Neville”, as an earlier volume of “Who’s Who” recorded, enjoyed “shooting”. “STALIN, Joseph” and “HITLER, Adolf” did not deign to send in their recreations (unlike “MUSSOLINI, Benito”, who liked “violin, horse-riding, fencing”). “CHURCHILL, Rt. Hon. Winston” did not find time to record his, either. After war broke out, though, he did find time to personally intervene and ensure that “Who’s Who” would still be printed despite paper shortages. It was, he considered, of “national importance”.
And it used to be. First published in 1849, “Who’s Who” is the world’s oldest biographical reference annual, one of its most influential and, arguably, its oddest. Its pillar-box red volumes were conceived to catalogue a certain sort of British elite and the occasional foreigner (the first entry listed in 1849 was “our Beloved SOVEREIGN”, Queen Victoria). But its influence, much like that of its elite, spread, and soon it had colonised other realms. “Who’s Who” was followed by “Wer ist wer?” for Germany, “Hvem er hvem?” for Norway and even “Who Was Who” for the afterlife. Leon Trotsky was included in the 1938 "Who’s Who”. In the current edition John McDonnell, a former Labour MP, lists his recreations as “fermenting the overthrow of capitalism”—with spelling, evidently, being less of an enthusiasm.
Now Bloomsbury, which publishes “Who’s Who”, has announced that it is selling it. It is uncertain who the buyer will be, or indeed whether it will continue to be printed. This matters. “Who’s Who” has lasted for so long, and gathered so much data—179 editions and over 125,000 entries—that it offers less mere anthology than anthropology. Past editions provide an unrivalled data source on that elusive species, the English elite. They list everything from habitats (each entry gives “Address” and “Clubs”) to hobbies (“Recreations” were added in 1897) and even elite humour: the comedian John Cleese listed his pastimes as “gluttony, sloth”.
How the “Who” are selected is complicated. Broadly speaking, entrants are split into two categories. One is bigwigs you mostly haven’t heard of (MPs, KCs, judges, peers, other types who wear tights), who gain automatic admission by virtue of their roles. The other is bigwigs you may know (actors, writers, business figures), whose entry is voted on by a board of advisers. Though quite who chooses the choosers is unclear: to stop bribery and corruption it is, says Sam Friedman, a professor of sociology at the LSE, “shrouded in secrecy”.
Its outcomes, by contrast, are illuminating. The elite of “Who’s Who” are, as Professor Friedman has shown, notably more male (over 80% are men) and pale (almost 97% are white) than Britain as a whole. They are also more likely to live in London (almost 36%, versus 13% for the average Briton), more likely to be privately educated (47% versus 6%) and far likelier to have gone to Oxbridge (35% versus 1%). Who is who in Britain feels rather similar to who was who—and both are largely who you would expect. In the 1850s a quarter of entrants listed “hunting” as a hobby. One later one liked hunting “tusker elephants” and another “hunting the Philistines”.
What for socialists is cause for handwringing is, for historians, cause for celebration. Such an archive is “absolute gold dust”, says Sir Tristram Hunt, director of the V&A museum. Even in an era of online oversharing “Who’s Who”, in its longevity, comparability and sheer triviality, offers the historian information that he says is “very, very hard to find elsewhere”. (Such as, perhaps, the fact that “HUNT, Tristram” enjoys “fresh-water swimming, ceramics [and] book-browsing”.) Some of the most telling details are incidental. Early volumes have telegram addresses, car number plates and a habit of referring to female writers as “authoress”.
Best of all it is still in print, for its volumes speak volumes. Whereas written history is, says Sir Tristram, “as much about the present as the past”, “Who’s Who” offers a yesterday unmediated by today. Open the 1938 volume and those entries—“HITLER, Adolf”, “STALIN, Joseph”, “CHURCHILL, Winston”—feel eerie in their unknowing; a cast list for a play that is yet to be played whose ending is yet to be written.
“Who’s Who” can feel like a monument to an unchanging elite.  But it shows Britain’s elites are changing: fewer list hunting as a hobby; now they like pets and displaying an awkward irreverence towards things like “Who’s Who”. (Several list “sex” as a recreation.) They are, probably, less likely to display a copy of “Who’s Who” at home. Britain’s elite will not disappear but it may, thinks Professor Friedman, be harder to spot if this “important window” is lost.
Like most monuments to magnificence, however, “Who’s Who” is also an Ozymandias-like monument to obsolescence. Pick up an old volume today and what strikes you most is not the entrants’ authority but their anonymity. Hitlers, Stalins and Churchills aside, you will hardly have heard of any of them.

epub_65.title: Mockery keeps Britain’s politicians honest. (Almost)
epub_65.text:
Mockery keeps Britain’s politicians honest. (Almost)
Britain
| Media mischief-makers
Mockery keeps Britain’s politicians honest. (Almost)
The ancient art of the parliamentary sketch is thriving in the digital era
Oct 22nd 2026
“The sluice gates of mediocrity opened. Before long the audience were up to their beaks in it, like chickens in a flash flood.” The Daily Mail’s verdict on a recent speech by Lucy Powell, Britain’s education secretary, was not kind. Nor was the Times’s on Sir Ed Davey, leader of the Liberal Democrats, who “looked and sounded, as he always does, like a smiley rural GP doling out cod-liver oil to old ladies” during his party-conference speech in September.
Both got off lightly compared with the Conservatives’ shadow chancellor. “Even 20 minutes of Andrew Griffith can rip your soul in half,” the Guardian wrote in October. “Griffith proceeded to give the worst speech ever heard. Not just in content but in delivery. It was like watching a less sentient version of the PG Tips monkey.”
Such indelicate sentiments are common on social media, but in most countries they rarely grace the pages of mainstream newspapers. On Fleet Street, however, they are positively encouraged. For that you can thank the ancient, still-thriving art of the British parliamentary sketch.
When John Healey, the chancellor, delivers his first budget on October 28th, he will care most about the responses of MPs, voters and the bond market. But he will probably keep half an eye on the sketches, too, since a well-turned phrase in a sketch can dog a politician for the rest of their career. Theresa May, while prime minister, never managed to escape the nickname of “Maybot”, attached to her by the Guardian’s John Crace after a particularly robotic set of interviews about Brexit.
A sketch has nothing to do with drawing. Rather, it is a comic but factual report of a political news event—usually parliamentary proceedings, a speech or an interview. It recounts what was said and what the sketch writer thought of it, along with plenty of jokes at the politicians’ expense. Four daily newspapers and two magazines employ sketch writers; in contrast, all British media outlets between them now employ only one trade-union correspondent. The practice began in the early 19th century and every sketch writer dreams of reaching the heights of their greatest predecessor, Charles Dickens, who wrote for the Mirror of Parliament.
Other Fleet Street traditions, such as spot-the-ball competitions and topless “page three girls”, have died in the age of the internet. But the sketch lives on. The chaos of the Brexit era helped, according to Mr Crace: “The sketch was reborn, because it was sometimes the only thing that could capture the hallucinogenic nature of politics at the time.” Another reason for its survival, says Rob Hutton, who writes sketches for the Critic, a magazine, is that practitioners of the art can be “more honest”. News reporters, by contrast, might feel uneasy about straightforwardly accusing politicians of lying.
What makes a good sketch? For Mr Crace, the important thing is to identify the issue of the day and shine a light on it. Quentin Letts of the Daily Mail takes a different approach: he files reports from the most obscure Commons debates, and enjoys bringing little-known politicians to life. (Keir Mather, a junior transport minister, “looks about 14 and is almost definitely yet to buy his first razor”, Mr Letts noted archly in a recent piece.)
The sketch squad agree that a good one does more than make readers laugh; it illuminates the psychology of the powerful. “The best sketch writer is a political thinker,” says Sir Peter Stothard, a former editor of the Times. Mr Hutton sees potential in exposing the gap between how Andy Burnham sees himself—as a blokey outsider to Westminster—and how the prime minister comes across to others.
Not all MPs fear being brutalised in a sketch. Sir Robert Buckland, a former Conservative cabinet minister, says he considered it a “badge of honour” to be mocked. Commons colleagues sit around in parliamentary cafés reading choice excerpts out loud to each other, he adds. He has no sympathy for the sketch writers’ victims: “It’s like sailors complaining about the sea, isn’t it, really? Don’t get on the water if you don’t like it.”

epub_66.title: How to help your child trounce the robots
epub_66.text:
How to help your child trounce the robots
Britain
| Upskilling Britain
How to help your child trounce the robots
Junior workers need to act like senior executives
Oct 22nd 2026
WHAT SKILLS does your child need on the cusp of an industrial revolution? That was the question Robert Campbell unwittingly sought to answer for parents in 18th-century London. His manual, published in 1747, contained useful advice on choosing an apprenticeship and the rather harder-to-follow injunction to “improve the genius, temper and disposition of their children”. Drawing could transform a mere cabinet-maker into a master craftsman; a prospective mercer (the luxury-fashion buyers of their day) should “by no means be an awkward clumsy fellow”. There were even tips on how to avoid “the many temptations to which youth are liable in this great City”: female artisans could make a good living if they didn’t succumb to gin.
Parents today need not contend with the gin craze of the 1740s. But a bigger threat to their children’s future, many worry, is artificial intelligence, which could revolutionise the world of work much faster than the steam engine did.
No one knows exactly how it might do so, and much doom-mongering has been premature at best. Take the prediction in 2016 by Geoffrey Hinton, a British AI pioneer, that the technology would replace radiographers within five years. Instead it has raised demand for them. Other bets have failed, too. “It wasn’t that long ago that people were saying, ‘we’ve got to train everyone in prompt engineering,’” says Euan Blair, who runs Multiverse, a training firm. “That now seems pretty pointless.”
Conventional career paths are already being disrupted. “Just become an accountant” seems like worse advice with much of that job being automated and 29% fewer people being hired for entry-level roles than last year. In Britain’s service-dominated economy many other junior jobs look exposed, too. What is a young person, or a helicopter parent, to do? A modern-day Campbell could offer a few pointers.
One is that people with the right technical skills will stay in high demand. Britain has too few AI specialists, so it pays to be one of them—especially in the already-lucrative financial-services sector. Manufacturing jobs that require AI skills command a lower wage premium in Britain than elsewhere. But this is still a hefty 25%, reckons PwC, a consultancy.
Second, even if most workers will not help to develop AI, they will benefit from understanding it. Today’s government is far more hands-on than in Campbell’s time, and aims to train 10m workers to use the technology. Quality is patchy, with some courses being little more than collections of outdated slide decks. But it is a start. A survey in June, by the Office for National Statistics, found that only 41% of adults said they had used AI in the previous 12 months for work or study. (Among 16- to 29-year-olds, that rose to 63%.)
Autodidacts will be especially keenly sought after, because employers are spending less on training their workers than at any time in over a decade. Only a few enthusiastic firms offer meaningful courses in AI. One is Evri, a logistics company which has quotes by Steve Jobs, Apple’s co-founder, on its office walls. At its industrial hub on the outskirts of Barnsley, in northern England, white-collar workers huddle around laptops. This is a “hackathon” led by a Multiverse instructor fond of change-management theories. Either side of a lunch of sausage rolls and scotch eggs, the teams clean up data sets and use AI in an exercise to optimise parcel deliveries, then finish the event by delivering AI-generated presentations. Bright youngsters can do this sort of thing on their own.
They will struggle more to develop soft skills in isolation—and communication, judgment and team-building may in fact be the most important qualities to cultivate in the age of AI. Data from LinkedIn show that the most sought-after skill among sales workers on its platform is building customer relations. In contrast, AI literacy comes fifth. Moreover, Sue Duke, LinkedIn’s head of global policy, notes that workers are seven times as likely to land a job when they have a connection with someone already at a company. Schmoozing, in other words, matters almost as much as in Campbell’s day.
This is bad news for Britain’s young people. One recent analysis found that 15- to 16-year-old Britons have worse social and emotional skills, such as co-operation and resilience, than their peers abroad.
The harsh reality is that youngsters must now demonstrate such qualities much earlier in their careers than earlier generations had to. With entry-level roles disappearing, junior staff need the leadership and decision-making capacity of much older managers. They will also have to be more adaptable in order to stay ahead. “We are entering an [unprecedented] age of skills and learning,” says Hugh Milward of Microsoft, a tech giant.
In theory, Britain should be well-placed for this revolution. The English education system gives students a decent grounding in numeracy and literacy (though Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales do less well). British universities tout their emphasis on critical thinking, which is useful for judging outputs from probabilistic large language models. Infusing vocational courses with such thinking will give young people many more options in the labour market.
The potential rewards are big. AI should bring many opportunities as well as liberation from drudgeries. “No one wants to write emails for a living anymore,” says Adam, a 19-year-old studying at Barnsley College, who has founded his own startup. Soon, they will no longer have to.

epub_67.title: Meet John Healey, Britain’s bald fraud
epub_67.text:
Meet John Healey, Britain’s bald fraud
Britain
| Bagehot
Meet John Healey, Britain’s bald fraud
As his upcoming budget will show, the chancellor is out of his depth
Oct 22nd 2026
Bald men ruled football in 2024. That year four of the big six managers in the Premier League had heads that gleamed like the trophies they won. A moniker was coined that is now beloved by football fans: the “bald fraud”. This charlatan is someone whose actions have little to do with their team’s performance on the pitch and who will, eventually and inevitably, be found out.
Bald dominance of football has since ended; the bald era of Britain’s public finances, however, is just beginning. In July John Healey, the new-ish chancellor and proud slaphead, greeted Treasury officials by noting familiar faces from his previous stint there in the 2000s. “Perhaps a little older, a little wiser, a little greyer,” he said. “Me, I’m still bald.” But what if Mr Healey is something worse? What if he is a bald fraud?
While accusations of bald fraudulence in football are made publicly, in Westminster they are private. “Pedestrian”, say the kinder ones who have worked with Mr Healey. “Slow”, say the meaner ones. Visibly out of his depth, remarks a veteran of Sir Keir Starmer’s era. Ministers do not pay Mr Healey much heed. What is the chancellor’s theory of growth? Who knows, replies one. Should they bother to find out? The chancellor has little influence on growth policy, shrugs a member of the cabinet. The caucus crying “bald fraud” is large.
Bald he may be but a fraud he is not, say others. “He’s got views!” says one mp, delightedly. After two frustrating years in power, Labour sets the bar low. Under Sir Keir, ministers treated their boss like a constitutional monarch, sitting mute while others ran the country for him. By contrast Mr Healey and Andy Burnham, Sir Keir’s successor, have politics. It is a parochial politics, focused on regional growth and hand-outs rather than the coming demise of the welfare state, but it is a politics nonetheless.
Gauging fraudulence is more art than science, in both football and politics. Some labelled bald frauds are nothing of the sort; others are lucky to be there at all. Often people decide based on trivia and vibes. Did you know Mr Healey came second among Labour mps when they voted for their shadow cabinet in 2010? The man has been around. He was first elected in 1997, becoming a Treasury minister when Gordon Brown was chancellor. Come 2024, this was executive manna to a party about to seize power with almost no governing experience. Mr Healey found himself as defence secretary, in the same way Sir Alex Ferguson’s former players were granted plum jobs even if they had achieved little. “Get Healey in. He knows the club.”
Pretty much everyone in top-flight football has won something, just as a senior politician has usually done a big job somewhere. How difficult is it to win the Eredivisie, the Dutch premier league, really? Some roles can make anyone look good. Is secretary of defence a real job? After all, the bulk of it comes down to asking the Treasury for money and then, if it refuses, sending uniformed generals to march up Downing Street and beg.
What being defence secretary does provide is instant gravitas. Sometimes appearance is all it takes. In 30 Rock, a sitcom about a television channel, one character ranted: “The television audience doesn’t want your elitist, east coast, alternative, intellectual, left-wing—” The recipient cut in: “Jack, just say Jewish, this is taking forever.” And so it was when Labour was casting around for a potential caretaker prime minister should Sir Keir have to quit. Mr Healey was tipped for it by senior party wallahs: steady, solid, looked the part. Just say “bald”, this is taking forever.
Asking for money and not getting it is Mr Healey’s main achievement in politics. His defining moment as defence secretary came when he left, resigning over Sir Keir’s refusal to raise defence spending to 3% by 2030. Mr Healey, hitherto known for resolute loyalty, called for the prime minister to go. It worked. Sir Keir left and Mr Healey landed the second-biggest job in government.
In football as in politics, frauds are exposed only once they climb high enough. The Peter principle—that everyone is promoted one level beyond their competence—is an iron law. After all, Mr Healey became chancellor because of who he was not. Shabana Mahmood was too useful as home secretary;  Ed Miliband, now the foreign secretary, was too alternative, intellectual and left-wing. Mr Healey resembles a hapless coach at a club whose megalomaniac chairman picks the team each week.
Even a bald fraud can prosper for a while. Some budgets mark sea changes; the one on October 28th will not, unless something goes badly wrong. Some money for defence will be found and lip service will be paid to growth. Should it go without a hitch, plaudits will come in anyway: “steady”, “solid”, “he looked the part”.
But in 2027 Mr Healey will have to cobble together the best part of £35bn ($47bn, or 1.1% of GDP) if he wishes to avoid steep cuts for a swathe of departments including for local government and prisons, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies, a think-tank. Anyone can manage a spending review when the economy is growing by 3% a year, in the same way any bald fraud can manage Bayern Munich, Germany’s richest club, and win the Bundesliga. Could they do it on a cold, wet night in Stoke? Can Mr Healey do it in a spring statement in April?
If a football team can thrive with a bald fraud at the helm, so can the British economy. The data are more hopeful than the vibes suggest; should the Strait of Hormuz fully reopen, they would be glowing. Whether Labour can hang on to power will be decided outside the chancellor’s office—in 10 Downing Street or far beyond. Should it fail, the next government will face the same fundamental questions. Andrew Griffith, another bald man, is the Conservatives’ new shadow chancellor. The debate can start again.

epub_69.title: The surprising popularity of AI
epub_69.text:
The surprising popularity of AI
International
| What backlash?
The surprising popularity of AI
Unlike rich Westerners, many around the world feel hopeful about the technology
Oct 22nd 2026
AS A BOY growing up in the aftermath of the Korean war, Bae Oh-do would venture out into the forest to gather firewood to heat his family’s home. “The manual era is completely ingrained in me,” says the 70-year-old violin salesman, sitting under a tree in a park in Seoul’s Jong-no district. He recalls having to use a foot-operated “treadle pump” to get water, as well as his delight when the first tractors rolled into the South Korean countryside.
In recent decades he has seen things “develop so conveniently”, with the internet and smartphones. And what about artificial intelligence? “It’s nothing for humans to worry about. This kind of thing is good,” he says. “They should keep developing the technology. Humanity has advanced so much up to our generation. There’s no telling how the world will change.”
Read the headlines in Western media and it may seem as though a backlash to AI is spreading fast everywhere. But so far, it is not. Mr Bae’s sunny disposition about AI is shared by almost two-thirds of South Koreans, according to a survey that GlobeScan, a polling firm, conducted for The Economist. Outside rich countries this good feeling is even more strongly shared: nearly nine in ten people in Nigeria and Vietnam, for example, said that AI will improve not only their own lives, but the lot of humanity (see chart 1).
The polling across 34 countries was carried out online, which could tilt attitudes in favour of AI. Yet in the same survey sentiment in rich Western countries was much gloomier. In America, Canada and France more people felt negatively than positively about AI’s future impact on humanity. In other Western countries sentiment was net-positive, but far less so than in the poor world. Another recent survey of 37 countries, carried out by Gallup with Microsoft, returned similar results: AI is broadly popular, but less so in rich Western countries.
Why the gap between the West and the rest? Some of the optimism may cool as more people in poor countries come into direct contact with AI or data centres, and see the technology helping or hurting some more than others. Around 9% of working-age Kenyans used AI in the second quarter of 2026, according to a study by Microsoft. Yet 85% told GlobeScan that it would change their lives for the better.
But plenty of people, poor and rich alike, are already at least vaguely conscious of AI’s pitfalls. In a survey by Pew Research Centre, South Koreans were most likely (along with Australians) to say they expect AI to generate massive job losses and worsen inequality. For now, though, such fears appear to be outweighed by intrigue about the technology’s promise.
Part of the explanation is that many workers outside the richest countries have less to lose from AI than do their counterparts in the West. In much of the poor world work is often informal and, compared with jobs in the West, precarious. The notion of losing a secure office job to technology is more of a rich-world problem (though in India, say, information-technology and other back-office workers look vulnerable to disruption).
The poor world has much to gain from AI, too. In countries where institutions and formal education can be lacking, AI helps some people help themselves. “Pessimism is a privilege for those who can afford to despair,” argues Payal Arora, author of “From Pessimism to Promise”, a book about diverging attitudes to technology.
In India users have gained cheap or free access to apps like Gemini from Google or ChatGPT from OpenAI; nearly one in five working-age Indians used generative AI in the second quarter of 2026, compared with a third of Americans, according to a recent Microsoft study. DeepSeek, a free Chinese alternative, is popular in Africa, where Microsoft estimates that in many countries about one in ten working-age people used generative AI in the second quarter.
A narrow street in a busy suburb of Mumbai illustrates the benefits. Many shops on it use ChatGPT to generate advertisements. Dinesh Chandra, an optician, asked the chatbot to produce a “gravity-defying” photo for his brand. It duly created an image, now printed on brochures, of glasses floating above clouds while riding a feather. Next door Omkar Sapre, who sells dried fruit, masalas and pickles, posts “beautiful pictures” from ChatGPT on Instagram and WhatsApp, and has noticed his sales pick up. Ashlesha, who works at a dry cleaner on the same street, says, “We work hard and AI is extra support for us. Everyone is on Instagram.”
All of them love the convenience of using AI; none worry about safety, privacy or data leaks, much less “AI slop”. The shaming of AI content seems less common outside America and Europe. Westerners “have historically monopolised knowledge and ideational production, but AI challenges that,” says Yuen Yuen Ang of Johns Hopkins University. “Is it a crisis only for those who lose from disruption?”
As Mr Bae illustrates, even in some rich and middle-income countries where there seems more to lose from disruption, AI is surprisingly popular. Singaporeans are among the world’s top AI users, says Microsoft; nearly two-thirds told GlobeScan they thought the technology would have a positive effect on their lives. In Malaysia, which is experiencing a big data-centre boom, minor protests against the sites have not yet turned into a wider backlash.
Some countries where AI-optimism runs high share common factors that seem to cut across socioeconomic lines. One is a looming shortage of workers. Parts of the world that have long had low fertility rates, like East Asia, are ageing rapidly. Many hope that AI (and AI-powered robots) can fill in for workers who do not exist, helping countries to care for greying populations.
Another feature of some AI-optimist countries is a living memory of technology radically transforming societies in the span of a lifetime. Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan went from poor to rich partly by rapidly adopting new technologies that originated abroad.
In China and India technological leaps, including through digital payment and delivery apps, have brought extraordinary convenience and autonomy. “At our age, we’ve lived through countless changes,” says Ms Meng, who works in advertising in Beijing and who, at 40, feels ancient. “Things haven’t even settled in China before another huge shift comes two or three years later.” In India smartphones have offered hundreds of millions of people a “God in their hand” over the course of just a few years, says Ms Arora.
In Western countries, by contrast, pessimism towards AI may reflect people’s perception that their lives are not getting much better, that AI could make their lives worse—and that politicians cannot be relied upon to protect their interests. Daniel Dobrygowski, author of the book “Technology Governance”, argues that this attitude is coloured by people’s experience of social media and Big Tech, which Western governments have struggled to rein in.
The ways in which politicians and firms talk about AI may also make a difference. Bosses of American labs warn of job losses and human extinction as they race towards “artificial general intelligence”. Asian politicians and tech bosses rarely talk like that, perhaps in part because they are not developing frontier capabilities of their own. Instead they tend to focus on the practical uses of AI—what they will do with the technology, rather than what it will do to them. You are unlikely to hear the boss of Samsung talking publicly about AI doom.
In China, where big advances in AI are being made, officials
do worry about risks
, from cyber-security threats to economic dislocation. But the general tenor of state media is boosterish.
It would be wrong to conclude, though, that people in more AI-positive countries have no worries at all. Some are more resigned to the advance of technology as a fate that cannot be avoided. “AI’s impact might be different from every previous shift. But the Earth has its own rhythms,” says Ms Meng in Beijing. “When it’s not meant for you to survive, you won’t. You can’t live every day worrying, right?”
Cho Kyu-jin of Seoul National University reckons that South Koreans are embracing AI despite their concerns because the “fear of being left behind is higher than that of losing stability”. Kim Ah-ran, a 40-year-old labour lawyer, says, “When changes came in the Industrial Revolution, there were positive and negative effects. We’ll find a way to live.” Her young son, standing next to her at the Galaxy Robot Park outside Seoul, is mimicking a humanoid that is practising Muay Thai moves, while clutching a workbook that explains how to use AI to code such robots.
Such pragmatic acceptance suggests that positive attitudes like Mr Bae’s could yet be fragile. Kim Jeong-nam of KAIST, a tech-focused university, serves on South Korea’s Presidential Council on National Artificial Intelligence Strategy. He thinks that South Koreans’ tolerance is conditional on “competently built” policy. If AI starts to “produce visible losers”, such as in exam fairness or jobs, he worries that leeway could vanish. The same could hold true elsewhere. “How are you going to invent an AI that can drive a motorbike?” asks Anderson Santos, a delivery driver in São Paulo, Brazil, who is later dismayed at a mention of driverless cars.
There are some nascent signs of data-centre backlash in other parts of the world, too, if nothing like the outright rebellion seen in many parts of America. In the Philippines people are marching against “Pax Silica”, an American-led initiative to develop AI and semiconductor supply chains. In Thane, a city near Mumbai, hundreds have protested against an Amazon hyperscale data centre that is planned for their neighbourhood. Rage is not yet all-consuming, though. “It’s just like any other factory,” says one resident. “AI is the future.”

epub_70.title: MAGA foreign policy is a mess
epub_70.text:
MAGA foreign policy is a mess
International
| The Telegram
MAGA foreign policy is a mess
Democrats disagree on what comes next
Oct 22nd 2026
“INEVER MEANT to start a war…I just closed my eyes and swung,” sings Miley Cyrus in “Wrecking Ball”, a break-up ballad that seemed to play on every American radio in 2013. Though melodically a bit relentless, the pop song deserves a revival as a guide to the second-term statecraft of President Donald Trump.
It is clear that traditional foreign-policy theories are a poor guide to Mr Trump. That offers both risks and opportunities to anyone running to be America’s next president.
This newspaper has noted Mr Trump’s wrecking-ball tendencies before, but in the two years before the next presidential election his yen for demolition has a specific impact. It has broken the “pendulum theory”, a once-reliable tool for predicting American foreign policy. Going back to Richard Nixon and his successor Jimmy Carter, most presidents have (over-)corrected for the biggest flaws of the guy who came before. In reaction to Tricky Dick’s devious realpolitik, the Carter presidency offered hairshirt moralising. Before long, voters felt that America was disrespected and chose can-do Reaganite optimism. When Americans wearied of George H.W. Bush, a wise but stiff statesman, they elected feel-your-pain Bill Clinton. After shoot-from-the-hip George W. Bush, Americans fell for cool, cerebral Barack Obama, before souring on haughty brainiacs and betting the country on Mr Trump.
Today the theory is less use, because Mr Trump swings every which way. When bullying Ukraine to settle with Russia, he is a might-makes-right realist. In Venezuela his rule-by-proxy would impress a 19th-century imperialist. In the Middle East he scorned regime change right up until his bungled war to bend Iran to his will. He declares that communism menaces America, but calls China’s party boss, Xi Jinping, his friend. The one constant is an impulse to smash the status quo. Cue mental images of Mr Trump atop a demolition ball (hopefully, unlike Ms Cyrus’s music video, the 80-year-old is wearing more than Dr. Martens boots).
It is quite plausible that this president will be hooted from office after wrecking America’s good name (though AI dominance could create riches and clout). Successors wishing to do the opposite will be spoiled for choice. For the foreign-policy pendulum to swing through a full arc, the 48th president could put the national interest ahead of personal profit. Alternatively his successor could avoid reckless wars and shun regime change. The next administration could work to rebuild alliances, pledging to help Europe confront Russia and friends in Asia deter China. All these options would break with some version of Trumpism.
The range of options is especially wide for Democrats. Whether Mr Trump’s vice-president, J.D. Vance, clears the field or faces a contested primary, Republicans will be wary of angering the MAGA faithful by repudiating Mr Trump.
Because Democrats are a self-indulgent bunch and—for a political party—surprisingly bad at politics, they are responding to this moment of opportunity with a navel-gazing argument. Conversations with foreign-policy heavy-hitters in Washington describe two broad camps, one centrist and one on the progressive left. These agree that voters care most about domestic and economic issues: there is much talk of heeding the kitchen-table concerns of working families. Yet each camp knows, too, that the outside world has a habit of intruding.
Responding to demand, delegations of Democratic thinkers and former officials have begun meeting foreign governments and politicians. One such group, involving both moderate and leftish Democrats, visited Brussels, London and Paris this month. A consistent message from these envoys is that the old post-1945 order is not coming back, and that some pillars of Trumpism—rhetoric about putting Americans first, and a focus on industrial production—will remain, whoever wins.
Trump-era tariffs are divisive. Polls suggest that voters blame them for high prices. Centrist Democrats cannot decide, though, whether it is better to juice the economy by scrapping most import taxes on taking office, or keep them temporarily as leverage over trade partners. The left believes in protected favoured industries (which will lobby to keep trade barriers) and likes tariff revenues.
A loud group would bar from future service those Biden-era officials who worked on Israel policy, deeming them steeped in Gazan blood. A cross-party consensus exists to deny Israel uncritical support. Some on the left would pull America out of the Middle East and offer only cautious support for Ukraine.
China sparks sharp disputes. Centrists believe that America is in an epochal contest with China for global leadership in technology and the world order. Prominent leftists call that overblown and hope to work with China on climate change and other global challenges. Some, ludicrously, imagine China will permit its workers to ally with America’s to agree on global minimum wages. Unfortunately for such China dreamers, their growing anxiety about AI safety and the power of big tech leads in another direction. Politically no Democrat can safely call for the slowing of American AI firms without calling for their Chinese rivals to be held back, too. That would involve imposing export controls on high-end computer chips and tools to make them, which would enrage China.
In some fields Democrats can break with Mr Trump while offering elements of continuity. Shrewd Democrats can keep tough border controls, which voters like, but promise less cruel enforcement of immigration laws inside America and a warmer welcome for legal migrants. His proposed defence budgets are so large that hawkish Democrats can spend less without much fear of seeming weak. Disruptive, unknowable change is coming: the thing to know about wrecking balls is that they are erratic.
