epub_82.title: Brazil’s weird economy needs serious reform
epub_82.text:
Brazil’s weird economy needs serious reform
Finance & economics
| A real problem
Brazil’s weird economy needs serious reform
Neither Lula nor Flávio Bolsonaro have the stomach for it
Oct 22nd 2026
DEMOCRATS OF THE world shuddered after the first round of Brazil’s presidential election. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of a coup-plotting former president, unexpectedly beat the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. He looks poised to carry the run-off against Lula, as the 80-year-old leftist icon is known, on October 25th. Capitalists, too, trembled—but with excitement. São Paulo’s stock-market index jumped by nearly 8% the next day, the real strengthened and yields on government bonds fell.
This was a brutal verdict on Lula’s economic stewardship. GDP growth has beaten (glum) forecasts, unemployment is low and inflation has stayed close to the 1.5-4.5% range targeted by the Central Bank of Brazil (BCB). But his fiscal abandon and anti-business rhetoric spook markets. The “primary” budget surplus (ie, before interest payments) he inherited is now a deficit and the IMF expects public debt to hit 97% of GDP this year, up from 84% in 2022. “We need to put an end to all this nonsense of running a surplus and maintaining fiscal discipline,” he recently averred.
Mr Bolsonaro, by contrast, styles himself on Javier Milei, Argentina’s chainsaw-wielding president whose free-market reforms have led to some success (and lots of pain). He, too, uses a cutting tool—a giant pair of scissors—as an electoral prop, vowing to slash taxes, red tape and graft. Yet his economic ideas are hazy. To offset his proposed tax cuts and 900bn reais ($179bn, or 6.6% of GDP) over four years in infrastructure spending, he wants to reduce the number of ministries, digitise public administration and sell federal buildings.
This is implausible—he would be lucky to get half his promised savings from such tinkering. It is also unequal to the task. It would take true Milei-like ardour to slice through Brazil’s economic troubles. These are caused by a gnarly mix of high public spending, stubborn inflation and low saving. The result is a crippling cost of capital. Some analysts put Brazil’s real interest rate, the BCB’s policy rate adjusted for next year’s expected inflation, at 9% or more. That is higher than in Russia and four times that in peaceful peers like Chile, the Philippines or South Africa.
It all starts with the public finances. Brazil’s 65,000-word doorstop of a constitution bars cuts to nominal public-sector wages and links pension, disability and unemployment benefits to the minimum wage, which is adjusted annually based on recent inflation and GDP growth. This ratchet has lifted mandatory spending to 90% of the federal budget.
It also perpetuates inflationary pressure. This plus a generous welfare state in turn make Brazilians unwilling to save. At 14% of GDP, the national savings rate is 12 percentage points below the world average. If price rises have regularly eroded your bank balance in the past and the state pays for your health care, school and pension, you may as well spend all the money you make right away—especially if, like most people in unequal Brazil, you do not make much to begin with.
No government in recent memory has had a serious go at belt-tightening. And Lula has been no less loose. He has repeatedly allowed the minimum wage (and so everything linked to it) to rise above inflation. He has also splurged nearly $260bn on cheap credit for arms-, chip- and drugmakers, among others, with little to show for it—between 2022 and 2025 industry shrank as a share of GDP. When he was still trying to balance the books earlier in his term, he raised taxes, piling more woe onto already woebegone businesses.
Lula’s stimulus also meant that the BCB had no choice but to raise interest rates. And because nearly half of all
lending
in Brazil is subsidised—including most mortgages, loans to farmers and infrastructure credit—the hikes must be higher than in other countries to have the same cooling effect on prices. Between mid-2024 and mid-2025 the policy rate rose seven times, to 15%. Though it has come down to 13.8%, it remains as high as it got in the wake of the post-pandemic price surges.
High real interest rates raise the cost of servicing public debt and push up the debt-to-GDP ratio (see chart). And with such juicy returns on offer, investors prefer to lend to the government, which for all its flaws seems a safer bet than most companies. This raises the cost of capital for everyone else. It also creates perverse incentives in the financial system, explains Monica de Bolle of the Peterson Institute for International Economics, a think-tank in Washington. Around half of government debt consists of floating-rate treasury bills (known as LFTs), which pay a daily return based on the BCB’s policy rate. Commercial banks have balance-sheets full of this easy money. The BCB could thus be cutting rates less than it otherwise might, for fear that deeper cuts hurt lenders’ profits and provoke a banking crisis.
LFTs blunt monetary policy in another way. Coupon payments to the banks and wealthy Brazilians who own them undercut the cooling effect on consumption that tightening aims to achieve. “The more I raise interest rates, the more income holders receive,” the BCB’s president, Gabriel Galipolo, complained earlier this year.
The one way out of the mess is through belt-tightening. It would bring down inflation, lower the real interest rate and make capital available for productive uses. Mr Bolsonaro’s team whisper about reform but the candidate himself has rejected changes to pensions or indexation. If Lula pulls off a surprise comeback in the run-off, he is unlikely to discover his inner fiscal hawk. And any president would struggle to persuade three-fifths of both houses of Congress required to dismantle the constitutional ratchet. Markets may prefer Mr Bolsonaro to Lula. Whomever they get will turn out to be a disappointment.

epub_83.title: It’s not just Commerzbank: Italians are eating up German business
epub_83.text:
It’s not just Commerzbank: Italians are eating up German business
Finance & economics
| Commerz all’italiana
It’s not just Commerzbank: Italians are eating up German business
The takeover of the bank by UniCredit is only the start
Oct 22nd 2026
“Die Italiener kommen”, screamed a headline in June in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ), a normally sober German daily. The Italians in question are not tourists coming for German sights or workers coming for German jobs. Rather, despite what the FAZ calls Italy’s “lower economic prestige”, it is Italian banks and businesses salivating over the giant German market and its choicest cuts.
On October 15th UniCredit, Italy’s second-biggest lender by assets and revenue, said it got the nod from the European Central Bank (ECB) to seal a €45bn ($51bn) hostile takeover of Commerzbank, its German opposite number. The banking deal is the biggest of recent Italo-German mergers. But it is part of a much larger feast.
Earlier this year Italo, an
Italian high-speed railway operator
, entered Germany. By 2028 it plans to challenge state-owned Deutsche Bahn along two lucrative routes: Munich-Cologne-Dortmund and Munich-Berlin-Hamburg. A year ago MediaForEurope, the empire controlled by the family of Silvio Berlusconi, a late former prime minister, paid €1.8bn for ProSiebenSat.1, Germany’s second-biggest private broadcaster—and immediately replaced Bert Habets, ProSieben’s Dutch boss, with an Italian, Marco Giordani.
Smaller Italian firms, meanwhile, are going after the Mittelstand. Last year the value of their foreign takeovers rose by 74%, to €24bn, according to Arkios, a Milanese investment bank. Germany is Italy’s biggest trading partner and behind only America and Britain as a takeover target.
In 2025 Polifarma, an Italian drugmaker, bought Hennig Arzneimittel, a competitor from Frankfurt, and
Bending Spoons
, a collector of tech startups, took over Komoot, a German route-planning app. (Bending Spoons has just sold a big stake in itself to Berkshire Hathaway, a legendary American investment firm.) In December DIESSE and EsseEmme Tecno, two other medium-size firms, bought parts of Mayer, an insolvent German textile-machinery manufacturer, to get hold of its industrial-braiding technology. And in March an Italian maker of machinery, Danese, swallowed a German one, Zwaans.
The Italian appetite for German firms reverses a historical trend. It used to be the Italians with the brands and the Germans with the money. Volkswagen bought Lamborghini (sports cars) in 1998 and Ducati (sports bikes) in 2012. Allianz, a German insurer, picked up RAS, an Italian one, in 2005. HeidelbergCement (now Heidelberg Materials) absorbed Italcementi in 2016.
Such deals are not entirely a thing of the past: last year Lufthansa acquired a 41% stake in ITA Airways and says it will increase that to 90% next year. But as Germany’s GDP has more or less stagnated since the covid-19 pandemic, more German companies, especially manufacturers competing with cheap alternatives from China, are receptive to foreign advances. As for the Italian acquirers, their domestic economy may have grown faster than Germany’s in recent years, but it is hardly pizza-oven hot. A slice of Europe’s biggest market, garnished with technology and engineering know-how, therefore looks appetising, says Jörg Buck of the German-Italian chamber of commerce in Milan.
This is not to everyone’s taste. The German government (which owns 13% of Commerzbank) is revulsed by the desire of UniCredit’s hard-charging boss, Andrea Orcel, to sack Bettina Orlopp, Commerzbank’s chief executive—pronto.
It also dislikes the tactics Mr Orcel has used in his pursuit of Commerzbank. He built UniCredit’s stake with the help of derivatives, which obscured his intentions. He also made a stingy bid for all shares his bank did not own just before its stake reached 30%. This let him circumvent the legal requirement to launch a full takeover bid on reaching 30% ownership while sidestepping the need to offer a decent premium such a bid would normally include. He could then keep buying up Commerzbank shares on the cheap in the open market.
The German finance ministry wants to change takeover law to prevent such “lowballing”, by requiring a second mandatory offer once an acquirer’s stake in a target firm reaches 50%. At that stage, an acquirer forced to make a full takeover bid would find it harder to get away with a stingy offer. The ministry also wants stricter rules on acquirers’ use of derivatives to build their stakes.
This looks like sour Riesling grapes. Even if the proposed rules were enacted, they would come too late to prevent the Commerzbank takeover—especially now that UniCredit has won the ECB’s blessing. And they are unlikely to keep other Italians away. From the south, Deutschland AG looks just too delectable.

epub_84.title: Who will buy $120bn-worth of fresh Japanese government bonds?
epub_84.text:
Who will buy $120bn-worth of fresh Japanese government bonds?
Finance & economics
| For sale, going cheap!
Who will buy $120bn-worth of fresh Japanese government bonds?
Japan wants its pension fund and households to buy more government debt
Oct 22nd 2026
OF THE MANY reinventions of Suzuki Airi, a singer-turned-model-turned-actress, one stands out. In an ad campaign released earlier this year by Japan’s finance ministry, an all-pink Ms Suzuki hawks government debt. Perched on her shoulder are the official mascots of its “retail government bonds plus” programme: Kokusai-sensei, a cartoon professor shaped like part of the Japanese word for government bond, and Koko-chan, his girlish companion. The pair encourages savers to “add peace of mind” with “plus-plus”.
Peace of mind is in short supply for those trading Japanese government bonds (JGBs) for a living. Last month the yield on ten-year JGBs passed 3% for the first time since 1996, up from 2% in January. Investors worry about persistent inflation—a novelty in a country until recently plagued by years of falling prices. This makes them less keen on government debt at a time when lots of bonds are hitting the market.
Takaichi Sanae, the prime minister,
has pledged
¥120trn ($700bn, or 18% of last year’s GDP) in new public investment by 2040. She is backing
strategic industries
, from shipbuilding to chipmaking, while raising spending on defence and cutting sales taxes on food. Her promises to do all this without funding government budget deficits through new bonds are taken with a generous dash of soy sauce. Goldman Sachs, a bank, expects that a “primary” deficit (before interest payments) of 1.5% of GDP will raise total JGB issuance by ¥19trn in fiscal year 2027. And investors also have their pick of corporate bonds, a record ¥17trn-worth of which was sold in the 12 months to March.
Who will buy all that? The usual buyers are not as reliable as they once were. Life-insurance companies, which bought loads before new accounting rules for assets took effect in March, have gone quiet. The Bank of Japan (BoJ), which owns 44% of all JGBs, is unwinding a balance-sheet bloated by more than a decade of bond-buying.
To help digest the rising supply, the government is targeting new sources of demand. One is the Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF), the country’s $1.9trn nest-egg. After a raft of economic reforms in 2014, low-yielding domestic bonds fell to a quarter of its portfolio, down from two-thirds in 2012 (see chart, top panel). The finance minister says that GPIF should make “substantially greater investments” in domestic assets. Were it to raise its domestic-bond allocation to 30% or so, as the current rules allow, that could create another ¥15trn in JGB demand, estimates Morgan Stanley, another bank.
The bigger potential pool of buyers are the everyday investors wooed by Ms Suzuki and her two sidekicks (see chart, bottom panel). They hold more than ¥1,100trn (around 165% of GDP) in cash savings in bank deposits, against ¥22trn in JGBs. Given that a two-year lockup deposit now returns around 0.7% a year, households may well be tempted by the 2% on offer from retail JGBs. Were they to raise their JGB allocations back to 4% of savings, the level in the late 2000s, from 2% today, it could create perhaps ¥20trn in fresh demand.
Yet both of these sources of demand face barriers. GPIF targets nominal investment returns of around 5%, higher than the 4% from the highest-yielding JGBs (with a maturity of 40 years). A bigger JGB allocation therefore risks undercutting GPIF’s goals. Savers, for their part, are sceptical that retail JGBs will protect their cash from inflation. “The state is trying to generate inflation so it can recover its debt while encouraging ordinary people to buy government bonds. It’s a trap, really,” warns Yohei, a Japanese fin-fluencer.
The government’s retail-JGB push is also in tension with NISA, popular tax-free stock-investing accounts. Though some politicians want to make JGBs eligible for NISA, that would muddy the programme’s aim of creating more home-grown risk capital that Japan has lacked lately.
Japan may, then, have little choice but to rely on the flightier demand from abroad. Hedge funds and other foreigners are buying 60% of JGBs on the secondary market, up from 36% in 2019 (excluding those sold to middlemen). In general they drive a harder bargain. Thankfully, though, they are drawn by Japan’s “yield curve”, the interest rates at which the government borrows over different time periods, which is one of the world’s steepest. Japan’s ten-year yield is 1.6 percentage points higher than its three-month yield. In America, the gap is around half that.
A steep yield curve appeals to foreign investors. A bond’s local-currency returns depend on its yield, which is rising for longer-duration JGBs, whereas the cost of hedging currency risk is set in part by differences in short-term rates, which have not moved enough to offset the yield gains. A currency-hedged American investor buying JGBs would now earn about 0.8 percentage points of additional returns above the equivalent Treasury bond, estimates Ralf Preusser of Bank of America. Having to compete for flighty foreign capital may feel uncomfortable for a country accustomed to sleepy bond markets. But at least Japan has something to offer.

epub_85.title: The late Perry Mehrling explained the hierarchy of money
epub_85.text:
The late Perry Mehrling explained the hierarchy of money
Finance & economics
| Buttonwood
The late Perry Mehrling explained the hierarchy of money
The course for par
Oct 22nd 2026
THERE IS A moment in Perry Mehrling’s opening lecture on money and banking, a course he taught for years at Barnard College in New York, when the professor recalls the origins of his intellectual passion. (Thanks to the magic of the internet, the recording is available for anyone to watch.) His eyes light up. His enthusiasm is laid bare. He went to the library, he remembers, saw a shelf full of treatises on money, and said to himself, “If I could have a life reading all of those books, just from left to right, that would be the best life ever.”
His best life set him apart from most mainstream economists. They read articles, not books. And their intellectual framework leaves surprisingly little room for money. They care about the production and exchange of stuff, not the pieces of paper that change hands along the way. A famous couplet sums up their creed: “promises of payment/Are neither food nor raiment”.
But if you have made a promise of payment, you will need money, not food or raiment, to fulfil it. That “settlement constraint” is a starting point of Mr Mehrling’s own school of thought, which he called “the money view”. It is a little school, he admitted. But he did not feel alone. He drew on a shelfful of intellectual ancestors, such as Hyman Minsky, a maverick American economist, and Walter Bagehot, the third editor of this newspaper. (“They’re pretty great guys, actually,” he assures his lecture audience.) He also inspired other adherents, such as Daniel Neilson, a data scientist, and Iñaki Aldasoro of the Bank for International Settlements, whose own interpretation, dedicated to Mr Mehrling’s memory, was published this month, shortly after the professor’s untimely death at the age of 67.
According to this tradition, money evolves out of promises of payment. Suppose I owe you something. Perhaps that obligation is written on a piece of paper. If you trust me, you might accept that paper in lieu of immediate satisfaction of my debt. You might even try offering it to someone else to clear a debt of your own. If they too trust me—or feel confident that everyone else does—they could take my paper from you as settlement of your obligation to them. My IOU begins to circulate like money.
A complex, hierarchical apparatus ensures that some promises are routinely accepted as money. Mainstream economists concentrate on only a few parts of this system. They obsess over the policy rules that curb inflation, ensuring that money holds its value against goods and services. Mr Mehrling was fascinated by the rest of the plumbing. What, he asked, ensures that the dollars in a bank account, a money-market fund or an offshore deposit hold their value, at par, with higher breeds of promise, such as reserves at the central bank? He treated “par”—the one-for-one exchange rate between different kinds of dollars—as one of “four prices” of money, as important as the familiar trio of the interest rate, exchange rate and price level of goods and services.
Par normally attracts little attention. The public is so confident it will hold, they barely know it exists. In good times banks happily extend loans and create deposits, adding new promises to pay. This “elasticity” helps the economy flourish. But it can create strains. And the scale of the system is not the only thing that grows. Its scope also expands. A wider range of actors issue a more exotic mix of claims in the hope they will circulate like money, with few questions asked. One historical example is the Eurodollar market created by offshore banks. Money-market funds are another. The “latest iteration” of this pattern, points out Mr Aldasoro, are
stablecoins
, crypto instruments that try to keep par with established currencies.
But when confidence is shaken, par is tested. Institutions that issue lower forms of money often cannot survive this test alone. They have to turn to institutions higher up the hierarchy for help. In the global financial crisis of 2007-09 foreign banks, issuing dollar claims, turned to their local central banks, which in turn received help from the Federal Reserve. When stablecoins have faced a similar test, they have so far had nowhere to turn. But the monetary apparatus may eventually domesticate them, too.
Mr Mehrling will sadly not be around to document this evolution. During his career he published four books of his own. Another treatise setting out his money view remains half-written. Perhaps it will still see the light of day in some form. There is room on that shelf of monetary classics for more.

epub_86.title: New research tries to defuse the “China shock”
epub_86.text:
New research tries to defuse the “China shock”
Finance & economics
| Free exchange
New research tries to defuse the “China shock”
An almighty fight over an influential finding
Oct 22nd 2026
IN AMERICA THE left and the right agree on little. But from the deepest-blue city to the reddest-of-red hamlet, almost everyone agrees that America suffered a “China shock” in the 2000s. Joe Biden’s top economic adviser said that surging Chinese imports had destroyed “nearly 1m” manufacturing jobs. Scott Bessent, Donald Trump’s treasury secretary, said last year that it was 3.7m American jobs. The economic research on which such claims are (in Mr Bessent’s case loosely) based is hugely influential. Yet it is controversial, too—and the argument about what exactly trade with China did to America’s economy is now hotting up once again.
The seminal paper was published in 2013 by David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson, a trio of academic economists. It examined what happened around China’s accession to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in 2001. Chinese imports flooded into America; manufacturing jobs fell. But was it China that made the difference? To work this out, the authors estimated the exposure of local areas to the shock based on the rise in industry-specific imports from China in other rich countries. So a place with many toymaking jobs, for example, was treated as vulnerable if imports of Chinese toys were surging in the rich world as a whole.
Their estimates implied that exposure to Chinese goods accounted for about a quarter of the fall in manufacturing employment from 1990 to 2007. Besides shut factories, affected areas were found to have lower wages, higher overall joblessness and more benefit claimants. Early drafts of the paper, circulated in 2011, came close to saying the overall costs of trade with China exceeded the benefits.
The findings became gospel among talking heads seeking to explain the rise of Donald Trump in 2016. They have also been pored over by economists. Some noted that, though the numbers seem large, they are a rounding error in an economy the size of America’s. Since 2001 Americans have left jobs more than 1.5bn times. Even if Mr Bessent is correct and China has cost America 3.7m jobs over 25 years, almost all job moves had nothing to do with it. In the 20 years before 2001 the share of American workers in manufacturing fell by 0.4 percentage points a year. In the ten years after 2001, it fell by roughly as much.
Other critics argue that the China-shock literature considers only the bad, not the good. Bits of research suggest that some places exposed to China lost jobs in manufacturing but gained others in services; that cheaper imports reduced American businesses’ costs, allowing them to expand; and that China’s accession to the WTO was a two-way street, giving American exporters better access to the Chinese market and boosting jobs that way.
The fiercest battle of all has been fought over the methods of the original paper. Its probably most-quoted statistic—that quarter of manufacturing job losses caused by Chinese competition—was an approximation. The authors’ statistical wizardry captured the relative effect of the China shock in different parts of America, not the aggregate national impact. The paper acknowledged that scaling the numbers from local to national required some crude assumptions—a caveat that commentators often ignored. Subsequent “general equilibrium” analysis seeking to identify the national effect produced a lower figure. In a paper from 2019 Lorenzo Caliendo of Yale University and co-authors estimated that the China shock explained 16% of manufacturing jobs lost between 2000 and 2007.
Then there is the question of whether Messrs Autor, Dorn and Hanson blamed China for destroying manufacturing jobs that were on the way out anyway. In 2022 Kirill Borusyak of the University of California, Berkeley, Peter Hull of Brown University and Xavier Jaravel of the London School of Economics showed that the original study inadvertently treated places as exposed to the China shock simply because they had a lot of factories. It might thus have picked up job losses in reality caused by a surge in sector-wide forces like automation. Controlling for this problem cut the effect of the China shock on employment roughly in half.
In a new paper Joseph Francis of Birmingham University extends this method to the supposed socioeconomic fallout of the China shock. Apply the statistical correction of Mr Borusyak and his colleagues, and these broader effects of the shock “disappear”, writes Mr Francis. Chinese imports are no longer proven to have pushed down household incomes; the impact on health, family structure and welfare payments looks smaller.
Messrs Autor, Dorn and Hanson say there is “no consensus that this specification is more appropriate than ours”. However, Mr Hull “strongly” believes that his and his co-authors’ approach is more appropriate, and points out that it “has been peer reviewed and published in two high-profile journals”.
Perhaps the two approaches put an upper and lower bound on the size of the China shock? The new statistical controls cleanse the numbers of trends, like automation, that might have affected all manufacturing-heavy places. However, the China shock probably had some across-the-board effect, too, which is no longer counted. Messrs Autor, Dorn and Hanson insist that “our core findings do not depend on the contested specification.” They point to other work tracing the misfortunes of individual factory workers after the China shock via tax and other administrative records.
It seems undeniable that the China shock destroyed jobs and hurt some workers. Yet the finding that it caused one in four manufacturing jobs lost from 1990 to 2007 has not aged well. Neither has the populist turn against free trade that began around the time of the original research—and for which doubtful claims about the shock’s size have, alas, provided intellectual cover.

epub_88.title: America’s new era of private science
epub_88.text:
America’s new era of private science
Science & technology
| Back to the bench
America’s new era of private science
The future of innovation may be research outside universities
Oct 22nd 2026
THE YEARS since the second world war have been good to American science. The country’s researchers sent men to the moon, invented the modern computer and led the sequencing of the human genome. Its government funded basic research in academia and national labs, which could then pass on findings with commercial promise to firms.
Now there are signs the innovation machine is breaking down. The system’s critics fret that America’s scientific infrastructure encourages groupthink, since a small number of committees distribute a large share of funding for basic research. They worry that universities are ill-suited to the interdisciplinary work that much of 21st-century science requires. And America is no longer an undisputed scientific superpower: China’s research and development (R&D) spending has caught up with Uncle Sam’s in purchasing-power terms, and is growing faster. In 2024 China overtook America in the Nature Index, a measure of publications in the most prestigious scientific journals.
Advocates of “metascience”, the study of scientific discovery, have spent years pointing out the foibles of the system. Lately they have been putting their ideas into practice. Private institutions, many of which were founded within the past five years, say they are building the future of science. The history of American innovation suggests they may be right.
Private science is nothing new. Many of the most exciting American discoveries of the 20th century were not dreamt up on university campuses, but within corporate research institutes. Scientists at Bell Labs (the research arm of AT&T), Xerox PARC (the copy-machine maker’s lab) and IBM Research came up with such marvels as the transistor, and won a handful of Nobel prizes in so doing.
Yet for all their successes, private labs failed to justify their upkeep. A paper published in 2004 by William Nordhaus, an economist at Yale University, estimated that, in the post-war period and across the whole economy, just 2.2% of value from innovation flowed to firms. In response, companies transitioned to “R&D by M&A,” buying startups spun out from universities rather than funding their own labs.
Corporate labs’ retreat led basic research to become much more reliant on government-backed efforts. In the view of private-science advocates, that is lamentable. The concentration of science funding means fewer innovative ideas can benefit society at large, says Caleb Watney of the Institute for Progress, a think-tank. To wit, a study of 100,000 National Institutes of Health (NIH) grant applications, conducted in 2025 by Pierre Azoulay of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Wesley Greenblatt of Harvard Medical School, found that projects which took out-of-consensus approaches were less likely to have their funding renewed. And seeking funding is onerous. According to one survey, researchers spend about 44% of their time doing administrative tasks like writing proposals and reports.
To illustrate these issues, many cite the example of Katalin Kariko, a biologist whose work provided much of the science underpinning mRNA vaccines, such as those for covid-19. For decades funders, notably the NIH, rejected her proposals, considering them too risky. She happened to stay in science, but not many in her position would have, says Stuart Buck of the Good Science Project, a lobby group.
Such concerns have made their way from metascientists’ lips to powerful ears. On July 21st the American government released a report arguing that universities should not be “the only home of America’s most innovative scientific research”. Instead, funding agencies should act more like venture capitalists, betting on a wide variety of institutions.
As part of this push, the National Science Foundation (NSF) is to allocate $1.5bn to a first round of “X-labs”, new organisations that “advance breakthrough science outside of traditional institutions”. A bipartisan bill in Congress would create a similar initiative at the NIH, which has a much larger budget, notes Josh Harder, a Democratic representative and one of the bill’s sponsors. Other changes would see federal agencies offer “golden tickets” to oddball projects that a committee would never back, or begin to give long-term money to individuals rather than projects.
Such ideas have discomfited scientists because of their source. As it attempts to spark “a new golden age” for American science, the Trump administration wants to fund it less. The White House’s proposed budget for fiscal year 2027 suggests halving the NSF’s budget. The worry is that the combination of less funding spread across more institutions will lead to university labs losing out.
Michael Kratsios, the White House science czar, says he “disagrees with that premise”. He notes that the administration has suggested boosting overall R&D spending, particularly in defence. (Defence-department programmes have spurred innovations such as epipens, bug spray and self-driving cars.) Nor does he think the bottom line is the right way to measure policy. Science advocacy groups “have this extreme fixation on budgets”, he says. “Academia just needs to get out of this zero-sum mindset.”
But separately from such squabbling, many private science experiments have already begun. One of the most notable of these is Convergent Research, a Massachusetts-based nonprofit founded in 2021 to fund “focused research organisations” (FROs). Its grantees often want to create a specific tool rather than answer a purely academic question, say co-founders Anastasia Gamick and Adam Marblestone. Convergent gives researchers $20m-50m and between three and seven years to carry out their project. Afterwards, its staff will help them decide what to do with the results. One FRO creates sets of tools that labs and companies can use to study non-model organisms. Another produces an interface that uses ultrasound waves to read brain activity.
Another entrant to the world of private science is Episteme, a company launched in 2025 by Sam Altman of OpenAI and Louis Andre, then a little-known researcher. Rather than demanding pre-set targets or papers, Episteme hopes to give its lead researchers near-total freedom. While the select few it funds often have an approach in mind to solving their chosen problem, Episteme offers them the flexibility to adapt. “If an idea fails, which in science is something that happens very often, you should be able to pivot and try a different angle,” says Mr Andre.
The approach is an appealing one. Charles Marcus, a physicist, says he left a tenured position at the University of Washington to work at Episteme because he felt it would enable him to work across disciplines without needing approval from staid bureaucrats. “We’re not building academic departments in which nobody talks to each other,” he says. Nor will he and other lab leads need to apply for grants or wait for months to hire junior researchers. And while publishing papers is encouraged, it is not mandated. The main constraint on their work is that it should represent a commercial opportunity.
Many important questions fall outside that scope and will have to remain within universities. And besides, not every attempt at private science has flourished. Arena BioWorks, a private biomedical institute founded in 2023, shut down after less than two years. But whereas Arena’s funders reportedly expected quick payouts, Mr Andre says his backers, who have funded Episteme from their personal fortunes, are committed for the long haul. And Episteme, unlike Arena, is not betting on one specific area of research, either. “If a programme fails, it’s okay. We can recycle it and repurpose the resources into something else,” he reckons.
Between federal support, independent experiments and a coming wave of AI-fuelled cash, private-science initiatives are “seeing the stars align,” says Mr Marble-stone. Historians of science and technology argue the post-war system cemented American hegemony. In the bet on private science the stakes are high, both for boffins and for America.

epub_89.title: Japan’s mission to Mars’s moons takes off
epub_89.text:
Japan’s mission to Mars’s moons takes off
Science & technology
| Phobophiles
Japan’s mission to Mars’s moons takes off
It will collect samples and search for signs of ancient life
Oct 22nd 2026
ORBITERS, LANDERS and rovers have travelled to Mars, but none has returned. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) intends for that to change. On October 20th its Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission lifted off from Tanegashima, an island in southern Japan. The probe will spend the next year travelling to Mars, where it aims to land on Phobos, the larger of the planet’s two moons, collect at least ten grams of rock and dust, and return the haul to Earth in 2031. Planetary scientists hope the mission will resolve a long-standing puzzle: how Mars’s moons were formed—and, in the process, reveal much about the planet itself.
Phobos and Mars’s other moon, Deimos, are small, respectively about 22km and 12km across, and look like lumpy potatoes. That might suggest they are asteroids that were captured by Mars’s gravitational field after straying too close. Captured asteroids, however, usually have tilted, elliptical orbits, whereas both moons follow nearly circular paths around the planet’s equator. That hints at another possible origin: a giant collision that threw debris into orbit that later gathered into moons.
JAXA has spent over a decade developing MMX, working with the space agencies of America, Europe and Australia. The mission builds on Japan’s record of returning samples from space. Its Hayabusa mission collected small amounts of grains from Itokawa, an asteroid which comes close to Earth, and brought them home in 2010. Its successor, Hayabusa2, brought back five grams of material—well above the mission’s target—from Ryugu, another near-Earth asteroid, in 2020. The samples proved rich in water-bearing molecules and organic compounds, offering clues to how asteroids may have carried the ingredients for life to Earth.
MMX’s mission is more demanding. Phobos’s surface gravity is roughly one-2,000th of Earth’s, but it is 40 times greater than Ryugu’s. That is strong enough to pose a crash risk for a delicate spacecraft, explains Erik Asphaug, a planetary scientist at the University of Arizona. The Hayabusa missions also followed a “touch-and-go” method in which the spacecraft briefly kissed the asteroids. In contrast, MMX will land on Phobos and extract samples from beneath its surface.
And MMX’s makers want to do a lot more during its three years orbiting Mars. An instrument called MEGANE (pronounced “meh-gah-neh”, like the Japanese word for spectacles), developed by NASA, will measure gamma rays and neutrons given off when cosmic rays hit Phobos, thus revealing its chemistry. A small European rover will explore its surface. After departing Phobos, MMX will conduct fly-bys of Deimos to observe it, too, up close.
If the samples make it safely back to Earth, scientists reckon they might settle which of the two origin stories is true. If Phobos is a captured asteroid, its rocks may resemble meteorites from elsewhere in the solar system. If it instead formed after a giant impact, it will contain melt fragments generated by intense heating.
Whatever Phobos’s history, its proximity to Mars means it should also have collected material blasted off the planet by asteroid impacts. Martian debris should make up about 0.1% of the samples MMX collects. Scientists already have Martian meteorites, but these are mostly hard volcanic rocks that survived the journey through space and Earth’s atmosphere. Sara Russell, a planetary scientist at the Natural History Museum in London who will help analyse MMX’s samples, hopes the mission could recover softer sedimentary material. “That’s the material where we might see biosignatures,” she says, offering clues to whether Mars was once habitable.
There is reason to wonder. Ancient riverbeds and lake deposits suggest Mars once had liquid water and a thicker atmosphere. Unlike the planet itself, its moons have undergone little geological change. They may therefore have preserved fragments of that distant past like a time capsule, says Elizabeth Tasker, an astrophysicist at JAXA. The two small moons could thus help answer a much bigger question: whether life existed on the red planet.

epub_90.title: The second may soon be redefined
epub_90.text:
The second may soon be redefined
Science & technology
| Time for a rethink
The second may soon be redefined
Several atomic clocks are competing for the job
Oct 22nd 2026
IT TAKES ABOUT a second to say “caesium atoms”. And, for nearly 60 years, caesium atoms have said how long a second lasts. That is because caesium-133, an isotope of caesium, switches between two energy states when exposed to microwave radiation, at a rate so regular you could set your watch by it. Indeed, atomic clocks use this steady rhythm to measure time. According to the International System of Units, a second is 9,192,631,770 cycles.
But not for much longer. On October 13th the world’s top metrologists convened in Versailles for the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM), as they have done roughly once every four years since 1889, to discuss the science of measurement. After three days of debate, they set themselves a deadline: by 2030 they will decide how to redefine the second.
The CGPM oversees the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM), which sets the global standard for the passage of time. It does so by combining measurements from hundreds of atomic clocks based in laboratories around the world, to account for small fluctuations which can cause errors in each individual reading. The result is a single standardised time that co-ordinates everything from financial transactions to satellite navigation.
But the BIPM has a problem. To check the accuracy of its standardised time it uses a set of newer clocks, based on different chemical elements, which can measure time more precisely than the best caesium clocks can. Checking the accuracy of the newer clocks requires a definition of the second itself. Using that from a caesium clock is like trying to measure the width of a hair using a ruler whose divisions are wider than the hair. To run the clockwork like clockwork the CGPM needs to untie the second from caesium.
Kyle Arnold, a physicist at the National University of Singapore, is part of a team developing a clock based on lutetium ions. While caesium clocks use microwave radiation to trigger transitions between the atom’s energy states, Dr Arnold’s device uses lasers. Such optical clocks “tick” more quickly, allowing time to be measured more finely. Writing in Nature, in September, Dr Arnold’s group reported its lutetium clock had a tick about 1,000 times more regular than the best caesium devices.
Atomic clocks must work reliably in different places around the world. Dr Arnold’s device, however, is the size of a room and yet to leave his Singapore lab. Other, more portable, contenders include optical clocks based on ytterbium and strontium atoms suspended by lasers. These come with their own issues. A study published in Physical Review Letters, in July, found that measurements comparing optical clocks based on these elements disagreed with earlier results by more than their known uncertainties could explain.
Metrologists must now decide which atomic transition is promoted to the official standard. That requires consensus among yet another team of time lords: the Consultative Committee for Time and Frequency, who are advising the BIPM and CGPM on the second’s fate. With the deadline set for 2030, they have about 100m seconds to reach an agreement.

epub_91.title: Is the internet still safe?
epub_91.text:
Is the internet still safe?
Science & technology
| Cyber-security
Is the internet still safe?
A string of cyber-security incidents has caused websites to go dark
Oct 22nd 2026
PITY THE cyber-defenders. Occasionally, the industry must burst into action following the unheralded revelation of a vulnerability in some widely used software. Rarely, however, must they do so several times in the same week.
On October 20th the security teams at major web browsers received an unusual email. It read “we have a problem here” and was accompanied by a file containing eight private security keys: randomly generated numbers used to encrypt communications across the entire internet. Such keys should be 116 digits long to ensure security. Those in the email, originally issued by an Indian authority, were no longer than three. One was a private key of just “4”. To top things off, the email was signed simply “Wayne”.
Revoking such keys from important central databases is manageable. Checking every system has updated accordingly is hard work. Major web browsers keep their blacklists up-to-date, but many internet-connected systems do not adjust so easily. Some, like many Linux systems, require an active software update; others, like some command-line tools on MacOS, must be manually fixed.
Defenders were busily plugging those gaps when, on the morning of October 21st, another problem arrived. A pair of vulnerabilities had been exposed in PHP, a venerable programming language which underpins tens of millions of web applications, including message boards, financial portals and government websites. A patch was promised for the same afternoon. In the meantime, affected organisations were advised by governments to take their systems offline entirely—an instruction not issued lightly. Several government websites in Europe went dark.
The advice proved to have been reasonable. Hours after news of the vulnerability broke, and with over 12 hours before a patch was due, its details leaked. The vulnerability was as bad as it gets: a recipe for unauthorised remote code execution (RCE), letting an attacker take control of machines running PHP. Exploiting the vulnerability, as demonstrated by at least one widely shared proof-of-concept, was simple.
There is no direct link between the two weaknesses, but one strong relationship: both vulnerabilities seem to have been discovered by AI. The PHP vulnerability was found independently by two members of an AI cyber-defence consortium led by OpenAI, an American firm. The dodgy security keys were “possibly” found using AI too, according to eMudhra, the Indian company which issued them. Certainly, the method of disclosure suggests an unusual approach to research.
By October 22nd two further vulnerabilities had been published. GitLab, a software development tool, announced a patch for a weakness affecting 12 years of releases that could allow its own RCE, ranking it ten on a ten-point severity scale. Oracle, a tech giant, fixed a similar weakness in Java, its widely used programming language, and ranked the severity 9.1. AI was probably used to uncover these flaws, too.
The episodes illustrate an uncomfortable reality of AI-powered cyber-security: fixing an issue sets a timer for its exploitation. The PHP bug was announced with 18 hours notice before a patch was released, in an effort to prepare defenders to install the update with alacrity. But an accidental release of a video demonstrating the vulnerability allowed others, ai in hand, to reverse-engineer the problem and work out how to exploit it. Shortly after, a security company published its version of the fix six hours early, allowing any attacker to examine exactly what was fixed, and therefore uncover more details of the weakness in unpatched systems.
Defenders once faced the difficult problem of finding the flaws in their own software before attackers did. Now they have a different challenge: with AI exposing a plethora of weaknesses, how can they spread news of the fixes to their users, without tipping off their enemies in the process?

epub_92.title: Can joggers outrun injury?
epub_92.text:
Can joggers outrun injury?
Science & technology
| Well Informed
Can joggers outrun injury?
Patience when training goes the extra mile
Oct 22nd 2026
KNEE PAIN in joggers is prevalent enough to be a term of art. “Runner’s knee”, an ache around the kneecap, was among the most common complaints in a study of 3,669 runners published in the Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine (OJSM) in 2021. But it is only one of an assortment of “overuse” injuries: those caused by training that, though tolerable in parts, cumulatively exceed the body’s capacity to recover.
Such problems can compound. The study found that a previous injury increased the odds of another by 62%. Hence a widespread worry that a lifetime of running will wear down joints and eventually lead to arthritis. How can runners keep injuries at bay?
Throwing money at the problem does not help. A review published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, in 2022, found little evidence that different running-shoe designs affect their owners’ susceptibility to injury. The OJSM study from 2021 concluded  that stretching before a jog did not help, either.
Instead, when taking up running or increasing the distance covered, the old adage of “slow and steady” is the one to follow. Novices report injuries more than twice as often as experienced runners, according to a review published in Sports Medicine in 2015. Some of this may be down to differences in expectations, says Rasmus Nielsen, an epidemiologist at Aarhus University in Denmark. A beginner might panic and report a twinge that a more experienced runner knows will pass on its own.
But doing too much too soon is a risk even for seasoned sprinters. A study of 5,205 runners published by Dr Nielsen and his colleagues in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, in 2025, found that running 10-30% farther in a single session than the previous month’s longest run was associated with a 64% higher rate of overuse injury.
Increasing training load slowly gives the body a chance to adapt. Using tendons stimulates collagen production, causing them to stiffen and thicken so that they are more resilient to strain. Repeated impact activates bone-strengthening cells known as osteoblasts, gradually increasing resilience to stress fractures. And, rather than damaging knee cartilage, running strengthens the muscles that help protect the joint.
Building resilience takes time. Changes in tendons occurred in studies lasting around 8 to 12 weeks, according to a review published in Sports Medicine in 2015. Increases in shinbone density have been detected after eight weeks of intensive military training. Another study found that bone mineral density improved after six months of resistance and jumping training.
To be on the safe side, Dr Nielsen recommends keeping any single run to no more than 5% longer than the past month’s longest run, and that any week’s total not exceed 110% of the previous week’s. For beginners, particularly those with high body-mass indices or a history of injury, 3km of cumulative walking and running in the first week of training is a safe starting point.
Happily, there is little evidence that running is associated with long-term joint problems. A study of 3,804 marathon runners published in Sports Health, in 2024, found no association between running history and the risk of arthritis. Accidents involving the knee, such as tears in its cartilage, can cause persistent issues. But as Dr Nielsen points out, such injuries can strike anyone. With sufficient caution, joggers can keep going for the long run.

epub_94.title: Are film critics as snooty and out of touch as people think?
epub_94.text:
Are film critics as snooty and out of touch as people think?
Culture
| The good and the (not) great
Are film critics as snooty and out of touch as people think?
We look at the data to find out
Oct 22nd 2026
Whether a film is good enough to warrant a trek to the cinema is not always easy to ascertain. Recently viewers have praised “Digger”, a satirical black comedy about a wealthy oil tycoon whose company triggers an environmental catastrophe. It has a 76% audience-approval score on Rotten Tomatoes, a review aggregator. But critics did not dig the film: only 53% reviewed it positively, complaining it was ponderous and preachy. Fans calling themselves “Digger Nation” have mobilised online to defend the movie.
Signals about films’ quality can be confusing to decipher. In April fans judged a biopic of Michael Jackson to be a thriller, with 97% of them enjoying it. But most critics thought
“Michael
” was bad. In January “
Melania
”, a documentary about America’s First Lady, reflected the politically polarised times, with a 90-point gap. “An absolute masterpiece!” gushed one audience member. “Gilded trash”, said the Guardian.
Critics and audiences have often failed to see eye to eye. The history of film criticism is littered with judgments that aged badly. (Pity the reviewer who dismissed “Citizen Kane”, now considered one of the greatest films ever made, as “well-intentioned, muddled, amateurish”.) Today many think that critics seem out of step—perhaps more than ever before.
But are they really? To test whether critical and popular opinion are drifting apart, The Economist compiled two decades of reviews of more than 10,000 films from Metacritic, an aggregator site. (We did not use Rotten Tomatoes because the website changed its audience-score methodology in 2019.) Then we matched the reviews with box-office data from The Numbers, a film-industry database.
Talk of a critic-audience divide, it turns out, is overblown. For most of the past 20 years, reviewers and moviegoers have been in broad agreement. Around a decade ago, their views began to diverge. But by 2025 critic and audience ratings were more aligned than at any point since 2005 (see chart 1).
The real difference is not how critics and audiences rate films, but which films they rate. For every ten audience reviews of a documentary, there are six from critics. For dramas and comedies there are around three, and for action less than one. Foreign-language and low-budget films attract disproportionately more attention from critics than from audiences.
Critics and audiences may gravitate towards different films, yet their judgments often align. Between 2005 and 2016 the correlation between critic and audience scores—where zero implies no relationship and one means the scores move perfectly in step—averaged around 0.6. Then opinions began to diverge. Before 2017 a ten-point increase in a film’s audience score was associated with a ten-point increase in its critic score. Over the next six years, that figure fell to just eight points. The correlation between critic and audience scores also dropped from 0.6 to around 0.5. In short, critics’ enthusiasm for a film told you less about how much viewers liked it.
To understand why, we tested a few hypotheses. The first was that the mix of films had changed, as film critics and audiences tend to agree more on some genres than others. But changes in genre, budget, sequel status and studio did little to explain the degree of disagreement.
In fact, much of the divergence happened within two of Hollywood’s biggest categories: big-budget action and
family films
. Before 2017 critics’ opinions of these films tracked audience opinions about as closely as they did for any other genre. Between 2017 and 2022, however, that relationship collapsed: critics’ scores on such releases were a poor guide to how audiences would rate them. All told, we estimate that roughly 43% of the divergence between critics and audiences was concentrated in these two types of film.
Most industry experts attribute the deviation to franchise fatigue. “Film reviewers got tired of
superhero movies
before the general audience did,” says Bruce Nash of The Numbers. “It gets boring”, says Mattias Frey of City St George’s, University of London, “if you’re seeing ‘Fast and Furious 23’ or ‘Avengers Part 27’.”
Political polarisation may have also played a part. When studios cast more female and minority actors in big-budget franchises, or embrace “woke” themes—as Marvel Studios did with “
Captain Marvel
”, its first female-led film, which was described as a “big feminist movie”—audiences tend to be more critical.
Since 2022 critics and audiences have found more common ground. Across all major genres, the correlation between their ratings now sits at nearly 0.7. Some reckon the film industry’s woes may be a factor: reviewers may be going easier on films they would once have panned. “There is this idea that there’s an existential crisis in movies, and that may be changing the way critics operate,” says Daniel Parris, a data scientist. James McMahon, an entertainment researcher, agrees: “As a critic, if you crap on every movie, you may be sinking the very thing that you really love.”
Journalism’s woes may be a factor, too. The era of the esteemed staff reviewer is long over. (“The Last Movie Critic”, a documentary about Roger Ebert, puts it bluntly.) Publications have laid off scores of arts journalists; those who remain must compete with influencers and podcasters to take part in the cultural conversation. They cannot afford to ignore the biggest blockbusters—or write only for the cognoscenti.
All this raises the question of what film critics are for today. Our data suggest they still have commercial clout. We found that higher critic scores are associated with significantly higher ticket sales in America, even after controlling for factors including genre and budget.
Their allure is also intellectual. Critics “get you thinking about things that you might not have thought about”, says Kevin Goetz, an entertainment researcher. Many read reviews only after they have seen a film as a way of extending the experience, positive or negative. Everyone can appreciate a good roast.

epub_95.title: The latest must-have movie memorabilia? Popcorn buckets
epub_95.text:
The latest must-have movie memorabilia? Popcorn buckets
Culture
| Kernel of an idea
The latest must-have movie memorabilia? Popcorn buckets
Novelty collectibles are lucrative for cinemas
Oct 22nd 2026
THE NEW
“Resident Evil”
film depicts a work assignment from hell. Bryan, a medical courier, is asked to deliver a package to a hospital in the mountains; on the way, he has to fight off mutant dogs, rats and people infected with a zombification virus. Fans have been coughing up around $20-25 for the official popcorn bucket, which takes the form of Bryan’s green, bespattered courier bag. (Talk about a bloody good snack.) It has sold out in many cinemas.
Popcorn buckets are popping off. AMC, a cinema chain, has estimated they will bring in $100m in revenue this year, almost double the amount in 2023.
“The Odyssey”
had buckets shaped like a Trojan horse (for a cool $70) and an imax film camera ($50).
“Spider-Man: Brand New Day”
, this year’s top-grossing film so far, offered fans the opportunity to dip into a tin shaped like the titular superhero’s head.
“The Devil Wears Prada 2”
went for a chic red handbag.
These novelty collectibles first went viral in 2024, with the bucket created for
“Dune: Part Two”
. Inspired by the sandworm that lives on the fictional desert planet of Arrakis, it featured a toothy creature emerging from the dunes. Some, however, felt it resembled a sex toy, and it was lampooned on
“Saturday Night Live”
and a late-night talk show. (It has become something of a cult item, having listed for $40-800 on resale sites.) Zinc Group, the marketing firm behind the dubious design, did not see the memes coming.
It was the enthusiastic reaction to a “Star Wars” R2-D2 collectible in 2019 that showed how turning a quintessential element of a film into memorabilia can delight fans. “It’s about the tangible experience with the movie that you’re going to see,” says Marcus Gonzalez, global creative director at Zinc. Creative keepsakes help fans feel connected with the film long after the credits roll.
Popcorn buckets are a “status symbol”, argues Calvin Innes, a creative strategist. Well, sort of. Often there is a limited supply, meaning that people who rush to the cinema on a film’s opening weekend are more likely to get their hands on one. Owning a limited-edition item signals to other obsessive fans that you are one of them.
The hype is great news for cinemas, which need to lure customers. Concessions—food and drinks—allow them to squeeze more profit from every moviegoer and popcorn buckets are a way to turn fans’ enthusiasm into high-margin sales. For Vue, a British cinema chain, sales of
collectible
merchandise have increased ten-fold since 2023.
Design is key. A “well-executed popcorn bucket is a really delightful kind of object” to people of all ages, avers Tim Sparrow, director of retail at Cineworld, another chain: it makes the film experience “so much richer”. The best popcorn buckets turn a movie reference into something playful and nostalgic. They have become such a successful marketing tool that fans are almost as excited to see the popcorn bucket for “Dune: Part Three” as they are to see the film itself in December. Now that’s something for film executives to chew on.

epub_96.title: How Ella Langley two-stepped to the top of the charts
epub_96.text:
How Ella Langley two-stepped to the top of the charts
Culture
| Choosin’ country
How Ella Langley two-stepped to the top of the charts
Country music is riding high, thanks to a new generation of stars and fans
Oct 22nd 2026
THE RECORD for the longest stint atop the
Billboard Hot 100
, a chart of America’s most popular songs, once belonged to Mariah Carey’s schmaltzy festive anthem, “All I Want For Christmas Is You”. No longer. “Choosin’ Texas”, a twangy country song by Ella Langley, now claims that distinction, having spent 24 weeks in the number-one slot. (Though it was recently bumped to second place by Taylor Swift’s new single.) Ms Langley’s track about being dumped in a honky-tonk may seem like a replay of the genre’s whisky-and-heartbreak trope. In fact, her ascent shows how the
country-music business
is finding a new rhythm.
Country music has traditionally relied on radio to reach its fans. But it is now America’s fourth-most-streamed genre, after R&B/hip-hop, rock and pop, according to Luminate, an analytics firm. Spotify reports that global streams passed 90bn last year and royalties have grown more than 130% since 2020. More labels are setting up shop in Nashville and Austin. Pop stars have climbed the charts after
donning cowboy boots
. This year Ms Swift, who started out as a country singer before turning to pop, returned to the genre with the single “I Knew It, I Knew You”. (There are rumours that her next album will offer more boot-scootin’ tunes.)
Ms Langley is currently touring her second album across America. Her monthly listeners on Spotify, the biggest streamer, have soared by 20m in a year. Her breakout success combines old-world pastoral charm with an astute use of social media.
She grew up in Hope Hull, Alabama, where the population is just over 7,000. (Her first audience, she has joked, was a bunch of cows.) She hunts and claims to have learned to read by singing hymns at church. In 2019, aged 20, Ms Langley moved to Nashville to become a songwriter. She signed a record deal in 2023 after performing at the Grand Ole Opry, a hallowed venue in the city that made stars of Loretta Lynn and
Dolly Parton
.
Yet Ms Langley has made her name on social-media platforms as well as Nashville’s stages. She posted a clip of herself singing in her car in 2021, which went viral; a publishing deal followed soon after. Her internet fame resulted in collaborations with more established stars. In 2024 a snippet of a single from her debut album, “Hungover”, again went viral on TikTok.
Gen Z is charmed by the aesthetics of Americana. So the arrival of digitally native stars like Ms Langley, now 27, came at a “perfect moment”, says Jaime Marconette of Luminate. The firm has found that country-music fans are 27% more likely than the average American to use TikTok, giving performers more opportunities to be discovered. They are also more likely to listen on repeat to their favourite songs and artists, which keeps the music in the charts. The mellow strains of “Choosin’ Texas” have no doubt worked in its favour: it can be listened to again and again without its hooks becoming grating.
People who listen to music on streaming platforms tend not to seek out a specific genre, but a
playlist
that suits a mood or activity, such as cooking, explains Emily Cohen Belote of Amazon Music. This can help songs reach unexpected audiences. The guitar riffs of “Choosin’ Texas” may appeal to fans of 1980s soft rock. Ms Langley’s husky voice recalls Sheryl Crow.
Still, the number of people choosing “Choosin’ Texas” is surprising. A country track usually has to blend with another genre to “have this massive pop crossover moment”, says Claire Heinichen of Spotify. That is not the case with Ms Langley’s hit, which declares: “A cowboy always finds a way to leave / Drinkin’ Jack all by myself.” The appeal is in the storytelling. The lyrics might portray a “very specific Southern experience”, admits Ms Heinichen. “But being sad in a bar is universal.”

epub_97.title: Leadership lessons from Napoleon
epub_97.text:
Leadership lessons from Napoleon
Culture
| The emperor’s close
Leadership lessons from Napoleon
How the French emperor’s management style ultimately led to his fall
Oct 22nd 2026
What management tips can you learn from conquerors? Put aside oppression, and there are lessons about delegation, motivation, recruitment and team building.
Alexander the Great
refused to drink water before battle to stand in solidarity with his men. Caesar marched on foot alongside his men, even swimming across rivers, to demonstrate his derring-do. When his army wobbled, he would fling himself in the way of his fleeing men, “even catching them by the throat and forcing them to face the enemy”, according to Suetonius, a Roman historian. Diocletian divided the
Roman Empire
into four, and shared power while keeping a firm central grip.
In 2014 Andrew Roberts, a prolific British historian and member of the House of Lords, published an excellent biography of
Napoleon
and his boldness on the battlefield. In a new book he examines Napoleon’s marshal system. The day after he proclaimed himself emperor of France in 1804, Napoleon appointed 18 “marshals of the empire”, later increasing the tally to 26. They were to be “the swords around Napoleon’s throne”, the army’s most venerated figures and the pinnacle of French society.
Some recruits came from the nobility; others were craftsmen’s sons. They were indulged with fortunes, land and even marriages into the imperial family. Each was given a deep-blue velvet high-collared uniform trimmed with golden embroidery, complete with a red silk sash, and a baton inscribed with the gold imperial eagles. Napoleon made six of them princes and crowned two kings.
The marshals’ elite leadership team was built to carry out Napoleon’s orders and bring glory to France by executing his new theory of warfare, with fewer set-piece sieges and more agile manoeuvres, thanks to an army that lived off the land. But Napoleon also devised an efficient modern management system, based on the recruitment of brilliant talent, doling out of lavish rewards, intolerance of weakness and a demand for total loyalty.
For all this Napoleon relied heavily on Louis-Alexandre Berthier, his chief of staff, first marshal and a skilled manager with a remarkable grasp of detail. A short, strong man who was said to be able to fall asleep with one eye open, Berthier was a former topographical engineer who had volunteered to sail across the Atlantic to help the Americans in their war for independence, drawing up a detailed map of the coast of Rhode Island.
Berthier divided the army staff into four branches, to cover everything from intelligence to supplies. Divisional commanders had to provide twice-daily updates on the whereabouts of every soldier; these dossiers, like proto-spreadsheets, were sent in 18 large volumes twice a month from the war ministry to Napoleon. In Berthier’s written orders “all names of places, rivers, enemy generals and regiments were underlined,” writes Lord Roberts. New information flowed constantly, from gunpowder stocks or the provision of shoes to the state of troops’ morale. Berthier and Napoleon travelled in a coach fitted with cupboards and drawers for books, maps and a card index listing the location of every unit of the Grande Armée.
To motivate his marshals, Napoleon issued performance reviews in campaign bulletins, showering praise for heroic achievements along with crushing criticism. Success was rewarded. An attentive manager, Napoleon also liked to offer his marshals personalised advice on how to galvanise the troops. “Do not neglect to fanaticise the soldier and to electrify his imagination to the utmost,” he wrote to André Masséna as he was facing the Austrian army.
Yet in the end the management system failed him. As the empire expanded, Napoleon insisted on total control, cramped his marshals’ autonomy and undermined their effectiveness. Worse, he came to weaken the very system he had built. His incentive scheme became capricious, as he overlooked those who deserved praise in some campaign bulletins, or used marshals as scapegoats.
Rather than generating creative tension, he fostered destructive rivalry. The danger, Lord Roberts notes, was “when marshals started to see warfare not as a team enterprise so much as a race among rivals for individual triumph and fame”. Napoleon even boasted of stoking “continual jealousy”: “I am careful to keep my ministers and generals at variance among themselves, in order that each may reveal to me the faults of the other.”
The marshals began to come to blows after Napoleon’s victory over the combined Russian and Austrian armies at Austerlitz in 1805, and things just got worse. For all his skill, writes Lord Roberts, “Napoleon had a great capacity for sheer spitefulness.” By the time the emperor rode into his last battle in 1815, only two marshals accompanied him. Napoleon’s “approach to leadership”, the author notes, “ultimately left him almost completely bereft of the support he so desperately needed as he faced his
Waterloo
”.

epub_98.title: How personal rivalries and clashes are shaping the AI race
epub_98.text:
How personal rivalries and clashes are shaping the AI race
Culture
| Chronicle of a tech foretold
How personal rivalries and clashes are shaping the AI race
A new book offers a rollicking tale of the people shaping Silicon Valley’s new obsession
Oct 22nd 2026
To someone who has not witnessed the
AI
scene in California’s Bay Area, it is hard to convey how utterly weird it is. The Curve, a recent conference, hosted sessions including “What’s the plan for keeping robots under control?” and “The Neural Frontier: what happens when AI can read your mind?” People lounged on couches and in gazebos with cold brews and
kombuchas
discussing how AI company staff made obscenely rich by forthcoming public offerings should channel their philanthropic giving—even as some of them conspired to hobble their own employers  to delay civilisational upheaval.
The goal of Kevin Roose, a former reporter for the New York Times, was not to write a grand treatise on what AI means for the world but merely to record this weirdness before it was lost to the vagaries of memory, disappearing message threads and obsolete media-storage formats. In “The AGI Chronicles” his focus is the nine years since Google researchers developed the transformer, the type of AI model that underlies ChatGPT and all its kin. Quickly the idea took hold that, given enough data and computing power, transformer-based systems would eventually attain the holy grail: a truly “general” AI, or
AGI
, matching human smarts and then outstripping them.
That doctrine has been the driving force of AI research ever since. And so its history in the West mostly boils down to the interwoven fates of a handful of brilliant, prickly people raising ever more money, panicking each time they get leapfrogged by rivals and  splitting off in a blaze of acrimony to start their own firms.
In outline, much of the story will be familiar. But Mr Roose captures the madness in a fast-paced style. His account is filled with gossipy anecdotes that highlight just how much the ambitions, ideological divides and
personality clashes
of a group small enough to fit in a couple of classrooms have shaped what may turn out to be the most consequential technology in modern history. As Mr Roose puts it, AGI is a “quest that half my sources thought was going to save the world, and the other half thought was going to end it”.
Consider Dario Amodei, who early in his tenure at OpenAI proposed the doctrine that more data and more compute equals more intelligence. He eventually left to form
Anthropic
, in part because he thought OpenAI was reneging on its original commitment to build AI safely, and in part because he considered Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president, “a bully, a credit hog, and a cut-throat capitalist”, in Mr Roose’s words. Mr Brockman, in turn, thought Mr Amodei was a “paranoid control freak who used safety as a pretext to win arguments”.
For years, AGI was seen as the prize in an all-or-nothing contest to whose winner all power in the world would accrue. But as the goal approached, definitions multiplied to the point where the term has lost all meaning. At some point in 2025, Mr Roose noticed a shift in rhetoric. There would never be a finish line, only an endless arms race. By then, some researchers were starting to be terrified by their creations’ power—but “they kept accelerating, because they had forgotten how to do anything else.”
Meanwhile, Mr Roose provocatively argues that AGI has, in fact, quietly arrived. A few dollars now buys you some time with an intelligence that is tolerably good at a growing number of things and extraordinary at a few; not human-level (yet), but already pretty general.
Perhaps that is why hardly anybody mentioned “AGI” at The Curve. The talk was of “extremely powerful AI” and “advanced superintelligence”. The names and goalposts change, the relentless pursuit of computing capability continues, and with it the efforts of a small group of people, alternately elated and horrified at the creation taking shape before them.

epub_99.title: Are there too many art fairs?
epub_99.text:
Are there too many art fairs?
Culture
| Scene and be seen
Are there too many art fairs?
Probably. But FOMO keeps collectors and dealers going to them
Oct 22nd 2026
ART COLLECTORS are like swallows. They flock together, preen and feed (on canapés and
champagne
). They also migrate seasonally. In October they roost in Paris during Art Basel, which runs from October 21st-25th. (The early birds landed in London for Frieze, another art fair, the previous week.) In December they head to Miami; in March to
Maastricht
; in May to New York; and in June to the original Basel in Switzerland. And that does not include the more adventurous ones, who zoom off to fairs in Doha, Hong Kong and Seoul.
It is as exhausting as it sounds. “Everyone is talking about art-fair fatigue,” says Aurelie Cauchy of the Twentieth, an advisory firm. In 2025 there were 370 major art fairs—more than one for every day of the year. That is up from around 55 in 2000, says Clare McAndrew, an art economist. Can collectors and dealers maintain their current pace? Beneath the glass roof of the sun-drenched Grand Palais, where Art Basel Paris takes place, there is more gloom than the Instagram posts would have you believe (and not just because of the recent
unrest in France
).
Gallerists are facing what the French call a choix cornélien (difficult choice), says Ms Cauchy. The cost of keeping a physical storefront is growing, but fewer clients are casually popping in. Recently, some have had to lay off staff or close up entirely. Dealers feel pressure to keep travelling to fairs in order to find new clients and keep the artists they represent happy.
But this carries an ever-growing price tag, which many struggle to afford. Shipping costs are triple what they were before covid-19, says Thaddaeus Ropac, a prominent gallerist. (It’s not just getting there; all unsold works have to be shipped back.) Gallerists’ own travel costs have travelled higher, too. And the booths themselves have become more expensive to rent and build. Art Basel, for example, charges around $29,000 for its smallest booth and more than $177,000 for the largest. (The square-metre price for large exhibitors is 32% more in real terms than in 2018.) Those fees just get you floor space: exhibitors need to rent carpet, lighting and add other design features. “Fairs are becoming a burden,” especially for smaller and mid-sized galleries, says Valentina Castellani, an art-market expert.
Costs have changed the art that appears in fairs. Sculptures are so expensive to ship that they rarely make financial sense. Nor do items with lower price tags, such as many photographs.
Since fairs first arrived on the art scene in the 1960s-70s, collectors have found them worthwhile because of their scale and efficiency (so much art is packed into a small space). But art enthusiasts now have fair complaints. One is crowds. Fairs have a lot of guests and such long queues that you’d be forgiven for thinking VIP stands for “very immobile people”. Basel has responded by launching a VVIP preview, Avant-Première, an evening before the VIP opening to offer buyers more quietude. Meanwhile, collectors are culling their calendars and choosing to attend fewer fairs. This month some Americans put the freeze on Frieze and opted to
attend only Art Basel Paris
instead.
In the future there may be fewer international fairs. People do not want to see the same gallerists everywhere. To lure collectors, organisers will need to offer a more distinctive experience, with more local galleries and artists. This is a broader trend beyond art. “We’ve gone from a moment where everything was meta-globalist to regionalisation,” says Noah Horowitz, the boss of Art Basel. Some gallerists are excited, thinking they may participate in fewer fairs but encounter new local collectors at the ones they do. In art and in commerce, sometimes less is more.
